p.seg: In ancient times, Shùn personally engaged in farming, pottery-making, and fishing while practicing filial piety and fraternal duty.
His father Gǔsǒu was obstinate,
his mother was insincere, and his younger brother Xiàng was arrogant,
all being incorrigibly foolish.
Shùn fulfilled his filial duties to the utmost,
providing for Gǔsǒu.
Gǔsǒu and Xiàng plotted to have Shùn dredge a well and plaster a granary,
intending to kill him,
yet Shùn's filial devotion grew even more sincere.
When working in the fields, he would weep and lament,
and at fifty years old,
he still yearned for his parents like an infant,
which can be called the ultimate filial piety.
Thus, when he farmed at Lìshān,
the farmers there yielded boundaries to one another;
when he made pottery by the river,
the potters there
produced vessels without flaws;
when he fished at Léizé,
the fishermen there shared the catch fairly;
and when he became the Son of Heaven,
the world was transformed by his influence,
with barbarian tribes submitting willingly,
reaching Běifā and Qúsōu in the north,
and pacifying Jiāozhǐ in the south,
all admiring his righteousness,
and qílín and phoenixes appeared in the suburbs.
Hence, Confucius said:
"The ultimate in filial and fraternal devotion
penetrates to the divine and luminous,
shining throughout the four seas."
This refers to Shùn.
Confucius, in his hometown,
diligently practiced filial piety,
residing at Quèdǎng,
where the local youth hunted and fished,
allocating more to those with parents,
transformed by his filial example.
Thus, seventy-two disciples came from afar,
submitting to his virtue.
In Lǔ, there was a man named Shěnyóu,
who fed his sheep heavily in the morning,
to cheat market buyers;
Gōngshěn had a wife who was licentious;
Shěnkuì was extravagant and arrogant;
and sellers of cattle and horses in Lǔ were skilled at inflating prices.
When Confucius was about to become the Minister of Crime in Lǔ,
Shěnyóu dared not morning-feed his sheep,
Gōngshěn divorced his wife,
Shěnkuì moved beyond the borders,
and sellers in Lǔ no longer inflated prices for horses and cattle,
awaiting his governance with corrected conduct;
after he became Minister of Crime,
Jì and Mèng dismantled the walls of Hòu and Fèi,
and the people of Qí returned the land they had seized from Lǔ,
all resulting from the accumulation of his rectitude.
Hence it is said:
"If he is personally upright,
he will be followed without orders being given."
When Sūnshū Áo was a child,
he went out to play,
saw a two-headed snake,
killed it and buried it;
returning home, he wept.
His mother asked the reason,
and Shū Áo replied:
"I heard that whoever sees a two-headed snake will die.
Earlier I saw one,
fearing I would leave you and die."
His mother said:
"Where is the snake now?"
He said:
"Fearing others might see it too,
I killed it and buried it."
His mother said:
"I have heard that those who perform hidden virtues
are rewarded by heaven with blessings,
you will not die."
When he grew up,
he became the Prime Minister of Chǔ,
and before governing, the people already trusted his benevolence.
Yǔ's rise was due to Túshān,
while Jié's fall was due to Mòxǐ;
Tāng's rise was due to Yǒushēn,
while Zhòu's fall was due to Dájǐ;
King Wén and King Wǔ's rise was due to Rén and Sì,
while King Yōu's fall was due to Bāosì.
Therefore, the "Odes" rectified with "Guān Jū",
and the "Spring and Autumn Annals" praised Bó Jī.
Fán Jī
was the consort of the King of Chǔ.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ returned late from court,
and she asked the reason.
The king said:
"This morning I spoke with a worthy minister,
and did not notice the lateness of the day."
Fán Jī said:
"Who is the worthy minister?"
The king said:
"It is Yúqiūzǐ."
Fán Jī covered her mouth and laughed,
and the king asked why.
She said:
"I am fortunate to serve you with towel and comb,
not that I do not wish to monopolize honor and affection,
but I believe it would harm your righteousness,
so I have recommended several to share my position.
Now Yúqiūzǐ has been prime minister for decades,
yet has never recommended one worthy person.
If he knows but does not recommend,
he is disloyal;
if he does not know,
he is unwise—
how can he be considered worthy?"
The next day at court,
the king told Yúqiūzǐ Fán Jī's words.
Yúqiūzǐ kowtowed and said:
"It is as Fán Jī says."
Thereupon,
he resigned his position and recommended Sūnshū Áo.
When Sūnshū Áo became prime minister of Chǔ,
King Zhuāng ultimately achieved hegemony,
in which Fán Jī played a significant role.
During the time of Duke Líng of Wèi,
Qú Bóyù was virtuous but unused,
while Mí Zixiá was unworthy yet held office.
The Wèi senior official Shǐ Qiū was troubled by this,
and repeatedly remonstrated with Duke Líng, but he would not listen.
Shǐ Qiū fell ill and was near death,
and said to his son:
"When I die,
hold the funeral in the northern hall.
Since I could not advance Qú Bóyù and remove Mí Zixiá,
I have failed to rectify my lord.
One who in life cannot rectify his lord
should not receive full rites in death.
Place my corpse in the northern hall—
that is sufficient for me."
When Shǐ Qiū died,
Duke Líng went to mourn,
saw the funeral in the northern hall,
and asked the reason.
His son fully reported his father's words to Duke Líng,
who, startled, changed expression,
stood up agitatedly from his seat,
and said:
"The master in life wished to advance the worthy and remove the unworthy,
and even in death did not relent,
using his corpse to remonstrate—
he can be called loyal without decline."
Thereupon,
he summoned Qú Bóyù and advanced him to minister;
removed Mí Zixiá,
moved the funeral to the main hall,
completed the rites, and then returned.
Wèi was thereby well-governed.
Shǐ Qiū's courtesy name was Zǐyú,
the one referred to in the "Analects" as "How upright was Shǐyú!"
When the Jìn minister Qí Xī grew old,
the ruler of Jìn asked him:
"Who can succeed you?"
Qí Xī replied:
"Xiè Hú is suitable."
The ruler said:
"Is he not your enemy?"
He responded:
"You asked about suitability,
not about enmity."
Jìn then promoted Xiè Hú.
Later the ruler asked again:
"Who can serve as Commandant of the State?"
Qí Xī replied:
"Wǔ is suitable."
The ruler said:
"Is he not your son?"
He responded:
"You asked about suitability,
not about sons."
The gentleman would say Qí Xī was capable of recommending the worthy:
praising his enemy,
this was not flattery;
establishing his son,
this was not favoritism.
The Documents say:
"Without bias or faction,
the Kingly Way is vast and expansive."
This describes Qí Xī.
In external recommendations not avoiding enemies,
in internal recommendations not bypassing relatives,
he can be called supremely impartial.
Only through goodness can one recommend one's kind.
The Poetry says:
"Only because he possesses it,
therefore he resembles it."
Qí Xī had this quality.
When King Gòng of Chǔ fell ill,
he summoned his Prime Minister and said:
"The regular attendant Guǎn Sū, who stayed with me,
constantly loyal to me through the Way,
corrected me with righteousness.
When I was with him,
I felt uneasy;
when not seeing him,
I did not miss him.
Even so,
I gained from him,
his contributions were not small -
you must richly ennoble him.
Shēn Hóu Bó, when with me,
constantly indulged my whims.
Whatever pleased me,
he encouraged me to pursue;
whatever I favored,
he would wear before me;
when with him,
I was joyful;
when not seeing him,
I felt sorrowful.
Even so,
I ultimately gained nothing from him,
his faults were not small -
you must quickly dismiss him."
The Prime Minister said:
"Yes!"
The next day,
the king passed away,
the Prime Minister immediately appointed Guǎn Sū as Senior Minister,
and expelled Shēn Hóu Bó beyond the borders.
Master Zēng said:
"When a bird is about to die,
its song is sorrowful;
when a man is about to die,
his words are good."
This speaks of returning to one's original nature,
as exemplified by King Gòng.
Therefore Confucius said:
"Having heard the Way in the morning,
one may die content in the evening."
Through this to inform later generations,
enlightening future ages,
is still better than passing away unawakened.
Formerly, when Marquis Wǔ of Wèi planned affairs appropriately,
and none of his ministers could match him,
he appeared joyful at court,
Wú Qǐ came forward and said:
"Has anyone today reported what King Zhuāng of Chǔ once said?"
Marquis Wǔ said:
"No.
What did King Zhuāng say?"
Wú Qǐ said:
"When King Zhuāng of Chǔ planned affairs appropriately,
and none of his ministers could match him,
he appeared worried at court.
Shēn Gōng Wū Chén came forward and asked:
'My lord appears worried at court,
why is this?'
King Zhuāng said:
'I have heard that,
feudal lords who select their own teachers become kings,
those who select their own friends become hegemons,
while those self-satisfied with no ministers their equal perish.
Now with my lack of virtue,
deliberating in court,
and yet no minister can match me,
my state must be close to perishing.
This is why I appear worried.'
This was why King Zhuāng worried,
yet you alone appear joyful -
why is this?"
Marquis Wǔ hesitated and apologized:
"Heaven has sent you, Master, to rectify my faults,
Heaven has sent you, Master, to rectify my faults!"
When Wèi expelled Duke Xiàn,
Duke Dào of Jìn said to Shī Kuàng:
"The people of Wèi have expelled their ruler -
is this not excessive?"
He replied:
"Perhaps their ruler was truly excessive.
Heaven gave birth to the people and established rulers for them,
to shepherd and oversee them,
not letting them lose their nature.
A good ruler will reward the good and remove the people's troubles,
loving the people as his children,
sheltering them like heaven,
containing them like earth.
The people serve their ruler,
loving him as parents,
looking up to him as sun and moon,
revering him as spiritual powers,
fearing him as thunder.
Now the ruler
is host to the spirits,
and hope of the people.
Heaven loves the people deeply -
how could it let one man run rampant over the people,
indulging his excesses,
and abandoning heaven and earth's nature?
This cannot be.
If he oppresses the people's nature,
neglects the spirits' sacrifices,
leaves the common people hopeless,
and the altars of state without a host,
what use is he then!
If not removed, what else?"
The Duke said:
"Well said!"
When Jiǎn Zǐ of Zhào ascended the steep slope of Yángcháng,
all his ministers bared their shoulders to push the chariot,
yet Hǔ Huì alone carried his halberd, singing while walking without pushing.
Jiǎn Zǐ said:
"As I ascend this slope,
all my ministers push the chariot,
yet Huì alone carries his halberd singing without pushing -
this means Huì as minister insults his lord.
For a minister to insult his lord,
what should the punishment be?"
Hǔ Huì replied:
"For a minister insulting his lord,
death upon death."
Jiǎn Zǐ said:
"What means 'death upon death'?"
Hǔ Huì said:
"He himself dies,
his wife and children also die -
this is called death upon death.
You have now heard the punishment for ministers insulting their lord;
have you also heard about rulers insulting their ministers?"
Jiǎn Zǐ said:
"What about rulers insulting their ministers?"
Hǔ Huì replied:
"When a ruler insults his ministers:
the wise will not offer counsel,
the eloquent will not serve as envoys,
the brave will not fight.
If the wise offer no counsel,
the altars of state are endangered;
if the eloquent serve not as envoys,
diplomacy fails;
if the brave do not fight,
the borders are invaded."
Jiǎn Zǐ said:
"Well said!"
He then dismissed the ministers
from pushing the chariot;
prepared wine for the officers,
drank with his ministers,
and honored Hǔ Huì as his foremost guest.
In the past, Zhōu Shě served under Zhào Jiǎnzǐ,
standing at Zhào Jiǎnzǐ's gate
for three days and three nights.
Jiǎnzǐ sent someone out to ask him:
"What instruction do you have for me, Master?"
Zhōu Shě replied:
"I wish to be a minister who speaks forthrightly,
holding ink brush and writing tablet,
following behind my lord,
observing and recording my lord's errors,
so there will be daily records,
monthly assessments,
and yearly achievements."
Jiǎnzǐ was pleased with him
and kept him in his company.
Not long after, Zhōu Shě died,
and Jiǎnzǐ buried him with great honors.
Three years later,
while drinking with his various ministers and becoming intoxicated,
Jiǎnzǐ wept.
The ministers rose and went out, saying:
"We deserve the death penalty,
though we were unaware of our offense."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Ministers, return.
You are not guilty.
In the past, my friend Zhōu Shě once said:
'A hundred sheepskins
are not worth one fox's armpit fur;
the yes-men of the crowd
are not worth Zhōu Shě's forthright speech.
In ancient times, King Zhòu was benighted and perished,
while King Wǔ had forthright advisors and prospered.'
Since Zhōu Shě's death,
I have never heard about my faults.
Therefore, when a ruler hears no criticism of himself, or hears it but does not reform, he will perish.
My state must be close to perishing,
that is why I weep."
Marquis Wén of Wèi was sitting with his scholar-officials
and asked:
"What kind of ruler am I?"
All the ministers said:
"My lord,
you are a benevolent ruler."
When it came to Dí Huáng's turn,
he said:
"My lord,
you are not a benevolent ruler."
The Marquis asked:
"How can you say that?"
He replied:
"When you conquered Zhōngshān,
you did not enfeoff it to your younger brother,
but instead enfeoffed it to your eldest son.
From this I know you are not a benevolent ruler."
Marquis Wén became angry and expelled Dí Huáng.
Huáng rose and went out.
When it came to Rén Zuò's turn,
Marquis Wén asked:
"What kind of ruler am I?"
Rén Zuò replied:
"My lord,
you are a benevolent ruler."
The Marquis said:
"How can you say that?"
He replied:
"I have heard that
when a ruler is benevolent, his ministers are straightforward.
Since Dí Huáng's words were straightforward,
I therefore know that you,
my lord, are a benevolent ruler."
Marquis Wén said:
"Excellent!"
He recalled Dí Huáng to return,
and appointed him as senior minister.
When Zhōngxíng Yín was about to be destroyed,
he summoned his Grand Invocator and wanted to punish him with a crime,
saying:
"You performed invocations for me -
were the sacrificial animals not plump and glossy enough?
Or were the purification rituals not reverent enough?
Why then is my state being destroyed?"
Invoker Jiǎn replied:
"In the past, our former lord Zhōngxíng Mùzǐ
had only ten leather-covered chariots,
yet he did not worry about their meagerness,
but worried about insufficient virtue and righteousness.
Now you, my lord, have a hundred armored chariots,
yet you do not worry about insufficient virtue and righteousness,
but only worry about insufficient chariots.
When boats and chariots are ornate,
then taxes and levies are heavy;
when taxes and levies are heavy, then the people resent, criticize, and curse.
Moreover, if you believe that invocations can benefit the state,
then curses must also harm it.
The state is lost.
With one person invoking for it,
and the whole state cursing it,
one invocation cannot overcome ten thousand curses.
The state's destruction
is only appropriate, is it not?
What crime has the Invoker committed?"
Zhōngxíngzǐ then felt ashamed.
Qín wanted to attack Chǔ,
and sent an envoy to observe Chǔ's precious vessels.
The King of Chǔ heard of this,
summoned Prime Minister Zǐ Xī and asked him:
"Qín wants to observe our precious vessels.
Should I show them
our Hé Shì's jade disc
and Suí Hóu's pearl?"
Prime Minister Zǐ Xī replied:
"I do not know."
He then summoned Zhāo Xīxù and asked him.
Zhāo Xīxù replied:
"They want to observe our state's strengths and weaknesses to plan against us.
It is not about precious vessels,
but about worthy ministers.
Pearls, jades, and objects of curiosity
are not what we treasure as important."
The king then sent Zhāo Xīxù to receive them.
Zhāo Xīxù deployed three hundred elite troops,
arrayed them inside the western gate,
built one platform facing east,
four platforms facing south,
and one platform facing west.
When the Qín envoy arrived,
Zhāo Xīxù said:
"You, sir,
are a guest;
please take the honored position facing east."
Prime Minister Zǐ Xī faced south,
Grand Minister Zǐ Áo next,
Lord Yè Gōngzǐ Gāo next,
and Minister of War Zǐ Fǎn next.
Zhāo Xīxù himself took the platform facing west,
and declared:
"Our guest wishes to see Chǔ's precious vessels.
What Chǔ treasures are its worthy ministers.
Governing the hundred surnames,
filling the granaries and storehouses,
enabling the people each to find their proper place -
Prime Minister Zǐ Xī is here;
holding the jade tablets,
serving as envoy to the feudal lords,
resolving difficulties of anger and resentment,
fostering friendship between two states,
preventing the worries of war -
Grand Minister Zǐ Áo is here;
guarding the borders,
securing the frontiers,
not infringing on neighboring states,
nor suffering infringement from them -
Lord Yè Gōngzǐ Gāo is here;
managing the armies,
organizing the troops,
to confront powerful enemies,
wielding the drumsticks,
to mobilize the masses of a million men,
making those under his command all charge into boiling water and fire,
tread upon naked blades,
face difficulties of ten thousand deaths without a thought for survival -
Minister of War Zǐ Fǎn is here;
cherishing the remaining discussions of the Hegemons and Kings,
grasping the lingering traditions of order and chaos -
Zhāo Xīxù is here.
These are what your great state may observe."
The Qín envoy was awestruck and had nothing to reply,
whereupon Zhāo Xīxù bowed and left.
The Qín envoy returned
and reported to the ruler of Qín:
"Chǔ has many worthy ministers;
it cannot be plotted against."
Thus they did not attack Chǔ.
The Book of Songs says:
"With many officers, gathered all around,
King Wén secured his state with peace."
This expresses what is meant here.
Jìn Pínggōng intended to attack Qí,
and sent Fàn Zhāo to observe the situation.
Jǐnggōng hosted him with wine,
and when they were in high spirits,
Fàn Zhāo said:
"I wish to request a drink from Your Majesty's cup."
The Duke said:
"Pour wine from my cup,
and present it to the guest."
After Fàn Zhāo had drunk,
Yànzǐ said:
"Remove this cup,
and replace it!"
New wine vessels were prepared.
Fàn Zhāo pretended to be drunk and displeased, then rose to dance,
saying to the Grand Music Master:
"Can you play the music of Chéngzhōu for me?
I shall dance to it for you."
The Grand Music Master said:
"Your humble servant has not learned it."
Fàn Zhāo hurriedly departed.
Jǐnggōng said to Yànzǐ:
"Jìn
is a great state,
they sent a man here
to observe our governance,
yet now you have angered the envoy of a great state -
what shall we do?"
Yànzǐ said:
"As for Fàn Zhāo's character,
he is not ignorant of ritual propriety,
but rather wished to test our ruler and ministers,
therefore I thwarted him."
Jǐnggōng said to the Grand Music Master:
"Why didn't you play the music of Chéngzhōu for our guest?"
The Grand Music Master replied:
"The music of Chéngzhōu
is the Son of Heaven's music,
if it were played,
only the ruler should dance to it.
Now Fàn Zhāo is a mere minister,
yet he wished to dance to the Son of Heaven's music -
therefore your servant would not play it."
Fàn Zhāo returned,
and reported to Pínggōng:
"Qí cannot be attacked,
for when I tried to test their ruler,
Yànzǐ saw through it;
when I tried to violate their rituals,
the Grand Music Master understood it."
Zhòngní heard of this and said:
"Without leaving the space between the wine vessels and sacrificial stands,
he knew what was happening a thousand lǐ away -
this describes Yànzǐ indeed!
He may be said to have repelled the enemy's chariots,
and the Grand Music Master contributed to this as well."
Jìn Pínggōng was sailing on the Western River,
when in midstream he sighed and said:
"Alas!
How can I find worthy scholars to share this pleasure with me?"
The boatman Gù Sāng came forward and replied:
"Your Majesty speaks incorrectly.
Swords are produced in Yuè,
pearls in the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
jade in the Kūnlún Mountains -
these three treasures
all come to us without feet.
If Your Majesty truly appreciates scholars,
then worthy scholars will come!"
Pínggōng said:
"Gù Sāng, come here!
At my gate I have over three thousand retainers being fed,
if their morning meal is insufficient,
I collect market taxes by evening;
if their evening meal is insufficient,
I collect market taxes by morning.
Can I still be said not to appreciate scholars?"
Gù Sāng replied:
"When the swan goose flies high and reaches the heavens,
it relies only on the six main feathers of its wings.
As for the down beneath its belly
and the feathers on its back,
whether you add or remove a handful,
its flight is neither higher nor lower.
I wonder if Your Majesty's three thousand retainers are the six main feathers?
Or are they just the down of belly and back?"
Pínggōng fell silent and made no response.
King Wēi of Chǔ asked Sòng Yù:
"Do you, sir, have some misconduct?
Why do the officials and common people speak so poorly of you?"
Sòng Yù replied:
"Yes,
indeed,
there is something.
I beg Your Majesty to pardon my offense,
and allow me to complete my explanation.
There was a visitor singing in Yǐng,
who began with 'Xiàlǐ Bārén',
and several thousand people in the capital joined in the chorus;
when he sang 'Yánglíng Cǎiwēi',
several hundred people in the capital joined in the chorus;
when he sang 'Yángchūn Báixuě',
only several dozen people in the capital joined in the chorus;
when he introduced shāng notes and delicate jué notes,
mixed with flowing zhǐ notes,
those in the capital who joined in the chorus
were no more than a few people.
Thus, the more elevated the song,
the fewer join in the chorus.
Therefore, among birds there is the phoenix and among fish there is the whale.
The phoenix soars nine thousand lǐ high,
piercing the floating clouds,
bearing the blue sky,
hovering in the vast emptiness above.
Could the quail in the manure field
possibly comprehend the height of heaven and earth?
The whale sets out at dawn from the foot of Kūnlún,
basks its fins at Jiéshí,
and rests by evening at Mèngzhū;
could the tadpole in a foot-deep pond
possibly measure the vastness of rivers and seas?
So not only do birds have phoenixes and fish have whales,
scholars also have their exceptional kinds.
The sage with magnificent ideas and extraordinary conduct
transcends ordinary life and stands alone -
how could the common people of this world
possibly understand what your servant does?"
Jìn Pínggōng was at leisure in his residence,
with Shī Kuàng in attendance.
Pínggōng said:
"You were born without pupils in your eyes,
how extreme is your darkness!"
Shī Kuàng replied:
"There are five kinds of darkness in the world,
and your servant doesn't share in even one of them."
Pínggōng said:
"What do you mean?"
Shī Kuàng said:
"Ministers bribe to gain fame and reputation;
the people suffer injustice,
with nowhere to appeal,
yet the ruler remains unaware -
this is the first darkness.
Loyal ministers are not employed,
employed ministers are not loyal;
incompetents hold high positions,
the unworthy govern the worthy,
yet the ruler remains unaware -
this is the second darkness.
Treacherous ministers practice deception,
emptying the state treasury,
using their petty talents
to cover up their evil deeds;
worthy men are expelled,
villains are honored,
yet the ruler remains unaware -
this is the third darkness.
The state is poor, the people exhausted,
upper and lower ranks are discordant,
yet the state delights in using wealth for warfare,
craving without satisfaction;
sycophants and flatterers
linger at your side,
yet the ruler remains unaware -
this is the fourth darkness.
The supreme Way is not illuminated,
laws and decrees are not implemented,
officials and people are not upright,
the common people are not at peace,
yet the ruler remains unaware -
this is the fifth darkness.
If a state has these five darknesses yet avoids peril,
such a thing has never occurred.
Your servant's darkness
is but minor darkness -
how could it harm the state?"
Zhào Wénzǐ asked Shū Xiàng,
"Among the six generals of Jìn,
who will perish first?"
He replied,
"It will likely be the Zhōngháng clan!"
Wénzǐ said,
"Why would they perish first?"
He replied,
"The Zhōngháng clan's governance
takes harshness for thoroughness,
deceit for clarity,
severity for loyalty,
numerous schemes for excellence,
and heavy taxation for good policy.
It is like stretched leather:
expanded it may be large,
but it is the way to tearing—
they should perish first."
When King Zhuāng of Chǔ had punished the murderer of Duke Líng of Chén,
executed Xià Zhēngshū,
and captured Xià Jī, he was pleased with her
and intended to take her as his consort.
Shēngōng Wūchén advised against it, saying,
"This woman brought chaos to the state of Chén,
corrupting its ministers.
A bewitching woman should not be approached."
The king heeded his advice.
The Ling Yǐn also wanted to take her,
but Shēngōng Wūchén advised against it,
and the Ling Yǐn complied.
Later, Xiāng Yǐn took her.
When King Gōng battled Jìn at Yānlíng,
the Chǔ army was defeated,
Xiāng Yǐn died,
and his body was not returned.
Repeated requests to Jìn were refused.
Xià Jī offered to go to Jìn to seek the body,
and as Chǔ was sending her off,
Shēngōng Wūchén, who was on a mission to Qí,
secretly persuaded Xià Jī
and plotted with her.
When Xià Jī departed,
Shēngōng Wūchén abandoned his mission,
fled along the way,
and followed Xià Jī to Jìn.
The Ling Yǐn then sought to exile his clan,
telling the king,
"Shēngōng Wūchén advised the late king not to approach Xià Jī,
yet now he has abandoned his mission
and fled with her to Jìn.
This is a betrayal of the late king.
I request to exile his clan."
The king said,
"Shēngōng Wūchén was loyal in counseling the late king,
but disloyal in his own plans.
He honored the late king but belittled himself.
What crime did he commit against the late king?"
Thus, he did not exile the clan.
In ancient times, Táng and Yú exalted and promoted nine worthies,
placing them in positions of authority,
and the realm enjoyed great peace.
Distant regions came as guests,
and qílín and phoenixes appeared in the suburbs.
Shāng Tāng employed Yī Yǐn,
while King Wén and King Wǔ used Tàigōng and Hóng Yāo.
King Chéng entrusted Zhōu and Shào,
and the realm was greatly well-governed.
Yuècháng sent interpreters through multiple languages,
auspicious signs descended together,
and peace lasted a thousand years—
all due to the merit of employing the worthy.
Without worthy ministers,
even the Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns
could not have prospered.
Duke Huán of Qí obtained Guǎn Zhòng
and enjoyed the glory of hegemony over the feudal lords;
losing Guǎn Zhòng,
he suffered the disgrace of danger and chaos.
Yú perished for not using Bǎilǐ Xī,
while Duke Mù of Qín used him and achieved hegemony.
Chǔ was defeated for not using Wǔ Zǐxū,
while Hé Lǘ of Wú used him and became hegemon.
Fū Chāi not only failed to use Zǐxū
but also killed him,
and his state ultimately perished.
King Zhāo of Yān employed Yuè Yì,
who led the weak army of Yān
to defeat the powerful enemy of Qí,
capturing seventy cities.
But King Huì dismissed Yuè Yì,
replacing him with Qí Jié,
and the army was immediately defeated,
losing seventy cities.
Here, the father used him,
the son did not—
the outcome is clear.
Thus, Hé Lǘ used Zǐxū to rise,
while Fū Chāi killed him and fell;
King Zhāo used Yuè Yì to triumph,
while King Huì expelled him and failed.
This is as clear as black and white.
Qín did not use Shūsūn Tōng,
and King Xiàng did not use Chén Píng and Hán Xìn, leading to their destruction,
while Hàn used them and greatly prospered—
this is not far in the past.
The calamity of losing the worthy is like that,
the blessing of employing them is like this.
No ruler fails to seek the worthy for assistance,
yet states fall into chaos and ruin because
those deemed worthy are not truly worthy.
Sometimes, the worthy are employed
but must deliberate with the unworthy;
the wise are tasked with planning
but must consult with the foolish.
The unworthy envy the worthy,
the foolish envy the wise—
this is why the worthy are obstructed,
and for a thousand years, they do not find alignment.
Sometimes, the unworthy employ the worthy but cannot persist,
or they persist but not to the end.
Sometimes, unworthy sons dismiss the loyal ministers of their worthy fathers.
The disasters and failures are too numerous to record in full,
but the crux lies in one's own lack of discernment and heeding everyone's words.
If slander and false accusations do not prevail,
that is true clarity.
When Wèi's Páng Gōng went as a hostage to Hándān with the crown prince,
he said to the King of Wèi,
"If one person came and said there is a tiger in the market,
would Your Majesty believe it?"
The king said,
"No."
He said,
"If two people said it,
would Your Majesty believe it?"
The king said,
"I would be suspicious."
He said,
"If three people said it,
would Your Majesty believe it?"
The king said,
"I would believe it."
Páng Gōng said,
"That there is no tiger in the market is clear,
yet three people can create a tiger.
Now Hándān is farther from Wèi
than the market;
those who speak against me
will exceed three.
I beg Your Majesty to discern this."
The King of Wèi said,
"I understand."
But when Páng Gōng returned from Hándān,
slanderous mouths indeed arose,
and he could not gain an audience.
Gān Mào
was a man of Xiàcài.
He went west to enter Qín,
and repeatedly achieved merit.
By the time of King Wǔ,
he was appointed Left Chancellor,
while Chūlǐzǐ served as Right Chancellor.
Chūlǐzǐ and Gōngsūnzǐ
were both scions of the Qín ruling house,
and their maternal relatives were from Hán.
Qín repeatedly attacked Hán.
King Wǔ of Qín said to Gān Mào:
"I wish for my carriage to reach the court of Zhōu,
but the route passes through Yíyáng of Hán."
He wanted to send Gān Mào to attack Hán,
capture Yíyáng,
and thus open the route to the Zhōu court.
Gān Mào said:
"I request to form an alliance with Wèi
to jointly attack Hán."
He had Xiàng Shòu assist him on the mission.
After Gān Mào had secured the alliance,
and Wèi had agreed to his proposal,
he returned to Xìrǎng,
and said to Xiàng Shòu:
"You return and tell the king
that Wèi has agreed to follow my plan,
but I hope the king will not attack."
Xiàng Shòu returned and reported this to the king.
The king went to Xìrǎng to meet Gān Mào,
and asked him the reason.
He replied:
"Yíyáng
is a large district;
it is called a district,
but in reality it is a commandery.
Now Your Majesty must pass through multiple perilous places,
traveling a thousand lǐ to attack it -
this is difficult.
In the past,
when Zēng Shēn was in Zhèng,
there was a man with the same name who killed someone.
Someone told his mother:
'Zēng Shēn has killed a man.'
His mother continued weaving calmly.
After a short while,
another person came to tell her,
and his mother said:
'My son would not kill anyone.'
After another moment,
a third person came to report it.
His mother then threw down the shuttle and left the loom,
climbed over the wall and fled.
Now with Zēng Shēn's virtue and his mother's trust in him,
when three people cast doubt,
his mother became afraid.
Now my virtue
is not equal to Zēng Shēn's;
Your Majesty's trust in me
is also not like Zēng Shēn's mother's trust in him;
and those who doubt me are not just three people.
I fear that Your Majesty will throw down the shuttle.
Marquis Wén of Wèi ordered Yuè Yáng to lead troops and attack Zhōngshān -
it took three years to capture it.
When Yuè Yáng returned and spoke of his achievements,
Marquis Wén showed him a whole chest of slanderous letters.
Yuè Yáng bowed twice and kowtowed, saying:
'This was not my achievement,
but the strength of my lord.'
Now I am a traveler from abroad;
Chūlǐzǐ and Gōngsūnzǐ, these two men,
will use Hán to make arguments,
and Your Majesty will surely believe them.
This would mean Your Majesty deceives Wèi while I incur Hán's resentment."
The king said:
"I will not listen to them."
He sent him to attack Yíyáng.
After five months, Yíyáng had not yet been captured.
Chūlǐzǐ and Gōngsūnzǐ indeed disputed the campaign,
and King Wǔ summoned Gān Mào,
wanting to withdraw the troops.
Gān Mào said:
"The pledge at Xìrǎng remains there."
The king said:
"It does exist."
Thereupon he mobilized all troops,
put Gān Mào in command,
and attacked,
finally capturing Yíyáng.
When King Wǔ died,
and King Zhāo ascended the throne,
Chūlǐzǐ and Gōngsūnzǐ slandered him,
Gān Mào faced accusations,
and eventually fled to Qí.
Thus, without utmost clarity,
who can avoid being affected by slander?
The King of Chǔ asked his ministers:
"I hear that the northern states fear Zhāo Xīxù -
what is the truth of this?"
Jiǎng Yǐ replied:
"A tiger was searching for various animals to eat
and caught a fox.
The fox said:
'You dare not eat me!
The Heavenly Emperor has appointed me leader of all animals.
If you eat me now,
you will be defying the Emperor's command.
If you doubt my word,
I will walk in front of you,
and you follow behind me,
and see how all animals flee at the sight of me.'
The tiger thought this reasonable,
and followed along,
and indeed all animals fled at their approach.
The tiger didn't realize the animals were fleeing from him,
but thought they were afraid of the fox.
Now Your Majesty's territory spans five thousand lǐ,
with a million armored troops,
and you have entrusted full authority to Zhāo Xīxù.
The northern states do not fear Zhāo Xīxù himself,
but actually fear Your Majesty's military might,
just as the animals feared the tiger.
Therefore, when a minister is feared,
it is because of the ruler's power.
If the ruler does not employ him,
then that power vanishes."
The ruler of Lǔ sent Mì Zǐjiàn to be magistrate of Shànfǔ.
Zǐjiàn took his leave to depart,
and requested to borrow two skilled scribes,
to have them write regulations and instructions.
The ruler of Lǔ granted them to him.
When he reached Shànfǔ,
he had them write,
but Zǐjiàn would pull at their elbows from the side.
When the writing turned out poorly,
he would scold them;
when they wanted to write well,
he would pull again.
The scribes found this troublesome,
asked to resign and leave,
and returned to report this to the ruler of Lǔ.
The ruler of Lǔ said:
"Zǐjiàn is suffering from my interference,
which prevents him from implementing his good governance."
Thereupon he ordered the officials
not to make unauthorized demands on Shànfǔ.
The transformation of Shànfǔ became greatly well-ordered.
Therefore Confucius said:
"What a gentleman is Zǐjiàn!
If Lǔ had no gentlemen,
how could we get such a man!"
He was praising his virtue.
A man of Chǔ presented fish to the King of Chǔ,
saying:
"Today's fishing catch -
I cannot eat it all,
cannot sell what remains,
and it would be wasteful to discard it,
so I have come to present it."
The attendants said:
"How crude his words are!"
The King of Chǔ said:
"You do not understand that this fisherman
is a benevolent man.
I have heard that when granaries have surplus grain,
the state has starving people;
when the rear palace has many secluded women,
the common people have many unmarried men;
when surplus goods accumulate in the treasuries,
the territory has many impoverished people -
all these mean failure in the way of ruling.
Thus when the kitchen has fat fish,
the stables have fat horses,
but the people have hungry faces,
this marks a ruler who will lose his state,
hoarding in his treasuries.
I have long heard of this principle,
but have not been able to practice it.
This fisherman understands it,
and is using this to admonish me.
I shall now implement it."
Thereupon,
he sent envoys to comfort widows and widowers and care for orphans and the childless;
distributed grain from granaries and issued silk and money to relieve the needy;
dismissed the unused women from the rear palace,
and sent them out to marry widowers.
The people of Chǔ were greatly pleased and joyful,
and neighboring states submitted to them.
Thus with one presentation of leftover fish,
the fisherman benefited the whole state of Chǔ -
he may be called both benevolent and wise.
In the past, Zōu Jì gained an audience with King Xuān of Qí by playing the zither,
and the king appreciated his performance.
Zōu Jì said:
"The zither serves to symbolize governance."
He then explained to the king how the zither represents governance and matters of hegemony,
which greatly pleased King Xuān.
After conversing for three days,
he appointed Zōu Jì as his chancellor.
In Qí, there were scholars at Jìxià
who enjoyed discussing state affairs.
After Zōu Jì became chancellor of Qí,
seventy-two scholars led by Chúnyuán Kūn from Jìxià
all looked down upon Zōu Jì,
thinking that if they engaged in debate,
Zōu Jì would not be able to match them.
So they went together to see Zōu Jì.
Chúnyuán Kūn and his followers behaved arrogantly,
while Zōu Jì remained humble.
Chúnyuán Kūn and others said:
"A robe of white fox fur
patched with worn-out sheepskin -
what would that be like?"
Zōu Jì replied:
"I respectfully acknowledge,
I shall not mix the worthy with the unworthy."
Chúnyuán Kūn said:
"A square peg in a round hole -
how about that?"
Zōu Jì replied:
"I respectfully acknowledge!
I shall carefully guard the inner gates,
and dare not retain unworthy guests."
Chúnyuán Kūn and others said:
"Three people herding one sheep,
the sheep doesn't get enough to eat,
and the people get no rest either -
what about that?"
Zōu Jì replied:
"I respectfully acknowledge!
Reduce officials and streamline staff,
so they won't harass the people."
Chúnyuán Kūn and his group made three metaphorical statements,
and Zōu Jì understood all three instantly as if responding to an echo.
Chúnyuán Kūn and the others, having run out of arguments, departed.
Zōu Jì's manner then became dignified,
while Chúnyuán Kūn and the others became humble.
The reason we value swords like Gānjiàng and Móyé
is because they cut decisively;
the reason we prize steeds like Qíjì
is because they arrive swiftly.
If we must take long and extensive time,
even silk thread can lift stones,
and inferior horses can travel far.
Therefore, intelligence and quick-wittedness
are admirable qualities in a person.
Zǐgòng said:
"Yán Huí, upon hearing one point, understands ten."
This praises quick comprehension.
In the past,
the Prime Minister of Yān offended his ruler,
and was about to go into exile.
He summoned all his retainers and asked:
"Is there anyone who will follow me into exile?"
After asking three times,
none of the retainers responded.
The Prime Minister of Yān said:
"Alas!
This shows that retainers are not worth maintaining."
A retainer came forward and said:
"There are also rulers who cannot properly maintain retainers.
How can you say retainers are not worth maintaining?
In years of famine and hunger,
when retainers cannot even get their fill of dregs,
the ruler's dogs and horses have surplus grain;
in the severe cold of deep winter,
when retainers lack even complete coarse clothing,
with their limbs exposed,
the ruler's towers and pavilions
have brocade curtains
that flutter in the wind until they decay.
Wealth is something
the ruler considers light;
death is something
retainers consider heavy.
If the ruler cannot give what he considers light,
yet expects to obtain what retainers consider heavy,
isn't that difficult?"
The Prime Minister of Yān then felt ashamed,
fled,
and dared not show himself again.
Duke Wén of Jìn went out hunting,
when his vanguard reported:
"Ahead there's a huge snake,
as tall as a dike,
blocking the path."
Duke Wén said:
"I have heard that
when feudal lords have bad dreams, they cultivate virtue;
when high officials have bad dreams, they improve their offices;
when scholars have bad dreams, they cultivate themselves.
By doing so, disaster does not come!
Now that I have faults,
Heaven is warning me.
Turn the chariots around and return."
The vanguard said:
"I have heard that
one should not reward based on pleasure,
nor punish based on anger.
Now fortune and disaster are already before us,
and cannot be changed.
Why not just drive forward?"
Duke Wén said:
"Not so.
The supernatural cannot overcome the Way,
and monsters cannot overcome virtue.
Before fortune and disaster manifest,
they can still be transformed."
He turned the chariots around and returned.
After fasting for three days,
he prayed at the temple:
"I, the unworthy,
have offered insufficiently fat sacrifices,
and inadequate offerings -
this is my first fault;
I am fond of hunting,
without moderation -
this is my second fault;
I have imposed heavy taxes,
and severe punishments -
this is my third fault.
From now on,
I will eliminate taxes at passes and markets,
remove levies from marshes and weirs,
pardon offenders,
reduce taxes on old fields by half,
and exempt new fields from taxation."
Before half a month had passed since implementing these decrees,
the official guarding the snake dreamed that the Great Emperor killed the snake,
saying:
"How dare you block the path of a sage?
Your crime deserves death."
When he awoke from the dream,
he saw the snake had putrefied and stank.
He reported this.
Duke Wén said:
"Indeed,
the supernatural truly cannot overcome the Way,
and monsters cannot overcome virtue.
Why should we not investigate principles but leave things to Heaven?
We should respond with virtue."
The ruler of Liáng went out hunting
and saw a flock of white wild geese.
He got off his chariot and drew his bow to shoot them,
but there was a traveler on the road.
The ruler told the traveler to stop,
but the traveler didn't stop,
frightening away the flock of white wild geese.
The ruler became angry
and wanted to shoot the traveler.
His charioteer Gōngsūn Xí got down, held the arrow and said:
"Please stop, my lord!"
The ruler, flushed with anger, said:
"Xí, you side with others instead of your lord -
why is that?"
Gōngsūn Xí replied:
"In the past, during the time of Duke Jǐng of Qí,
there was a great drought for three years.
Divination indicated:
'A human sacrifice must be made
before it will rain.'
Duke Jǐng stepped down from his hall, kowtowed and said:
'The reason I seek rain
is for my people.
If I must now sacrifice a human
to get rain,
I will offer myself.'
Before he finished speaking, rain fell over a thousand li - why was that?
Because he had virtue toward Heaven and benevolence toward the people.
Now, because of some white wild geese,
my lord wants to shoot a person.
I say my lord's words are no different from those of a tiger or wolf!"
The ruler of Liáng took him by the hand,
and they mounted the chariot together.
Returning,
upon entering the temple gate,
he shouted 'Long live!' and said:
"How fortunate I am today!
Others hunting get game,
but I return having gained wise counsel."
King Wǔ of Zhōu, having defeated the Yīn,
captured two prisoners and questioned them,
saying:
"Does your state have any ominous phenomena?"
One prisoner replied:
"Our state does have an ominous phenomenon—
stars appearing during the day and blood raining from the sky,
this is the ominous phenomenon of our state."
The other prisoner replied:
"That is indeed an ominous phenomenon,
however,
it is not the most significant one.
The ominous phenomenon of our state,
the most significant one,
is that sons do not obey their fathers,
younger brothers do not obey their elder brothers,
and the ruler's commands are not carried out.
This is the most significant ominous phenomenon."
Duke Wén of Jìn went out hunting,
chasing game,
and ventured into a great marsh,
becoming lost with no way out.
There was a fisherman there,
to whom Duke Wén said:
"I
am your ruler.
Which way leads out?
I will richly reward you!"
The fisherman said:
"Your subject wishes to offer something."
The Duke said:
"Let's exit the marsh and then I'll receive it."
Thereupon,
they exited the marsh.
The Duke commanded:
"What is it you wish to teach me?
I am willing to receive it."
The fisherman said:
"When swans and geese dwell in rivers and seas,
if they grow weary and wish to move to small marshes,
they will surely face the worry of arrows and strings;
when giant sea turtles dwell in deep abysses,
if they grow weary and come out to shallow banks,
they will surely face the worry of nets, hooks, and arrows.
Now you, my lord, were chasing game
and ventured here—
how far you have strayed!"
Duke Wén said:
"Well said!"
He told his attendants to record the fisherman's name.
The fisherman said:
"Why should you record my name?
If you, my lord, honor heaven and serve earth,
revere the altars of soil and grain,
secure the four borders,
show kindness and love to the myriad people,
lighten taxes and levies,
and reduce rents and duties,
then I too will share in this.
If you do not revere the altars of soil and grain,
do not secure the four borders,
are discourteous to the feudal lords abroad,
and go against the people's will at home,
causing the entire state to flee and scatter,
then even if I, a fisherman, were to receive rich rewards,
I would not be able to keep them."
He then declined to accept anything,
saying:
"Please return to your capital quickly, my lord,
and I will return to my fishing grounds."
Duke Wén of Jìn was chasing a deer and lost it,
so he asked an old farmer named Lǎo Gǔ:
"Where is my deer?"
Lǎo Gǔ pointed with his foot and said:
"It went that way."
The Duke said:
"I asked you a question,
why did you point with your foot?"
Lǎo Gǔ shook his clothes, stood up, and said:
"I never expected a ruler to be like this.
When tigers and leopards dwell,
if they grow tired of seclusion and approach people,
they are captured;
when fish and turtles dwell,
if they grow tired of the depths and move to shallows,
they are caught;
when feudal lords grow tired of their people, they lose their states.
The Book of Songs says:
'The magpie has a nest,
but the cuckoo occupies it.'
If you, my lord, roam abroad and do not return,
others will take your place as ruler."
Thereupon,
Duke Wén became alarmed,
and on his return, he met Luán Wǔzǐ.
Luán Wǔzǐ said:
"Did you catch any game on your hunt?
You look pleased."
Duke Wén said:
"I was chasing a deer and lost it,
but I gained some wise words,
hence my pleased expression."
Luán Wǔzǐ said:
"Where is that person now?"
The Duke said:
"I did not bring him with me."
Luán Wǔzǐ said:
"To hold high position but not care for those below—that is arrogance;
to issue orders slowly but punish urgently—that is tyranny;
to take someone's advice
but abandon the person themselves—that is theft."
Duke Wén said:
"Well said!"
He turned back, took Lǎo Gǔ in his carriage, and returned with him.
Biǎn Què visited Marquis Huán of Qí
and stood for a while.
Biǎn Què said:
"You have an illness,
located in the pores and skin.
If not treated, I fear it will deepen."
Marquis Huán said:
"I have no illness."
After Biǎn Què left,
Marquis Huán said:
"Doctors are fond of profit—
they want to treat nonexistent illnesses to claim credit."
After ten days,
Biǎn Què visited again,
saying:
"Your illness
has reached the muscles and skin.
If not treated, it will deepen."
Marquis Huán did not respond.
Biǎn Què left,
and Marquis Huán was displeased.
After another ten days,
Biǎn Què visited again,
saying:
"Your illness
has reached the stomach and intestines.
If not treated, it will deepen."
Marquis Huán did not respond.
Biǎn Què left,
and Marquis Huán was again displeased.
After another ten days,
Biǎn Què visited again,
took one look at Marquis Huán, and turned to flee.
Marquis Huán sent someone to ask him why,
and Biǎn Què said:
"When the illness is in the pores and skin,
it can be reached by hot baths and poultices;
when in the muscles and skin,
it can be reached by needles and stone probes;
when in the stomach and intestines,
it can be reached by strong decoctions;
but when it reaches the bone marrow,
the Director of Fate can do nothing about it.
Now it is in the bone marrow,
therefore I have nothing more to request."
After five days,
Marquis Huán experienced bodily pain,
and sent people to search for Biǎn Què,
but Biǎn Què had already fled to Qín.
Marquis Huán then died.
Thus, when a good doctor treats illness,
he attacks it while it is in the pores and skin—
this shows that all matters should be dealt with while they are still small.
The fortune or misfortune of events
also has its 'pores and skin' stage,
therefore the sage acts early.
Zhuāng Xīn admonished King Xiāng of Chǔ, saying:
"Your Majesty has Zhōu Hóu on your left,
Xià Hóu on your right,
followed by Xīn'ān Jūn,
sharing the same carriage with Shòulíng Jūn,
indulging in excessive luxury and extravagance,
while forgetting the affairs of state.
Yǐng is in danger!"
The King said:
"Are you senile, sir?
Or are you falsely prophesying doom for Chǔ?"
Zhuāng Xīn replied:
"I dare not prophesy doom for Chǔ,
but truly foresee it.
If Your Majesty continues to keep these four men close,
then Chǔ will surely perish.
I request to remain in Zhào to observe this."
Thereupon,
within ten months,
the King indeed lost the territories of Wūshān, Jiānghàn, and Yānyǐng.
Then,
the King sent for Zhuāng Xīn,
who was in Zhào.
When Zhuāng Xīn arrived,
the King said:
"Alas!
You have come, sir!
Because I did not heed your advice, I have reached this state.
What should I do now?"
Zhuāng Xīn said:
"If Your Majesty follows my advice, it may still be possible;
if not,
the situation will become even worse than this.
There is a common saying:
'To repair the pen after the sheep are lost
is not too late;
to call the hounds upon seeing the hare
is not too late.'
Tāng and Wǔ became kings with only a hundred lǐ,
while Jié and Zhòu lost the entire world.
Now although Chǔ is small,
if you measure its length and breadth,
it amounts to a thousand lǐ,
how can it be compared to just a hundred lǐ?
Moreover, has Your Majesty not seen the dragonfly?
With six legs and four wings,
it flies between heaven and earth,
seeking mosquitoes and gnats to eat,
drinking the sweet dew when available,
believing itself free from troubles,
and having no conflict with people.
It does not know that a child barely five feet tall,
with a glued silk thread attached to a pole over twenty feet high,
will bring it down to be eaten by insects.
The dragonfly is but a small example.
The sparrow, pecking at white grains below,
perching in lush trees above,
flapping its wings,
and shaking its body,
believes itself free from troubles,
and having no conflict with people.
It does not know that young nobles,
holding a slingshot in the left hand,
and pellets in the right,
steadily aiming,
carefully aligning the shot,
so that though it frolics in lush trees by day,
by evening it is seasoned with sour and salty flavors.
The sparrow is but a small example.
The swan plays in the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
rests in large marshes,
pecking at bream and carp below,
soaring over hills and marshes above,
spreading its six wings to ride the clear breeze,
soaring high and fluttering,
covering a thousand lǐ in one flight,
believing itself free from troubles,
and having no conflict with people.
It does not know that the archer is preparing his bow and crossbow,
adjusting his aim,
attaching the silk line to its neck,
shooting from hundreds of feet above,
pulling the fine thread,
stirring gentle waves,
it falls with the clear breeze.
Thus, it swims in the rivers in the morning,
and by evening is cooked in the cauldron.
The swan is but a small example.
The affair of the Marquis of Cài is similar.
The Marquis of Cài traveled south over high hills,
north through Wūshān,
chasing deer and game,
shooting arrows in the streams,
following seasonal birds,
frolicking in the parks of Gāocài,
overflowing without limits,
not attending to state affairs.
He did not know that Zǐ Fā had received orders from King Xuān,
blocking him with the Huái River,
filling in Wūshān,
on the morning of the Gēngzǐ day,
binding him with red silk,
and presenting him as a captive to King Xuān.
The affair of the Marquis of Cài is but a small example.
Now Your Majesty's situation,
with Zhōu Hóu on the left,
Xià Hóu on the right,
followed by Xīn'ān Jūn and Shòulíng Jūn,
indulging in excessive luxury and extravagance,
enjoying pleasure and amusement,
galloping through Yúnmèng,
not attending to the world and state affairs,
not knowing that Ráng Hóu is plotting with the King of Qín,
to trap you at Miǎn'è,
and cast you beyond Miǎn Sài."
Then King Xiāng was greatly afraid,
his body trembling with fear,
and said:
"I respectfully accept your instruction."
He then enfeoffed Zhuāng Xīn as Chénglíng Jūn and employed his strategies,
restoring the twelve states of the Huáiběi region.
Wèi Wén Hóu was traveling,
when he saw a passerby wearing his fur coat inside out while carrying fodder.
Wén Hóu asked:
"Why are you wearing your fur coat inside out while carrying fodder?"
The man replied:
"I cherish the fur."
Wén Hóu said:
"Don't you know that if the lining wears out, the fur will have nothing to rely on?"
The following year, when Dōngyáng submitted its financial report,
the revenue in coins and cloth had increased tenfold,
and all the officials came to congratulate him.
Wén Hóu said:
"This is not something to congratulate me on.
It is no different from that passerby wearing his fur coat inside out while carrying fodder:
he cherished the fur,
but did not realize that when the lining is worn out,
the fur has nothing to rely on.
Now my land has not expanded,
my people have not increased,
yet the revenue has increased tenfold.
This must have been extracted from the officials and people.
I have heard that
when those below are not secure,
those above cannot rest easy.
This is not something to congratulate me on."
King Zhuāng of Chǔ asked Sūnshū Áo:
"I have not yet found the right way to govern the state."
Sūnshū Áo said:
"The right course for the state
is what the multitude dislikes and opposes.
I fear Your Majesty may not be able to establish it."
The King asked:
"Does the inability to establish it
lie solely with the ruler?
Or also with the ministers?"
Sūnshū Áo replied:
"When a ruler is arrogant toward his scholars, he says:
'Without me, the scholars would have no means to wealth and honor.'
When scholars are arrogant toward their ruler, they say:
'Without scholars,
the state would have no means to peace and strength.'
Some rulers lose their states without realizing why,
some scholars suffer hunger and cold without advancing,
when ruler and ministers are at odds,
the right course for the state cannot be established.
Jié of Xià and Zhòu of Yīn
failed to establish the right course for the state,
but considered whatever suited their preferences as right,
and whatever did not suit their preferences as wrong,
thus they brought about their own downfall without knowing it."
King Zhuāng said:
"Well said!
I wish the Prime Minister and the various nobles and officials would together establish the right course for the state.
How dare I, with this narrow state, be arrogant toward the scholars and people?"
King Zhuāng of Chǔ assumed governance,
yet for three years he did not administer,
preferring instead riddles and games.
The state altars were in peril,
and the kingdom faced imminent collapse.
Shì Qìng asked the assembled ministers and attendants:
"The king has assumed governance,
but for three years he has not administered,
preferring riddles and games.
The state altars are in peril,
and the kingdom faces collapse.
Why has no one remonstrated with him?"
The attendants replied:
"You should go in."
Shì Qìng entered,
bowed twice, and presented himself, saying:
"There is a great bird in seclusion,
that came to rest on the southern slope of the Nánshān.
For three years it has neither flown nor cried out.
May I inquire the reason for this?"
The king said:
"You may leave now,
I understand."
Shì Qìng said:
"Whether I speak, I die;
whether I remain silent, I die.
I wish to hear your explanation."
The king said:
"This bird does not fly
to grow its wings;
it does not cry out
to observe the faults of its ministers.
Though this bird does not fly now,
when it does, it will soar to the heavens;
though it does not cry out now,
when it does, it will startle all."
Shì Qìng kowtowed and said:
"This is what I wished to hear."
The king was greatly pleased with Shì Qìng's question,
and appointed him as Lìng Yǐn,
bestowing upon him the prime minister's seal.
Shì Qìng, overjoyed,
went out and, turning to the attendants, laughed and said:
"Our king
is a true king."
The Zhōng Shùzǐ heard of this,
knelt and wept, saying:
"I have served in the court for thirteen years,
standing guard in front with sharp arrows,
and shielding from behind like a barrier.
The king bestowed the prime minister's seal upon Shì Qìng but not upon me.
My death is near."
The king said:
"When I was in difficult circumstances,
the conversations you had with me
touched neither on internal state affairs
nor external relations with the feudal lords.
Someone like you
can be enriched but not honored."
Thereupon,
he brought out the state's treasure of jade and bestowed it upon him,
saying:
"Loyalty and trustworthiness
are the conduct of a gentleman;
speech and words
are the path of a gentleman.
If the path is not maintained,
the gentleman has nowhere to tread."
Jìngguō Jūn wished to fortify Xuē,
and many guests came to remonstrate.
The lord instructed the usher:
"Do not admit any guests on business."
Thereupon,
a man from Qí said:
"I wish to speak but one sentence.
If I exceed one sentence,
I request to be boiled."
The usher introduced the guest,
who said:
"The sea has a big fish."
Then he turned to leave.
Jìngguō Jūn said:
"Please, come a little closer."
The guest said:
"No,
I dare not jest with my life."
Jìngguō Jūn said:
"Alas,
I have no choice,
try to explain it further."
The guest said:
"Have you not heard of the sea's big fish?
Nets cannot stop it,
lines cannot pull it,
but if it is stranded and loses the water to live on land,
then even ants can overpower it.
Moreover, Qí
is your water.
Since you already have Qí,
what use is Xuē to you?
If you lose Qí,
fortifying Xuē would still be of no benefit."
Jìngguō Jūn was greatly pleased,
dismissed the laborers,
and did not fortify Xuē.
In the state of Qí, there was a woman
so extremely ugly that she had no equal,
known as the Wú Yán woman.
Her physical appearance was such that
she had a head like a mortar and deep-set eyes,
a tall, stout frame with large joints,
an upturned nose and a protruding Adam's apple,
a fat neck with sparse hair,
a bent waist and a protruding chest,
and skin as dark as lacquer.
Having reached the age of thirty,
she found no place to belong,
unable to marry despite her efforts to promote herself,
cast aside with no one to take her in.
Thereupon,
she brushed off her coarse short robe
and went personally to King Xuān,
wishing for an audience.
She said to the usher:
the unmarriageable woman of Qí,
hearing of Your Majesty's sagely virtue,
wish to serve in the sweeping and cleaning of the rear palace.
I kowtow outside the Sima Gate,
hoping only that the King might graciously grant this."
The usher reported this.
King Xuān was just then hosting a banquet at the Jiàn Terrace,
and those around him, upon hearing of it,
could not help but cover their mouths and laugh heartily, saying:
"This is the most brazen-faced woman in the world!"
Thereupon,
King Xuān summoned her for an audience,
and said to her:
"In the past, the former king arranged marriages for me,
and all positions are already filled.
Today, I listen to the music of Zhèng and Wèi,
singing and sighing with emotion,
exalting the lingering customs of the stirring Chǔ.
Now, you, madam, are not accepted by the common folk of your village,
yet you wish to approach the lord of ten thousand chariots.
Do you possess some extraordinary ability?"
The Wú Yán woman replied:
"I have none,
I merely privately admire the great king's righteous virtue."
The King said:
"Even so,
what do you enjoy?"
After a long while, she said:
"I have privately enjoyed riddles."
The King said:
"Riddles—
that is indeed what I wish for.
Try performing one."
Before she finished speaking,
she suddenly vanished.
King Xuān was greatly astonished,
immediately took out a book of riddles and read it,
retreated to ponder it,
but still could not grasp it.
The next day, he summoned her again to ask,
but she did not respond with a riddle,
instead raised her eyes, clenched her teeth,
raised her hand, and slapped her elbow, saying:
"Perilous!
Perilous!"
She did this four times.
King Xuān said:
"I wish to hear your message fully."
The Wú Yán woman replied:
"Now, great king, in your rule of the state,
to the west, you face the threat of the powerful Qín,
to the south, the enmity of the strong Chǔ,
externally, there are troubles from three states,
internally, you gather treacherous ministers,
and the masses do not support you.
At forty years of age,
you have not established a mature heir,
not attending to producing many sons but to keeping many consorts,
honoring what you fancy while neglecting what you should rely on.
Once the mountains and hills crumble,
the altars of state will be unstable—
this is the first peril.
The Jiàn Terrace, five layers high,
adorned with gold and white jade,
Lánggān and dragon patterns,
kingfisher feathers and pearls,
interwoven and continuously decorated,
exhausts the strength of the common people to the extreme—
this is the second peril.
Worthy men hide in the mountains and forests,
while flatterers force themselves upon you left and right,
wicked and false men stand in your court,
and those who would remonstrate cannot gain access—
this is the third peril.
You indulge in flowing wine,
carrying night into day,
with female musicians and comedians,
running wild with uproarious laughter,
externally, not cultivating the rites of the feudal lords,
internally, not upholding the governance of the state—
this is the fourth peril.
Therefore I say:
'Perilous!
Perilous!'"
Thereupon,
King Xuān fell silent,
his thoughts sinking into the netherworld,
then suddenly he raised his head,
sighed deeply, and said:
"How painful are the words of the Lady of Wú Yán!
Only now do I hear of my perils.
My perils nearly left me incomplete!"
Thereupon,
he immediately halted work on the Jiàn Terrace,
dismissed the female musicians,
removed the flatterers,
did away with ornate carvings,
selected troops and horses,
filled the treasuries and arsenals,
opened the public gates wide on all sides,
invited forth blunt advice,
and extended reach to the humble and obscure.
He chose an auspicious day,
established the crown prince,
honored the caring mother,
brought the reclusive woman to prominence,
appointed the Lady of Wú Yán as queen,
and the state achieved great peace—
all through the power of the ugly woman.
King Huì of Liáng said to Mencius:
"I have a fault;
I am fond of women."
Mencius said:
"If the king is truly fond of women,
what difficulty is there for the king?"
The King said:
"How can being fond of women lead to true kingship?"
Mencius said:
"The Great King was fond of women.
The 'Book of Songs' says:
'The ancient Gǔgōng Dǎnfù,
came in the morning, galloping on his horse,
along the western bank of the river,
until he reached below Qí Mountain,
along with his lady Jiāng,
came to survey the dwellings.'
The Great King loved his consort,
and whenever he went out or came in, he always accompanied her.
At that time,
there were no pining women within,
no unmarried men without.
If the king is fond of women,
let the people share in it,
and the people will only fear that the king is not fond of women!"
The King said:
"I have a fault;
I am fond of valor."
Mencius said:
"If the king is fond of valor,
what difficulty is there for the king?"
The King said:
"How can being fond of valor lead to true kingship?"
Mencius said:
"The 'Book of Songs' says:
'The king blazed with anger,
and thereupon marshaled his troops,
to stop the invading army,
to strengthen the blessings of Zhōu,
and to respond to the world.'
This was the valor of King Wén.
King Wén, with one burst of anger, brought peace to the people of the world.
If now the king too could, with one burst of anger, bring peace to the people of the world,
the people would only fear that the king is not fond of valor!"
Xúnqīng and Línwǔjūn debated military affairs before King Xiàochéng of Zhào,
the King said:
"May I ask about the essentials of warfare?"
Línwǔjūn replied:
"Above, gain the advantage of heaven's timing;
below, secure the benefits of earth's configuration.
To move after the enemy,
yet arrive before them—
this is the essential art of employing troops."
Xúnqīng said:
"Not so.
What I have heard,
from the ancient way,
is that in all warfare,
the art of using troops
lies in uniting the people.
If the bow and arrows are unadjusted,
even Yì could not hit the mark;
if the six horses are uncoordinated,
even Zàofǔ could not drive far;
if the officers and people are not attached,
even Tāng and Wǔ could not achieve victory.
Therefore, those skilled in using troops
focus solely on being good at winning the people's allegiance."
Línwǔjūn said:
"Not so.
What is valued in warfare is strategic advantage,
what is exalted is deception and surprise attack.
Those skilled in its use
move so swiftly none know whence they come.
When Sūn and Wú employed this,
they were invincible under heaven.
From this perspective,
must one really wait to win the people's allegiance?"
Xúnqīng said:
"Not so.
What I speak of
is the military of a true king,
the affairs of a ruler of men;
what you speak of,
is strategic advantage,
what you exalt
is deception and surprise attack.
The troops of a benevolent ruler
cannot be deceived;
those who can be deceived
are the negligent and idle,
those isolated and alone,
where between ruler and minister, high and low,
there is disunity and divergent purposes.
If Jié deceives Jié,
there might be chance of success;
but if Jié deceives Yáo,
it is like throwing an egg at a stone,
like stirring boiling water with a finger,
like stepping with feathers into fierce flames—
one would be scorched and sunk upon entry.
How could deception possibly work?
Thus, the troops of a benevolent ruler,
when deployed, are like Mòyé's sharp blade—
whatever meets it is severed;
when sharp, like Mòyé's keen edge—
whatever opposes it crumbles.
Whether arrayed circularly or squarely,
they are like a solid rock;
those who touch it tumble and retreat.
How could they be deceived?
Therefore, under the command of a benevolent ruler's troops,
the three armies unite their strength,
high and low are of one mind.
The ministers towards the ruler,
the subordinates towards their superiors,
are like sons serving their father,
like younger brothers serving their elder,
like hands and feet defending the head and eyes or covering the chest and belly.
To deceive and launch a surprise attack
is no different from first alarming them and then striking—
it is the same.
How could deception work then?
Moreover, with a tyrannical and chaotic ruler,
who would follow him to war?
Those who would accompany him
must be his own people.
But if the people feel towards me as joyfully as towards their parents;
if they are as fond of me as of the fragrance of pepper and orchid,
then looking back at their own ruler,
they see him as a branded criminal,
as a hated enemy.
By human nature, even if they were like Jié or Zhí,
would they willingly harm those they love for the sake of one they detest?
It would be like making a man's grandchildren harm their own parents.
The Book of Songs says:
'King Wǔ set out his banners,
grasped his axe with reverence;
his fury was like blazing fire,
and none dared oppose us.'
This expresses it."
King Xiàochéng and Línwǔjūn said:
"Excellent!
May we ask about the military of a true king?"
Xúnqīng said:
"Generals and commanders
are matters of lesser importance.
Allow me to enumerate the affairs of a true king,
the methods of a ruler of men."
Formerly, Qín and Wèi were allied states,
when Qí and Chǔ made a pact to attack Wèi.
Wèi sent envoys to seek help from Qín,
their carriages and caps in constant sight,
yet Qín sent no rescue.
There was a man of Wèi named Tángjū,
over ninety years old,
who said to the King of Wèi:
"This old minister requests to go west and persuade Qín,
to have their troops depart before I do.
May I?"
The King of Wèi said:
"Respectfully, yes!"
So he prepared a carriage and sent him.
Tángjū met the King of Qín,
and the King of Qín said:
"Sir, you are weary and confused,
yet have come all this way—
it must have been very hard.
Wèi has sought help many times;
I know well Wèi's urgency!"
Tángjū replied:
"Since Your Majesty knows Wèi's urgency yet sends no rescue,
this is a failure of your strategic ministers.
Moreover, Wèi,
a state of ten thousand chariots,
proclaims itself your eastern vassal,
receives your caps and girdles,
and offers seasonal sacrifices—
it is because Qín's strength
makes it a worthy ally.
Now the troops of Qí and Chǔ
are already at Wèi's outskirts;
if Your Majesty's rescue does not come,
in desperation, Wèi will cede territory and ally with Qí and Chǔ.
Even if you then wish to save it,
how could you reach in time?
This would mean losing a ten-thousand-chariot Wèi
and strengthening two enemies, Qí and Chǔ.
I humbly believe your strategic ministers have failed in this!"
The King of Qín, startled, awoke to realization,
immediately dispatched troops to rescue,
riding swiftly forth.
Qí and Chǔ, hearing this,
withdrew their armies and left.
Thus, the state of Wèi was restored.
With one persuasion, Tángjū settled the strategy of powerful Qín,
resolved the crisis for Wèi,
dispersed the armies of Qí and Chǔ,
and in one move averted conflict and dissolved calamity—
all through the power of rhetoric.
Confucius said:
"In speech, there are Zǎi Wǒ and Zǐgòng."
Thus the Book of Songs says:
"When words are well composed,
the people are in harmony;
when words are pleasing,
the people are at peace."
Tángjū had such words,
and Wèi relied on them—
thus, rhetoric cannot be dismissed.
During the reign of King Yì of Yān, the state fell into great turmoil.
King Mǐn of Qí raised an army to attack Yān,
massacred the people of Yān,
and carried off its treasures and ritual vessels upon returning.
After King Yì's death,
when Yān had recovered,
the crown prince was established as the King of Yān,
known as King Zhāo of Yān.
King Zhāo was virtuous;
upon ascending the throne,
he humbled himself and offered generous rewards to attract worthy men,
saying to Guō Kuǐ:
"Qí took advantage of our state's turmoil to invade and destroy Yān.
I am well aware that Yān is small and weak,
and insufficient to seek revenge.
However, if I can obtain worthy scholars to govern the state together,
to wash away the shame of the former king,
that is my wish.
Sir, if you see anyone suitable, I will personally serve him."
Kuǐ replied:
"I have heard of an ancient ruler who offered a thousand pieces of gold for a thousand-lǐ horse,
but could not obtain one for three years.
A palace attendant said to the ruler:
'Allow me to seek it.'
The ruler sent him,
and in three months,
he found a thousand-lǐ horse,
but the horse had already died.
He bought its bones for five hundred pieces of gold.
Returning to report to the ruler,
the ruler was furious,
saying:
'What I sought was a live horse;
what use is a dead horse,
wasting five hundred pieces of gold!'
The attendant responded:
'If a dead horse is bought for five hundred gold,
how much more a live one?
The world will surely believe that the king is capable of buying horses;
horses will arrive soon!'
Thereupon,
within a year, two thousand-lǐ horses arrived.
Now if the king truly desires to attract scholars,
I beg you to start with me.
If even I am treated with respect,
how much more those worthier than I?
Would they begrudge traveling a thousand lǐ?"
Thereupon,
King Zhāo built a palace for Kuǐ and honored him as a teacher.
Yuè Yì came from Wèi,
Zōu Yǎn came from Qí,
Jù Xīn came from Zhào,
and scholars competed to go to Yān.
The King of Yān mourned the dead and cared for the orphaned,
sharing joys and hardships with the common people.
After twenty-eight years,
Yān became prosperous and wealthy,
and its soldiers were eager and light-hearted for battle.
Thereupon,
he appointed Yuè Yì as the supreme general,
and joined forces with Qín, Chǔ, and the Three Jìn to attack Qí.
Yuè Yì's strategy
was the achievement of obtaining worthy men.
Yuè Yì advised King Zhāo
that they must wait for the troops of the feudal lords
before Qí could be attacked.
Thereupon,
he sent Yuè Yì as an envoy to the feudal lords,
who then assembled the combined armies of four states to attack Qí,
routing them utterly.
King Mǐn fled in exile,
barely escaping with his life to hide in Jǔ.
Yuè Yì pursued him,
subsequently slaughtering over seventy cities,
with Línzī surrendering entirely.
Only Jǔ and Jímò remained uncaptured.
He recovered all of Yān's precious artifacts and returned,
avenging the humiliation of King Yì.
Yuè Yì dismissed the armies of the feudal lords with thanks
and solely besieged Jǔ and Jímò.
At that time, Tián Dān was the magistrate of Jímò,
and he worried that Yuè Yì was skilled in using troops,
making Tián Dān unable to employ deceit against him.
He wanted to remove him,
but King Zhāo was also wise
and unwilling to listen to slander.
It happened that King Zhāo died,
and King Huì ascended the throne.
Tián Dān had someone slander Yuè Yì to King Huì,
who sent Qí Jié to replace Yuè Yì.
Yuè Yì left for Zhào,
not returning to Yān.
Once Qí Jié became the general,
Tián Dān was greatly pleased
and set a trap, decisively defeating the Yān army,
killing Qí Jié,
and fully recovering over seventy cities.
At this time,
King Mǐn of Qí had already died,
and Tián Dān found the crown prince in Jǔ,
establishing him as King Xiāng of Qí.
Meanwhile, King Huì of Yān felt deep shame,
regretting his own replacement of Yuè Yì,
which had led to this disaster.
King Huì then sent someone to deliver a letter to Yuè Yì, saying:
"I, the unworthy one,
was unable to adhere to your intentions,
so you abandoned the state and left.
My lack of virtue is evident.
I dared to express my wishes, but you were unwilling to listen,
so I have sent an envoy to convey my foolish thoughts;
I earnestly hope you will understand them.
There is a saying:
'The benevolent do not lightly sever ties,
the wise do not lightly bear grudges.'
Your relationship with the late king
is clearly known to the world.
If I had faults,
I hoped you would cover for me,
not expect you to openly abandon me;
if I had errors,
I hoped you would instruct me,
not expect you to openly condemn me.
My crimes
were unknown to the common people,
yet you secretly departed,
openly expressing resentment to abandon me.
I must have been at fault,
but I fear you have not acted with full generosity.
A proverb says:
'The generous do not harm others to benefit themselves,
the benevolent do not endanger their lives to seek fame.'
Thus, covering others' wrongs
is the way of generosity;
saving others from errors
is the path of benevolence.
In this world, to cover my wrongs
and save me from errors—
whom else could I hope for but you?
Now you, having richly received virtue from the late king to achieve honor,
lightly abandon me to satisfy your heart—
then covering wrongs and saving errors
would be hard to expect from you.
Moreover, the world has depth and shallowness,
hence actions differ;
conduct has gains and losses,
thus troubles arise alike.
Now I bear the blame for my lack of virtue,
and you have the burden of failing in generosity;
in choosing how to act, there is nothing to be gained.
A state has its borders,
just as a home has its walls,
meant to unite in goodwill and conceal faults.
If a household cannot harmonize internally
and takes disputes to the neighbors,
that is not a wise plan;
when resentment and faults are not yet apparent,
to openly abandon them
is not fully generous.
Though I am unworthy,
I am not as chaotic as King Zhòu of Shāng;
though you have not achieved your ambitions,
you are not as burdened as Shāng Róng or Jīzǐ.
Yet, without first exhausting internal efforts with me,
you openly expressed resentment abroad,
fearing it may only injure lofty righteousness and thin your conduct.
If not so,
if it could enhance your nobility
and clarify your righteousness,
even if I bear a bad name,
I would not find it hard to accept.
But to think that exposing my shortcomings
would not bring you generosity;
publicizing my ruin
would not bring you glory—
this is one act with two losses.
The righteous do not ruin others to benefit themselves,
let alone harm others to their own detriment.
I hope you will not, due to my unworthiness,
tarnish the beauty of past affairs.
In ancient times,
Liǔxià Jì served as an official in Lǔ,
thrice dismissed yet not leaving.
Someone said:
'You may leave now!'
Liǔxià replied:
'If I differ from others,
where can I go without being dismissed?
Since I would still be dismissed,
I'd rather it be in my homeland.'
Liǔxià Jì did not let dismissal burden him,
so he did not forget his former duties;
not making departure his intent,
he had no criticism far or near.
My crimes
are unknown to the people of the state,
yet the whole world criticizes me.
A proverb says:
'The benevolent do not lightly sever ties,
the wise do not dismiss achievements.'
To dismiss achievements and abandon greatness is to make enemies;
to lightly sever ties and forfeit great benefits is to incur resentment.
To make an enemy and abandon them,
to bear a grudge and burden them—
this should apply to distant relations,
not what I hope from you.
Now, if I am without fault,
would you still resent me?
I wish you would cast aside anger and harmonize your rage,
follow and comply with the late king,
and return to instruct me.
I suspect you might say:
'I will satisfy my heart to complete your errors,
disregarding the late king to expose your evils,'
leaving me unable to advance in following my initial path,
nor retreat to change my faults.
This is within your control;
I ask you to consider it.
This is my foolish intent,
respectfully presented in this letter."
Yuè Yì sent someone to present a letter to the King of Yān in reply, saying:
"Your servant is unworthy,
unable to carry out Your Majesty's commands
to satisfy the hearts of those around you,
and fearing to incur the punishment of the axe and battle-axe,
thereby tarnishing the late king's brilliance,
and harming Your Majesty's righteousness.
Therefore, I fled and took upon myself the crime of unworthiness,
not daring to offer any explanation.
Now that Your Majesty enumerates my offenses,
I fear that those in your service may not understand the reason the late king nurtured me,
nor comprehend the heart with which I served the late king.
Hence, I dare not refrain from replying by letter.
I have heard that a wise and sagacious ruler
does not bestow emolument on his personal favorites,
but grants it to those with great achievements;
he does not appoint officials according to his affections,
but places the capable in position.
Thus it is said:
'He who examines ability and confers office accordingly
is a ruler who achieves success;
he who judges conduct and forms friendships accordingly
is a scholar who establishes his name.'
Through what I have learned,
I observed the late king's actions
and found he had a mind surpassing ordinary rulers.
Therefore, I borrowed credentials from Wèi
to personally come under scrutiny in Yān.
The late king, in excessive favor,
raised me from among the guests,
setting me above the multitude of ministers,
without consulting the paternal uncles and elder brothers,
and made me Assistant Minister.
I considered that by obeying orders and accepting instructions,
I might fortunately avoid offense,
so I accepted the command without declining.
The late king commanded me, saying:
'I have accumulated deep resentment and fierce anger against Qí.
Despite our lightness and weakness,
I wish to make Qí our objective.'
I replied:
'Now Qí,
possesses the remnants of hegemony,
the legacy of past victories,
