is experienced in arms and armor,
and practiced in warfare and attack.
If Your Majesty wishes to attack it,
you must plan with all under heaven.
In planning, nothing is better than directly allying with Zhào,
and moreover, the Sòng territory north of the Huái,
is desired by Chǔ and Wèi.
If Zhào agrees to the covenant,
and Chǔ and Wèi exert their strength,
with four states attacking it,
Qí can be greatly defeated.'
The king said:
'Excellent!'
Thereupon I received the command,
prepared the tally and credentials,
went south as envoy to Zhào,
and upon my return,
raised troops to attack Qí.
By the way of Heaven,
and the spirit of the late king,
the lands north of the Yellow River
followed the late king and were raised;
the troops at the Jì River,
received commands and were victorious.
With light foot soldiers and sharp troops,
we drove straight through to Qí.
The King of Qí fled and escaped to Jǔ,
barely saving his own person.
Pearls, jades, goods, and treasures,
chariots, armor, and precious vessels,
were all gathered into Yān.
The Dàlǜ bell was displayed in Yuányīng,
the old cauldrons were returned to Lìshì,
Qí vessels were set up in Níngtái,
and what was planted at Jìqiū was planted in the Wèn bamboo groves.
Since the time of the Five Hegemons,
the flourishing of achievements and deeds
has never reached that of the late king.
The late king, considering his will gratified,
and that I had not failed his command,
therefore divided the land and enfeoffed me,
making me comparable to the lords of small states.
I have heard that a wise and sagacious ruler,
once he establishes achievements, does not let them decay,
and thus is recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals;
a far-seeing scholar,
once his name is established, does not let it be destroyed,
and thus is praised by later generations.
As for the late king avenging grievances and washing away shame,
subduing the mighty Qí of ten thousand chariots,
and gathering eight hundred years of accumulated wealth,
and on the day he left his assembled ministers,
his remaining commands instructed his successors in righteous models,
those who hold administration and undertake affairs,
follow laws and orders,
pacify the collateral branches,
and extend benefits to the common people and servants,
all can serve as instruction for later generations.
I have heard that a good starter is not necessarily a good finisher,
and a good beginner is not necessarily a good ender.
In the past, Wǔ Zǐxū's advice was heeded by Hé Lǘ,
and Wú reached as far as Yǐng;
Fū Chāi did not approve,
and gave him a leather sack to sink him in the river.
Thus, Fū Chāi did not consider that earlier counsel could achieve merit,
and sinking Zǐxū, he did not repent;
Zǐxū did not early perceive that the king's measure was different,
and thus entered the river without transformation.
Now, to preserve myself and complete my achievements,
and to illuminate the traces of the late king,
is my best plan;
to incur slander of disgrace and dishonor,
and ruin the late king's brilliance,
is my great fear.
Facing an immeasurable crime,
and hoping to turn it to advantage,
is something righteousness dares not produce.
I have heard that a noble man, in cutting off relations, uses no harsh words,
and in leaving his lord, utters no abusive sounds.
Although I am unworthy,
I have repeatedly received instruction from noble men.
I fear that those in your service may heed the words of close associates,
and not examine the conduct of one distant and estranged,
therefore I dare to offer this letter in apology."
Zōu Yáng of Qí,
while traveling as a guest in Liáng,
was slandered by someone to King Xiào,
who became enraged,
imprisoned him, and intended to execute him.
Zōu Yáng, feeling wronged after being slandered during his travels,
submitted a petition from prison.
His words read:
"I have heard that loyalty is always rewarded,
and trust never doubted;
I once believed this to be true,
but now see it as empty words.
In the past, Jīng Kē admired Prince Dān of Yān's righteousness,
yet when a white rainbow pierced the sun,
the Crown Prince grew fearful.
When Master Wèi devised the Chángpíng strategy for Qín,
and Venus eclipsed the Pleiades,
King Zhāo doubted him.
When such essence moves heaven and earth,
yet trust fails to reach two rulers,
is it not tragic!
Now I have exhausted loyalty and sincerity,
fully devoted to righteousness hoping for recognition.
But those around you lack clarity,
leading to interrogation by officials,
and suspicion from the world—
this would make even Jīng Kē and Master Wèi rise again,
only to find Yān and Qín unenlightened.
I beg Your Majesty to examine this carefully.
In the past,
when the jade craftsman presented a treasure,
the King of Chǔ executed him;
when Lǐ Sī exhausted his loyalty,
Hú Hài subjected him to extreme punishment.
Thus, Jīzǐ feigned madness,
and Jiē Yú withdrew from the world,
fearing such misfortunes.
I urge Your Majesty to consider the intent of the jade craftsman and Lǐ Sī,
and then reflect on the judgments of the King of Chǔ and Hú Hài,
lest I be lamented by Jīzǐ and Jiē Yú.
I heard of Bǐ Gān having his heart cut out,
and Zǐ Xū being stuffed into a leather sack—
I once disbelieved it,
but now I understand.
I beg Your Majesty to examine this,
and show some compassion.
A proverb says:
'Some meet as white-haired strangers,
others as instant old friends.'
Why so?
It lies in understanding or not.
In the past,
Fán Wūjī fled Qín for Yān,
lending his head to Jīng Kē for Prince Dān's cause;
Wáng Shē left Qí for Wèi,
cutting his throat at the city wall
to repel Qí and save Wèi.
Wáng Shē and Fán Wūjī were not new to Qí and Qín or old to Yān and Wèi;
their reasons for leaving two states and dying for two rulers
were alignment in purpose and boundless admiration for righteousness.
Thus, though Sū Qīn was distrusted by all under heaven,
he became a Wěi Shēng for Yān;
though Bái Guī lost six cities in battle,
he captured Zhōngshān for Wèi.
Why?
Because there was genuine mutual understanding.
When Sū Qīn served as Yān's minister,
and Yān people slandered him to the King of Yān,
the king gripped his sword in anger,
and fed him swift steeds.
When Bái Guī rose to prominence in Zhōngshān,
and Zhōngshān people slandered him to Marquis Wén of Wèi,
he was gifted a luminous night-shining pearl.
Why?
Because both rulers and ministers
laid bare their hearts and trusted each other,
unswayed by frivolous words.
Thus, whether a woman is beautiful or plain,
in the palace, she incites jealousy;
whether a scholar is worthy or unworthy,
at court, he faces envy.
In the past, Sīmǎ Xǐ had his kneecaps removed in Sòng,
yet became minister of Zhōngshān.
Fàn Jū had his ribs broken and teeth smashed in Wèi,
yet became Marquis of Yìng.
These two men
held firm to their inevitable plans,
abandoned partisan selfishness,
and maintained solitary integrity,
so they could not avoid envious people.
Thus, Shēntú Dí drowned himself in the river;
Xú Yǎn carried a stone into the sea.
Unaccepted by the world,
they would not compromise their principles for gain.
Those who form cliques at court
seek to sway the ruler's mind.
Thus, Bǎilǐ Xī begged for food on the road,
yet Duke Mù entrusted him with governance;
Nìng Qī fed oxen under a cart,
yet Duke Huán gave him the state's affairs.
These two men—
did they rely on official posts at court,
or borrowed praise from attendants,
before the two rulers employed them?
Hearts moved,
actions aligned,
bond stronger than glue and lacquer,
even brothers could not separate them—
how could they be misled by public gossip?
Thus, biased listening breeds treachery,
sole reliance causes chaos.
In the past, Lǔ heeded Jì Sūn's words to expel Confucius,
Sòng believed Zǐ Rǎn's scheme to exile Mò Dí.
With the eloquence of Confucius and Mòzǐ, they could not avoid this—
why?
For many mouths melt metal,
and accumulated slanders dissolve bones.
Thus, Qín employed Yóu Yú to dominate the central states,
Qí used Zǐ Zāng of Yuè to strengthen under Kings Wēi and Xuān.
Did these two states bind themselves to customs,
be constrained by the times,
or cling to one-sided words?
They listened broadly and observed collectively,
earning fame in their era.
Thus, when minds unite, Hú and Yuè become brothers,
as with Yóu Yú and Zǐ Zāng;
when not, flesh and blood turn enemies,
as with Zhū, Xiàng, Guǎn, and Cài.
If a ruler today can adopt the clarity of Qí and Qín,
and avoid the hearings of Sòng and Lǔ,
then the Five Hegemons would pale,
and the Three Kings be easily matched.
Thus, when a sage king awakens,
he discards the heart of a Zǐ Zhī,
and does not delight in the worth of a Tián Cháng;
he enfeoffs Bǐ Gān's descendants,
repairs the graves of pregnant women,
so his achievements cover the world.
Why?
Because his desire for goodness is insatiable.
Duke Wén of Jìn cherished his enemy,
and strongly dominated the feudal lords;
Duke Huán of Qí employed his foe,
and unified and rectified the world.
Why?
Because of compassionate diligence,
and sincere hearts,
not borrowed through empty words.
As for Qín using Shāng Yāng's laws,
weakening Hán and Wèi in the east,
establishing dominance under heaven,
yet finally tearing Shāng Yāng apart by chariots;
Yuè employing the strategies of Minister Wén Zhǒng,
capturing strong Wú,
dominating the central states,
yet ending in his execution.
Thus, Sūn Shū Áo thrice resigned his ministry without regret;
Zhòngzǐ of Yúlíng declined the rank of one of the three highest ministers,
to water gardens for others.
If rulers today can truly discard arrogant hearts,
hold intentions worthy of reciprocity,
lay open their innermost thoughts,
reveal true feelings,
bare their livers and gallbladders,
bestow generous virtue,
and share weal and woe with scholars to the end,
unchanging toward them,
then even Jié's dog
could be made to bark at Yáo;
Zhí's follower
could be sent to assassinate Yóu.
How much more, with the power of ten thousand chariots,
and the resources of a sage king?
Then, the sinking of Jīng Kē's seven clans,
or Yāo Lí burning his wife and children—
would these even be worth mentioning to Your Majesty!
Luminous pearls,
night-shining jades—
if thrown at someone in the dark on the road,
all would clutch their swords and glare.
Why?
Because they appear without cause.
Twisted roots of trees,
gnarled and peculiar,
become vessels for ten thousand chariots—
because attendants first adorn them.
Thus, without cause before you,
even presenting the pearl of the Marquis of Suí,
or a night-shining jade,
only earns resentment, not favor.
But if someone speaks for you first,
then even a withered tree or decayed stump
can achieve merit and be remembered.
Now, if poor scholars living in obscurity under heaven,
though possessing the methods of Yáo and Shùn,
the eloquence of Yī Yǐn and Guǎn Zhòng,
lack the adornment of roots from the start,
and wish to exhaust their spirit and
To open up loyalty and trustworthiness,
and assist the ruler in governance,
then the ruler is bound to follow the precedent of grasping his sword and casting sidelong glances.
This prevents commoners from serving as even withered trees or rotten stumps.
Therefore, the sage king governs the world and guides customs,
transforming alone upon the potter's wheel,
able not to be swayed by base and chaotic words,
nor confused by numerous opinions.
Thus, the Emperor of Qin heeded the words of his attendant Méng Tián,
trusting the tales of Jīng Kē,
hence the dagger was secretly drawn.
King Wén of Zhōu hunted in Jīng and Wèi,
carried Lǚ Shàng back with him,
and thereby ruled the world as king.
Qin trusted his close aides and was assassinated;
Zhōu employed a chance encounter and became king.
Why is this?
Because the latter could transcend restrictive speech,
gallop beyond the bounds of conventional discussion,
and gaze solely upon the bright and vast Way.
Now, if a ruler is submerged in flattering words,
restrained by the confines of his inner court,
causing untrammeled scholars
to share the same trough as oxen and steeds,
this is why Bào Jiāo resented the world and did not linger for the joys of wealth and honor.
I have heard that those who dress grandly to attend court
do not act righteously for private gain;
those who cultivate their reputation
do not harm their conduct for profit.
Thus, though a village was named Shèngmǔ (Surpassing Mother),
Zēngzǐ would not enter;
though a city was called Zhāogē (Morning Song),
Mòzǐ turned his carriage around.
Now, if the broad-minded scholars of the world
are caged by the power of authority,
intimidated by the prestige of high position,
turning their faces to defile their conduct
to serve flatterers,
seeking closeness to those around the ruler,
then the king will only have those who lie dead in rugged caves and mountain marshes—
how could there be any who exhaust their spirit and hasten to your majesty's court!"
The letter reached King Xiào of Qín,
who immediately released him,
and he ultimately became a honored guest.
Guǎn Zhòng said to Duke Huán of Qí:
"For reclaiming fields and establishing settlements,
opening lands and growing grain,
exhausting the benefits of the earth,
I am not as good as Nìng Qì,
I ask to appoint him as agricultural officer;
for ascending and descending, bowing and yielding,
advancing and retreating with ease and practice,
I am not as good as Xí Péng,
I ask to appoint him as master of ceremonies;
for entering early and leaving late,
braving the ruler's countenance,
offering loyal advice,
not valuing wealth and honor,
not shunning death,
I am not as good as Dōngguō Yá,
I ask to appoint him as remonstrance official;
for deciding cases and judging fairly,
not falsely accusing the innocent,
not killing the guiltless,
I am not as good as Xián Nìng,
I ask to appoint him as chief judge;
on open plains and vast hunting grounds,
where chariots do not halt their tracks,
soldiers do not turn their heels,
and when drums beat, the troops of the three armies
see death as returning home,
I am not as good as Wángzǐ Chéngfǔ,
I ask to appoint him as grand marshal.
If you wish to govern the state and strengthen the military,
then these five are sufficient;
if you wish to become hegemon and king,
then I, Yíwú, am here."
Guǎn Zhòng could recognize talent,
and Duke Huán could employ the worthy,
thus they assembled the feudal lords nine times,
unifying and rectifying the world,
without using military chariots—
this was Guǎn Zhòng's achievement.
The Book of Songs says:
"With many scholars in great array,
King Wén found peace."
Duke Huán resembled this.
An official requested instructions from Duke Huán of Qí,
who said:
"Report it to Zhòngfù."
The official requested again,
and Duke Huán said:
"Report it to Zhòngfù."
This happened three times.
Someone at his side said:
"Once report to Zhòngfù,
twice report to Zhòngfù—
how easy it is to be ruler!"
Duke Huán said:
"Before I obtained Zhòngfù it was difficult;
having obtained Zhòngfù,
why should it not be easy?"
Thus, the king labors in seeking people
but rests in obtaining the worthy.
Shun elevated many worthies to positions,
let his robes hang down,
reverently maintained himself without action, and the world was governed.
Tāng and Wén used Yī and Lǚ,
King Chéng used Zhōu and Shào,
and punishments were set aside unused,
weapons rested unmoved—
this was employing many worthies.
Duke Huán's use of Guǎn Zhòng was minor,
thus he reached hegemony but could not become king.
Therefore, Confucius said:
"How small was Guǎn Zhòng's capacity!"
Praising his encounter with Duke Huán,
but regretting his inability to become king.
The enlightened ruler, however, is different,
his employment is great.
The Book of Songs says:
"With many scholars in great array,
King Wén found peace."
This refers to this.
Gōng Jìchéng said to Marquis Wén of Wèi:
"Though Tián Zǐfāng is a worthy man,
he is not a ruler with territory;
yet you often treat him with equal courtesy.
If there were someone worthier than Zǐfāng,
how would you treat him further?"
Marquis Wén said:
"Someone like Zǐfāng
is not someone Chéng can discuss.
Zǐfāng
is a benevolent man.
A benevolent man
is the treasure of the state;
a wise scholar
is the vessel of the state;
a broadly learned and penetrating scholar
is the honor of the state.
Thus, if a state has a benevolent man,
then the ministers do not contend;
if it has wise scholars,
then there is no trouble from neighboring feudal lords;
if it has broadly learned scholars,
then the ruler is honored.
This is certainly not something for Chéng to discuss."
Gōng Jìchéng withdrew to the outskirts for three days,
seeking punishment.
Marquis Wén of Wèi's younger brother was named Jìchéng,
his friend was named Zhái Huáng.
Marquis Wén wished to make one of them chancellor but could not decide,
so he asked Lǐ Kè.
Lǐ Kè replied:
"If you wish to appoint a chancellor,
then ask whether Yuè Shāng or Wángsūn Gǒuduān is more worthy?"
Marquis Wén said:
"Good!"
Wángsūn Gǒuduān was considered unworthy,
and Zhái Huáng had recommended him;
Yuè Shāng was considered worthy,
and Jìchéng had recommended him,
so he made Jìchéng chancellor.
Thus, to know people is wisdom,
and to recommend the worthy receives high reward.
Jìchéng, because he knew the worthy,
was made chancellor by Marquis Wén.
Jìchéng and Zhái Huáng
were both close ministers and relatives,
distinguished by the worthiness of those they recommended—
thus Lǐ Kè's words were correct.
Mèng Cháng Jūn asked Bái Guī:
"Marquis Wén of Wèi's reputation surpassed Duke Huán's,
yet his achievements fell short of the Five Hegemons,
why is that?"
Bái Guī replied:
"Marquis Wén of Wèi studied under Zǐ Xià,
befriended Tián Zǐfāng,
and respected Duàn Gān Mù,
this is why his reputation surpassed Duke Huán's;
but when divining for a chancellor he asked:
'Which is better - Chéng or Huáng?'
this is why his achievements fell short of the Five Hegemons.
Letting personal affection interfere with public appointments,
caused those in office to be incompetent in their duties,
thus his achievements were ruined;
yet his fame and glory remained illustrious,
because three scholars assisted him.
Had he made these three scholars his chancellors,
then royal achievements would have been accomplished,
how could he have been merely a hegemon!"
Duke Píng of Jìn asked Shū Xiàng:
"In the past, Duke Huán of Qí nine times assembled the feudal lords,
unifying the world,
was this due to the ruler's strength
or his ministers' strength?"
Shū Xiàng replied:
"Guǎn Zhòng excelled at cutting the cloth,
Xí Péng excelled at sewing it,
Bīn Xūwú excelled at finishing the edges,
Duke Huán only knew how to wear the clothes,
so it was his ministers' strength."
Shī Kuàng who was attending said:
"Allow me to use flavors as an analogy:
Guǎn Zhòng excelled at cutting ingredients,
Xí Péng excelled at cooking them,
Bīn Xūwú excelled at seasoning them.
When the soup was ready,
presented and offered to the ruler,
if the ruler would not eat it,
who could force him?
So it was also the ruler's strength."
Once Duke Huán of Qí and Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ made a covenant at Kē.
The Lǔ minister Cáo Guì said to Duke Zhuāng:
"Qí's invasion of Lǔ
has reached our city walls,
with walls crumbling and borders pressed,
will Your Lordship not plan something?"
Duke Zhuāng said:
"Alas!
I'd rather be dead than live like this!"
Cáo Guì said:
"Then let Your Lordship deal with their lord,
and let me deal with their ministers."
At the meeting,
the two lords ascended the platform,
the two ministers exchanged bows.
Cáo Guì drew his sword and advanced on Duke Huán on the platform,
saying:
"With walls crumbling and borders pressed,
will Your Lordship not plan something?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Then what does Your Lordship want?"
Cáo Guì said:
"I wish to request the Wènyáng fields."
Guǎn Zhòng said to Duke Huán:
"Your Lordship should agree."
Duke Huán agreed.
Cáo Guì requested the covenant,
Duke Huán then made the covenant with him,
after the covenant Cáo Guì sheathed his sword and left.
The attendants said:
"Coerced covenants can be broken,
Cáo Guì can be punished,
we request to break the covenant and punish Cáo Guì."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Coerced covenants may be broken,
but our lord does not break them;
Cáo Guì may be punished,
but our lord does not punish him,
thus establishing trust throughout the world."
So they did not break the covenant.
The feudal lords of the world uniformly turned to him,
holding the Juàn meeting,
the Yōu covenant,
with no feudal lord absent;
holding the Yánggǔ meeting,
the Guànzé covenant,
with distant states all coming.
He campaigned south against powerful Chǔ,
securing the tribute of sacred grass;
campaigned north against the Shānróng,
opening the way for Yān.
He preserved three doomed states,
restored one extinguished lineage,
honored and served the Zhōu court,
nine times assembled the feudal lords,
unified the world,
his achievements ranked next to the Three Sovereigns,
becoming chief of the Five Hegemons,
all originating from the trust established at the Kē covenant.
Duke Wén of Jìn attacked Yuán,
setting a five-day deadline with his ministers.
After five days Yuán had not surrendered.
Duke Wén ordered withdrawal,
an officer said:
"Yuán will surrender within three days,
Your Lordship should wait."
The lord said:
"To gain Yuán but lose trust,
I will not do."
The people of Yuán heard this and said:
"With a lord so righteous,
we cannot but surrender."
So they surrendered.
The people of Wēn heard this,
and also requested to surrender.
Thus it is said:
"Attacking Yuán caused Wēn to surrender,"
this refers to this event.
Thereupon,
the feudal lords turned to him,
then he invaded Cáo and attacked Wèi,
holding the Jiàntǔ meeting and Wēn covenant,
later defeated powerful Chǔ in the south,
honored and served the Zhōu court,
thus achieving hegemonic success,
ranking next to Duke Huán of Qí.
This originated from the trust shown in attacking Yuán.
When Zhào's Zhōngmóu rebelled,
Zhào Xiāngzǐ led troops to attack it.
Before the encirclement was complete, ten sections of city wall collapsed by themselves.
Xiāngzǐ sounded the gongs to withdraw his troops,
a military officer said:
"Your Lordship punishes Zhōngmóu's crime and the walls collapse by themselves,
this is heaven's help,
why does Your Lordship withdraw?"
Xiāngzǐ said:
"I heard from Shū Xiàng:
'A gentleman does not take advantage of others' profits,
nor press others in danger.'"
He let them repair the walls before attacking.
Zhōngmóu, hearing of his righteousness,
then requested to surrender.
The Book of Songs says:
"The king's plans were truly sincere,
the Xú region then submitted."
This refers to this.
Xiāngzǐ then destroyed the Zhì clan and annexed Dài,
becoming powerful in the world.
This originated from attacking Zhōngmóu.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
and conquered it.
The Earl of Zhèng bared his shoulder,
holding a yak-tail banner in his left hand,
and a ceremonial knife in his right,
to welcome King Zhuāng,
saying:
"I, the unworthy one, have incompetent border ministers,
who have provoked Heaven's calamity,
thus causing Your Majesty trouble,
and disgracing you to come to my humble state.
If you would pity this bereaved man,
granting me barren land,
I will follow Your Majesty's command."
King Zhuāng said:
"Your unruly ministers repeatedly made statements,
thus enabling me to see Your Majesty's noble face,
and leading to this situation."
King Zhuāng personally took the banner and directed his troops left and right,
withdrawing his army seven lǐ.
General Zǐchóng advised him:
"Between Nányǐng and Zhèng,
the distance is several thousand lǐ,
several of our senior officials have died,
and hundreds of soldiers perished in this campaign.
Now that we have conquered but do not possess it,
is this not wasting the people's strength?"
King Zhuāng said:
"I have heard that,
in ancient times, if the water vessel was not broken,
and the leather not moth-eaten,
one did not travel to the four directions,
showing that the nobleman values ritual and despises profit.
We want the people,
not their land.
If people submit and we do not pardon them,
it is inauspicious.
If I establish myself in the world through inauspicious means,
disasters befalling me—
how long would it take?"
Soon after, the Jìn troops coming to rescue Zhèng arrived,
requesting battle,
and King Zhuāng agreed.
General Zǐchóng advised:
"Jìn
is a powerful state,
with short supply lines and fresh strength;
our Chǔ army is weary,
I beg you not to agree."
King Zhuāng said:
"No.
If I avoid the strong,
and intimidate the weak,
then I have no way to establish myself in the world."
So he turned his army to confront the Jìn invaders.
King Zhuāng took the drumstick and beat the drum himself,
and the Jìn army was utterly defeated.
The Jìn men came,
crossing the river southward;
when defeated and fleeing,
wanting to cross northward,
they scrambled for boats and hacked at grasping hands with blades,
until fingers in the boats could be scooped up by the handful.
King Zhuāng said:
"Alas!
That our two rulers cannot get along—
what crime have the common people committed?"
So he withdrew his troops to let the Jìn invaders escape.
The Book of Songs says:
"The soft she does not devour,
the hard she does not spit out,
she does not bully the widowed and solitary,
nor does she fear the strong and powerful."
This describes King Zhuāng.
The people of Jìn attacked Chǔ,
advancing ninety lǐ without stopping.
The senior officials said:
"We request to attack them."
King Zhuāng said:
"In the time of my predecessor,
Jìn did not attack Chǔ;
now in my time,
Jìn attacks Chǔ—
this is my fault.
How can I let the senior officials suffer disgrace!"
The senior officials said:
"In the time of our former lord,
Jìn did not attack Chǔ;
now in our time,
Jìn attacks Chǔ—
this is our crime.
We request to attack them."
King Zhuāng bowed weeping and rose,
then bowed to his senior officials.
When the people of Jìn heard of this, they said:
"Ruler and ministers compete to take the blame upon themselves,
and the ruler humbles himself before his ministers to such an extent—
this is what is called 'ruler and subjects of one mind,
the three armies united in strength.'
They cannot be attacked."
So that night they withdrew their army.
Confucius heard of this and said:
"King Zhuāng of Chǔ achieved hegemony,
and he had his methods.
With one statement he humbled himself before his officers and made the enemy withdraw,
thereby securing the altars of soil and grain.
His hegemony—
was it not fitting?"
The Book of Songs says:
"Pacifying the distant and亲和 the near,
to make our king secure."
This describes it.
Duke Wén of Jìn was about to attack Yè,
and Zhào Cuī explained how to defeat Yè.
and was going to reward Zhào Cuī.
Zhào Cuī said:
"Will you reward the branch, my lord,
or the root?
If you reward the branch,
then the cavalry and charioteers remain;
if you reward the root,
then I heard it from Xì Hǔ."
The duke summoned Xì Hǔ and said:
"Cuī explained how to defeat Yè,
and we succeeded,
I was going to reward him,
but he said:
'I actually heard it from you,'
so you should be rewarded."
Xì Hǔ replied:
"Speaking is easy,
acting is difficult—
I was merely the one who spoke of it."
The duke said:
"Do not decline."
Xì Hǔ did not dare firmly refuse,
and so accepted the reward.
There was a senior official of Liáng named Sòng Jiù
who once served as the magistrate of a border county,
adjacent to Chǔ.
The border stations of both Liáng and Chǔ grew melons,
each having their own plots.
The people of Liáng's border station diligently watered their melons frequently,
so the melons were excellent;
the people of Chǔ were lazy and watered their melons sparingly,
so the melons were poor.
The magistrate of Chǔ, angered by the quality of Liáng's melons, became furious about the poor state of his own station's melons.
The people of Chǔ's station resented that Liáng's station outperformed them,
so they went at night to stealthily trample Liáng's melons,
leaving many withered and dead.
When Liáng's station discovered this,
they reported to their captain,
intending to sneak over and retaliate by trampling Chǔ's melons.
The captain sought Sòng Jiù's advice,
and Jiù said:
"Ah!
How can this be done?
It is the path to enmity and disaster.
If others do wrong, and you do wrong too,
how narrow-minded that would be!
If I may advise you,
you should send people every evening
to secretly go and properly water Chǔ's melons at night,
without letting them know."
Thereupon,
Liáng's station began secretly watering Chǔ's melons every night.
When Chǔ's station checked their melons in the morning,
they found them all watered again,
and the melons improved daily.
Puzzled, Chǔ's station investigated,
and found it was Liáng's station.
The magistrate of Chǔ heard of this,
was greatly pleased,
and reported the matter in detail to the King of Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ, upon hearing it,
felt deeply ashamed,
and reflected on himself with remorse.
He told his officials:
"Investigate the melon tramplers—could they have other offenses?"
"This is Liáng's subtle remonstrance."
He then apologized with generous gifts,
and sought to establish friendly relations with the King of Liáng.
The King of Chǔ often praised and toasted the King of Liáng for his sincerity.
Thus, the harmony between Liáng and Chǔ
began with Sòng Jiù.
As the saying goes:
"Turn defeat into achievement,
transform disaster into blessing."
Lǎozi said:
"Repay enmity with virtue."
This is what it means.
If others are not good,
why should one imitate them!
Liáng once had a doubtful legal case,
with half the ministers believing the accused should be punished,
and half believing them innocent,
so even the King of Liáng was uncertain.
The King said:
"Táo Zhī Gōng,
though a commoner, amassed wealth rivaling a state's,
so he must possess extraordinary wisdom."
He summoned Gōng and asked:
"Liáng has a doubtful case;
half the officials think the accused should be punished,
half think not,
and even I am uncertain.
How would you, sir, decide this,
and what should be done?"
Gōng replied:
a humble man,
know nothing of judging cases.
However,
my household has two white jades,
identical in color,
equal in diameter,
and similar in luster,
yet one is worth a thousand gold pieces,
the other five hundred."
The King asked:
"If their diameter and luster are the same,
why is one worth a thousand gold,
the other five hundred?"
Why is that?"
Gōng said:
"View them from the side;
one is twice as thick,
hence the thousand gold value."
The King of Liáng said:
"Excellent!"
Thus, in doubtful cases, acquit;
in doubtful rewards, give.
The state of Liáng was greatly pleased.
From this we see:
a thin wall quickly collapses,
thin silk quickly tears,
thin vessels quickly break,
thin wine quickly sours.
What is thin and can last long
is probably nonexistent.
Therefore, those who govern a state and nurture its people with policies and teachings
should do so generously and appropriately.
King Huì of Chǔ found a leech in his cold pickles while eating,
so he swallowed it,
and developed an abdominal illness that prevented him from eating.
The Prime Minister came and asked:
"How did Your Majesty contract this illness?"
The King replied:
"I ate cold pickles and found a leech.
If I thought to reprimand but not enforce the penalty,
that would undermine the law and diminish authority,
unfitting for the state's reputation;
if I reprimanded and executed the punishment,
then the cook and food supervisor
would both deserve death by law,
but my heart could not bear it.
So, fearing the leech would be discovered,
I swallowed it."
The Prime Minister stepped back from his mat, bowed twice, and congratulated him:
"I have heard the Way of Heaven favors none,
but supports only the virtuous.
Your Majesty possesses benevolent virtue,
heaven upholds you,
and this illness will not harm you."
That very night,
the leech passed out of King Huì,
and his long-standing heart and abdominal ailments were all cured.
The sight and hearing of Heaven
cannot be ignored.
The people of Zhèng gathered at the village school,
to discuss the merits and faults of the government.
Rán Míng said to Zǐ Chǎn:
"Why not close down the village school?"
Zǐ Chǎn replied:
"Why?
People gather there morning and evening,
to discuss the government's merits and faults.
What they approve,
I will implement;
what they criticize,
I will correct.
They are my teachers.
Why close it?
I have heard that to govern a state,
one uses loyalty and good faith to reduce resentment,
not authority to prevent it.
It is like damming a river:
if a major breach occurs,
many will be harmed,
and I cannot save them;
better to make a small opening to channel it,
so I can hear and remedy it as with medicine."
Rán Míng said:
"I, Miè,
now know that you, sir, are truly fit to govern.
I am indeed incompetent.
If this is truly implemented,
the whole state of Zhèng will rely on it,
not just a few ministers."
Zhòngní (Confucius) heard of this and said:
"From this,
if anyone says Zǐ Chǎn is not benevolent,
I do not believe it."
Duke Huán was drinking with Guǎn Zhòng, Bào Shū, and Nìng Qī.
Duke Huán said to Bào Shū:
"Please offer a toast for me!"
Bào Shū raised his cup and rose, saying:
"I toast our lord:
may you not forget when you fled and were in Jǔ;
may Guǎn Zhòng not forget when he was bound and brought from Lǔ;
may Nìng Zǐ not forget when he fed oxen beneath a cart."
Duke Huán left his mat, bowed twice, and said:
"I and these two ministers
will never forget your words;
the altars of Qí
will surely not fall."
This means that by often recalling times of hardship and narrow straits,
one will never become arrogant.
Duke Huán was on a hunting excursion,
and when he reached Màiqiū,
he saw an elder from Màiqiū village,
and asked him:
"What do you do?"
The elder replied:
"I am a man of Màiqiū village."
The Duke said:
"How old are you?"
He replied:
"I am eighty-three years old."
The Duke said:
"How wonderful is such longevity!
Please use your longevity to offer me blessings."
The Màiqiū elder said:
"I bless our lord,
may our lord enjoy great longevity,
and value people as treasures over gold and jade."
Duke Huán said:
"Excellent!
Perfect virtue does not stand alone,
good words must come twice,
please repeat your blessing."
The Màiqiū elder said:
"I bless our lord,
may our lord never feel ashamed to learn,
nor dislike consulting those below,
may worthy men be at your side,
and advisers be truly capable."
Duke Huán said:
"Excellent!
Perfect virtue does not stand alone,
good words must come thrice,
please give one more blessing."
The Màiqiū elder said:
"I bless our lord,
may our lord never give offense to your ministers and the common people."
Duke Huán flushed with anger and said:
"I have heard that
sons may offend fathers,
and ministers may offend rulers,
but I have never heard of rulers offending ministers.
This saying
does not match the previous two,
please change it."
The Màiqiū elder knelt, bowed, rose and said:
"This saying
surpasses the previous two.
If a son offends his father,
he can seek reconciliation through aunts, uncles or other relatives,
and the father can pardon him;
if a minister offends his ruler,
he can apologize through close attendants,
and the ruler can pardon him.
But when Jié offended King Tāng,
and Zhòu offended King Wǔ,
these were cases of rulers offending their ministers -
no one could mediate,
and they remain unforgiven to this day."
The Duke said:
"Well said!
Thanks to the fortune of our state
and the power of our altars of land and grain,
I have met you here today."
He helped him into his carriage,
drove him back personally,
honored him at court,
and enfeoffed him with Màiqiū to administer its affairs.
Duke Āi asked Confucius:
"I was born in the deep palace,
raised by women's hands.
I have never known sorrow,
never known worry,
never known toil,
never known fear,
never known danger."
Confucius rose from his mat and said:
"My lord's question
is that of a sage ruler.
I, Qiū,
am but a petty man,
how could I be qualified to answer?"
Duke Āi said:
"No,
please return to your mat,
without you,
I would have no one to learn from!"
Confucius returned to his mat and said:
"Very well.
When you enter the temple gate,
ascend the eastern steps,
look up at the beams and rafters,
look down at the tables and mats,
the vessels remain,
but the people are gone -
if you reflect on this to understand sorrow,
how could sorrow not come to you?
When you wash and crown at dawn,
and hold court at daybreak,
if one matter goes unaddressed,
it becomes the start of disorder -
if you reflect on this to understand worry,
how could worry not come to you?
When you hold court at daybreak
and retire at sunset,
the descendants of feudal lords
must be waiting at your court -
if you reflect on this to understand toil,
how could toil not come to you?
When you leave Lǔ's four gates
and look over Lǔ's four borders,
among the ruins of fallen states
surely there are several -
if you reflect on this to understand fear,
how could fear not come to you?
I have heard that
the ruler is like a boat,
the common people are like water -
water can carry the boat,
water can capsize the boat -
if you reflect on this to understand danger,
how could danger not come to you?
He who holds the state's reins,
standing above the people,
trembles as if driving runaway horses with a rotten rein.
The Yì Jīng says:
'Treading on a tiger's tail.'
The Shī Jīng says:
'As if treading on thin ice.'
Is this not perilous!"
Duke Āi bowed twice and said:
"Though I am not clever,
I shall endeavor to follow these words."
Once Duke Huán of Qí was traveling in the countryside,
and saw the ruins of a fallen city, the Guō family's remains,
so he asked a villager:
"What ruins are these?"
The villager said:
"These are the Guō family's ruins."
Duke Huán asked:
"Why did the Guō family become ruins?"
The villager said:
"The Guō family praised goodness but hated evil."
Duke Huán said:
"Praising goodness and hating evil
is virtuous human conduct,
so why did they become ruins?"
The villager said:
"They praised goodness but could not practice it,
hated evil but could not eliminate it -
that is why they became ruins."
Duke Huán returned
and told Guǎn Zhòng about this.
Guǎn Zhòng asked:
"Who was this man?"
Duke Huán said:
"I don't know."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"You, my lord, are also a Guō."
Thereupon,
Duke Huán summoned the villager and rewarded him.
Duke Wén of Jìn was hunting in Guó,
when he met an old man and asked him:
"Guó has existed as a state for long,
and you have lived here since old times.
Now that Guó has fallen,
is there any explanation?"
The old man replied:
"The ruler of Guó could not make decisions himself,
and had no one to advise him.
Unable to decide,
and unable to employ capable men -
this is why Guó fell."
Duke Wén stopped hunting and returned,
meeting Zhào Cuī on the way and telling him.
Zhào Cuī asked:
"Where is this man now?"
The Duke said:
"I didn't bring him with me."
Zhào Cuī said:
"The noble men of old
would listen to someone's words and employ the person;
the noble men of today
listen to the words but discard the person.
Alas!
This is Jìn's sorrow."
Duke Wén then summoned and rewarded the old man.
Thereafter,
Jìn became willing to accept good counsel,
and Duke Wén ultimately achieved hegemony.
Jìng Pínggōng passed by Jiǔyuán and sighed, saying:
"Alas!
This land holds so many of my good ministers!
If the dead could rise,
with whom would I return?"
Shūxiàng replied:
"It would be Zhào Wǔ!"
Pínggōng said:
"You are partial to your teacher."
He responded:
"I dare to speak of Zhào Wǔ's character:
he stood as if unable to bear his clothes,
spoke as if words hardly left his mouth.
Yet he raised forty-six scholars from humble cottages,
all realizing their aspirations,
and the state greatly relied on them.
When Wénzǐ died,
all forty-six took their places as guests,
showing he held no private favors.
Therefore, I consider him worthy."
Pínggōng said:
"Well said."
Indeed, Zhào Wǔ was a worthy minister;
as prime minister of Jìn,
the world knew no war for nine years.
The Spring and Autumn Annals say:
"Through Zhào Wǔ's strength in Jìn,
he fully won people's hearts."
Shègōng Zhūliáng asked Yuè Wángfù:
"What kind of man is Zhào Wénzǐ, a senior official of Jìn?"
He replied:
"He loves learning and accepts admonition."
Shègōng said:
"I suspect there's more to it."
He answered:
"To love learning is wisdom;
to accept admonition is benevolence.
The river emerging from Wénshān
has a source as narrow as a jar's mouth,
yet by Chǔ,
it spans ten lǐ wide.
For no other reason
than its downstream abundance.
A man who loves learning and accepts admonition
is rightly established.
The Book of Songs says:
'Only the wise man,
when told good words,
follows virtuous conduct.'
This refers to him."
Zhōng Zǐqī heard someone playing the qìng at night sorrowfully
and summoned him at dawn, asking:
"Why?
Your qìng playing is so mournful."
He replied:
"My father committed murder but escaped,
my mother was caught and made a state slave,
and I became the state's qìng player.
I haven't seen my mother
for three years now.
Yesterday, while near the market, I saw her;
I wished to ransom her but had no wealth,
and I myself belong to the state—hence my sorrow."
Zhōng Zǐqī said:
"The sorrow is in the heart,
not in the hands,
nor in the wood or stone.
The heart's grief resonates through wood and stone
due to utmost sincerity."
If a ruler can be moved by inner sincerity,
the people will respond and be transformed.
Yáo and Shùn's sincerity
moved all states,
stirred heaven and earth,
so even remote lands followed like the wind,
phoenixes and qilins danced,
down to the smallest creatures,
all finding their place.
The Book of Changes says:
"Sincerity reaches even piglets and fish—auspicious."
This refers to it.
A brave warrior's single shout
makes three armies retreat—
such is the power of a warrior's sincerity.
Once, Chǔ's Xióng Qúzǐ walked at night,
saw a recumbent stone,
mistook it for a crouching tiger,
drew his bow and shot it,
the arrow embedding up to its feathers.
Looking down,
he realized it was stone;
shooting again,
the arrow broke without a trace.
Xóng Qúzǐ's sincere heart
made metal and stone yield—
how much more so human hearts?
To lead without response,
to act without followers,
indicates some inadequacy within.
One who corrects the world without leaving his mat
seeks it in himself.
Confucius said:
"If the ruler is upright,
he need not command to be followed;
if not,
even commands are ignored."
The ancient kings ruled the world with a mere gesture
because their perfect virtue,
manifested outwardly,
made all seas submit.
Thus the Book of Songs says:
"The king's plans truly filled,
the Xú region came."
This refers to it.
A comet appeared in Qí,
and the Lord of Qí ordered prayers to avert it.
Yànzǐ said:
"It's useless,
only deceptive.
Heaven's way is not fickle,
its decree unchangeable—
how can prayers avert it?
Moreover, comets exist
to sweep away filth;
if you have no vile virtue,
why pray against it?
If your virtue is vile,
how can prayers reduce it?
The Book of Songs says:
'This King Wén,
cautious and reverent,
brightly served God,
thus securing much blessing;
his virtue unwavering,
he received the states.'
If you avoid wickedness,
states will come—
why fear a comet?
The Book of Songs also says:
'I have no mirror
but Xià and Shāng;
due to their chaos,
the people fled.'
If virtue is corrupt and chaotic,
the people will flee,
and the prayers of priests
cannot remedy it."
The duke was pleased
and desisted.
During the reign of Duke Jǐng of Sòng,
the Mars was in the Heart constellation,
which frightened him.
He summoned Zǐ Wéi and asked:
"Mars is in the Heart constellation,
what does this mean?"
Zǐ Wéi replied:
"Mars
represents Heaven's punishment;
the Heart constellation
corresponds to Sòng's celestial division,
so the disaster will fall upon Your Highness.
However,
it can be transferred to the prime minister."
The Duke said:
"The prime minister
is appointed to govern the state,
yet to transfer death to him
is inauspicious.
I would rather bear it myself."
Zǐ Wéi said:
"It can be transferred to the people."
The Duke said:
"If the people die,
who will I rule over?
I'd prefer to die alone."
Zǐ Wéi said:
"It can be transferred to the harvest."
The Duke said:
"If the harvest fails,
the people will starve and die.
As a ruler,
to seek survival by killing my people -
who would then accept me as their lord?
This must be the end of my destined lifespan.
Say no more."
Zǐ Wéi stepped back,
faced north and bowed twice,
saying:
"I dare to congratulate Your Highness.
Heaven, though high above, hears what is below.
You have spoken three benevolent statements,
so Heaven will reward you three times.
Tonight the star will surely move its position,
and Your Highness will gain twenty-one years of extended life."
The Duke asked:
"How do you know this?"
He replied:
"You have three virtues,
thus three rewards,
the star must move three positions.
Each position covers seven stars,
each star represents one year -
three times seven makes twenty-one,
hence twenty-one years of extended life.
I request to remain at the palace steps to observe this.
If the star doesn't move,
I ask to die for it."
The Duke said:
"So be it."
That night,
the star moved three positions,
just as Zǐ Wéi had said.
Lǎo Zǐ stated:
"One who can bear the state's misfortunes
is called the king of the world."
During the reign of King Kāng of Sòng,
a sparrow gave birth to a sparrowhawk at the city corner.
He ordered the historian to divine it, who said:
"The small producing the large
signifies you will dominate the world."
King Kāng was greatly pleased.
Thereupon he destroyed Téng, attacked Xuē,
and seized lands north of the Huái River.
He grew even more self-confident,
wanting to hasten his hegemony.
Thus he shot at heaven and whipped the earth,
chopped up and burned the altars of soil and grain, saying:
"My majesty subdues heaven, earth, and the spirits."
He called the admonishing elderly ministers "headless coffins"
to display his courage.
He split the backs of hunchbacks,
cut the shins of morning waders,
and the people were terrified.
Qí heard of this and attacked him.
The people scattered,
the city became undefended,
the king fled to Érhóu's residence,
where he fell ill and died.
Thus, when seeing an omen but acting improperly,
the omen turns into disaster.
Your subject Xiàng foolishly applies the Hóng Fàn Zhuàn to deduce that
the Sòng historian's interpretation was wrong.
This was a black omen,
what the tradition calls "black calamity."
It resembles Lǔ having the myna as black omen,
belonging to those who don't consider their faults critically.
The sparrowhawk is black,
eats sparrows,
is larger than sparrows,
harms sparrows -
a creature of seizing and attacking,
of greedy and rapacious kind.
A sparrow giving birth to a sparrowhawk
meant the Sòng ruler would practice hasty, violent attacks and greedy actions,
rejecting advice to create great disaster that would harm himself.
Thus, a sparrow giving birth to a sparrowhawk at the city corner
presaged the state's destruction,
clearly showing disaster would harm the state.
King Kāng failed to understand,
leading to his destruction -
this proves the effect.
Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Zǐ Xià:
"Must one study before being able to stabilize the state and protect the people?"
Zǐ Xià replied:
"I have never heard of anyone
able to stabilize the state and protect the people without studying."
Duke Āi said:
"Then,
did the Five Emperors have teachers?"
Zǐ Xià said:
"Yes.
I heard Huáng Dì studied with Dà Zhēn,
Zhuān Xū studied with Lǜ Tú,
Dì Kù studied with Chì Sōng Zǐ,
Yáo studied with Yǐn Shòu,
Shùn studied with Wù Chéng Fū,
Yǔ studied with Xī Wáng Guó,
Tāng studied with Wēi Zǐ Bó,
King Wén studied with Jiǎo Shí Zǐ Sī,
King Wǔ studied with Guō Shū,
the Duke of Zhōu studied with Tài Gōng,
and Zhòng Ní studied with Lǎo Dān.
Had these eleven sages
not encountered these teachers,
their achievements wouldn't have been renowned under heaven,
nor their names transmitted through millennia.
The Shī says:
'Commit no fault, forget nothing,
follow the ancient statutes.'
This expresses the idea.
Not to study,
not understand the ancient Way,
yet be able to stabilize the state -
this has never occurred."
Master Lǚ said:
"Shén Nóng studied with Xī Lǎo,
Huáng Dì studied with Dà Zhēn,
Zhuān Xū studied with Bó Yí Fù,
Dì Kù studied with Bó Zhāo,
Emperor Yáo studied with Zhōu Wén Fù,
Emperor Shùn studied with Xǔ Yóu,
Yǔ studied with Dà Chéng Zhí,
Tāng studied with Xiǎo Chén,
King Wén and King Wǔ studied with Tài Gōng Wàng and the Duke of Zhōu Dàn,
Duke Huán of Qí studied with Guǎn Yí Wú and Xí Péng,
Duke Wén of Jìn studied with Jiù Fàn and Suí Huì,
Duke Mù of Qín studied with Bǎi Lǐ Xī and Gōng Sūn Zhī,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ studied with Sūn Shū Áo and Shěn Yǐn Zhú,
King Hé Lǘ of Wú studied with Wǔ Zǐ Xū and Wén Zhī Yí,
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè studied with Fàn Lǐ and Dà Fū Zhǒng.
These are all whom the sage kings learned from.
Moreover, Heaven creates humans with ears that can hear,
but without study,
their hearing is worse than deafness;
with eyes that can see,
but without study,
their sight is worse than blindness;
with mouths that can speak,
but without study,
their speech is worse than muteness;
with minds that can think,
but without study,
their intellect is worse than madness.
Therefore, all learning
doesn't merely add to one's abilities,
but realizes innate nature.
To fully preserve what Heaven has endowed without ruining it -
this may be called being a good learner."
Tāng saw a man setting up a net on all four sides while praying,
who said:
"Those falling from the sky,
those emerging from the earth,
those coming from all directions,
all enter my net."
Tāng said:
"Alas!
This is too thorough!
If not for Jié, who would do such a thing?"
Tāng then removed three sides of the net,
leaving only one side,
and taught him a new prayer:
"In the past, spiders made webs,
now people follow order.
Those wishing to go left, go left;
those wishing to go right, go right;
those wishing to go high, go high;
those wishing to go low, go low.
I only take those who violate fate."
When the states south of the Hàn River heard this,
they said:
"Tāng's virtue extends even to birds and beasts!"
Forty states submitted to him.
Setting nets on all four sides
may not necessarily catch birds;
Tāng removed three sides
and set only one side,
yet he netted forty states -
this was not merely about netting birds.
King Wén of Zhōu built the Líng Terrace,
and when digging ponds,
they excavated the ground
and found the bones of a dead person.
The official reported this to King Wén.
King Wén said:
"Rebury them."
The official said:
"These have no owner."
King Wén said:
"He who possesses the world
is the master of the world;
he who possesses a state
is the master of that state.
I am certainly their master,
why seek another?"
He then ordered the official to rebury them with clothes and a coffin.
When the world heard this,
they all said:
"King Wén is virtuous indeed!
His kindness reaches decaying bones,
how much more so to people?"
Some obtain treasures and endanger their states,
but King Wén obtained decaying bones to manifest his intent,
and the world turned their hearts to him.
Guǎn Zhòng tutored Prince Jiū of Qí,
while Bào Shū tutored Prince Xiǎo Bái.
When Gōngsūn Wúzhī of Qí killed Duke Xiāng,
Prince Jiū fled to Lǔ,
and Xiǎo Bái fled to Jǔ.
After the people of Qí executed Wúzhī,
they welcomed Prince Jiū back from Lǔ.
Prince Jiū and Xiǎo Bái raced to return.
Guǎn Zhòng shot an arrow at Xiǎo Bái,
hitting his belt hook.
Xiǎo Bái pretended to be dead,
thus entering first
and becoming Duke Huán of Qí.
After Prince Jiū died,
Guǎn Zhòng fled to Lǔ.
When Duke Huán was established
and the state settled,
he sent men to bring Guǎn Zhòng from Lǔ,
then appointed him as Zhòng Fù,
entrusting the state and following his advice.
He assembled the feudal lords nine times,
unified and corrected the world,
becoming the leader of the Five Hegemons.
Lǐ Fú Xū
was the keeper of Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn's treasury.
When Prince Chóng'ěr went into exile from Jìn,
Lǐ Fú Xū stole his treasures and fled.
When Prince Chóng'ěr returned to his state
and was established as ruler,
Lǐ Fú Xū came to the gate wishing to see him.
Duke Wén was washing his hair,
and his attendant reported this.
Duke Wén, holding his hair, responded:
"Is it my Fú Xū?"
The reply was:
"Yes."
"Tell Fú Xū:
'Do you still have the face to see me again?'"
The attendant told Lǐ Fú Xū,
who responded:
"I have heard that
when one washes hair, their heart is overturned;
when the heart is overturned, words become perverse.
Is my lord washing his hair?
Why so perverse?"
The attendant reported back,
and Duke Wén received him, saying:
"You stole my treasures and fled,
I said how could you still have the face to see me,
yet you say my lord is perverse -
what does this mean?"
Fú Xū said:
"Indeed,
my lord has returned to the state,
but half the state feels insecure.
Would my lord rather abandon half the state?
Or would he prefer to have the whole of Jìn?"
Duke Wén said:
"What do you mean?"
Fú Xū said:
"Among those who have offended you,
none is greater than Fú Xū.
If you pardon Fú Xū
and prominently appoint him to high position -
if even someone as guilty as Fú Xū
can be pardoned by you,
how much more those less guilty than Fú Xū?"
Duke Wén said:
"I understand your meaning."
He then pardoned him.
The next day when touring the state,
he made him his attendant,
and suddenly the whole state of Jìn became peaceful.
As the saying goes:
"Duke Huán employed his assassin, and Duke Wén used his thief."
Therefore it is said:
"An enlightened ruler follows strategy, not anger;
a foolish ruler follows anger, not strategy.
Where strategy overcomes anger, there is strength;
where anger overcomes strategy, there is ruin."
This refers to this case.
Nìng Qì wished to seek service with Duke Huán of Qí,
but was too poor to present himself.
Therefore,
he hired himself as a merchant's cart driver to go to Qí,
staying overnight outside the city gate.
Duke Huán was welcoming guests in the suburbs,
opening the gates at night for cart drivers,
with torches burning brightly
and many followers.
Nìng Qì was feeding his ox beneath the cart,
gazed at Duke Huán with sorrow,
struck the ox's horn,
and urgently sang a merchant's song.
Duke Huán heard this,
tapped his servant's hand and said:
"How extraordinary!
This singer is no ordinary man."
He ordered him to be carried in a following carriage.
When Duke Huán returned,
his followers requested instructions.
Duke Huán said:
"Grant him robes and cap,
I will receive him."
When Nìng Qì appeared,
he advised Duke Huán on governing the territory;
the next day he appeared again,
advising Duke Huán on ruling the world.
Duke Huán was greatly pleased
and planned to appoint him.
The ministers objected:
"This guest
is from Wèi,
five hundred lǐ from Qí -
not far.
Why not send someone to inquire about him?
If he is truly worthy,
it won't be too late to appoint him."
Duke Huán said:
"Not so.
If we inquire, we might learn of minor faults;
because of minor faults,
we would forget his great virtues -
this is how rulers lose the talents of the world.
Moreover, people are inherently imperfect;
we should employ their strengths."
He then promoted him,
greatly employed him,
and appointed him as a minister.
In this action,
Duke Huán was correct,
which is why he became hegemon.
Duke Huán of Qí visited the commoner Jì,
going three times in one day,
but was unable to see him.
His attendant said:
"A ruler of ten thousand chariots,
visiting a common scholar,
three times in one day
without gaining an audience -
you may stop now."
Duke Huán replied:
"Not so.
When scholars disdain ranks and emoluments,
they naturally look down upon their rulers;
if a ruler despises hegemony and kingship,
he would likewise belittle his scholars.
Even if this gentleman scorns rank and wealth,
how dare I disregard hegemony and kingship?"
After five visits, he finally obtained an audience.
When the world heard of this,
all said:
"Even Duke Huán humbled himself before a common scholar,
how much more should other state rulers?"
Thereupon,
they came in succession to pay court,
with none failing to appear.
The reason Duke Huán could nine times assemble the feudal lords
and unite the world under one standard
was because he treated scholars in this manner.
The Book of Songs says:
"With upright conduct and virtue,
all states will follow."
Duke Huán indeed embodied this.
Marquis Wén of Wèi passed by the lane where Duàngān Mù lived and bowed to his crossbar.
His driver asked:
"Why does my lord bow?"
He replied:
"Is this not Duàngān Mù's lane?
Duàngān Mù is a worthy man,
how dare I not bow?
Moreover, I've heard Duàngān Mù never considered exchanging places with me,
how dare I act superior?
Duàngān Mù shines with virtue,
while I shine with territory;
Duàngān Mù is rich in righteousness,
while I am rich in wealth;
territory cannot match virtue,
wealth cannot equal righteousness.
I should serve him."
Thereupon he sent him a million in stipends and regularly visited him.
The people of the state were all pleased,
and together they chanted:
"Our lord loves rectitude -
hence his respect for Duàngān Mù;
our lord values loyalty -
hence his reverence for Duàngān Mù."
Not long after,
Qín raised troops intending to attack Wèi.
Minister Sīmǎ Tángjū advised the ruler of Qín:
"Duàngān Mù
is a worthy man,
and Wèi honors him -
this is known throughout the world.
Would it not be inappropriate to attack?"
The ruler of Qín agreed,
and halted his troops, ceasing the attack.
Marquis Wén of Wèi may be said to have excelled at using military force.
When a gentleman excels at using military force,
no visible form appears,
yet the victory is already achieved -
this describes exactly that situation.
When crude men use military force,
their drumbeats resemble thunder,
their shouts shake the earth,
dust fills the sky,
flying arrows fall like rain,
they carry the wounded and collect the dead,
treading through intestines and wading through blood.
Innocent people
lie dead in quantities sufficient to fill marshes,
yet the survival of the state
and the life or death of its ruler
remain uncertain.
Such methods are far removed from benevolence and righteousness.
King Zhāo of Qín asked Xúnzǐ:
"Confucians are of no benefit to a state."
Xúnzǐ replied:
"Confucians emulate ancient kings,
honor ritual principles,
are meticulous as subjects,
and can bring honor to their superiors.
If employed by a ruler,
they advance at court;
if neglected and unused,
they retire among common people,
inevitably becoming obedient subordinates.
Even in poverty and hunger,
they would never seek food through wicked means.
Though without enough land to stick an awl into,
they understand the great schemes for maintaining the state.
Though their calls may go unanswered,
they comprehend the principles governing all things and nourishing the people.
In positions above others,
they possess the talent of kings and dukes;
in subordinate positions,
they serve as ministers to the state,
treasures to the ruler.
Even when hidden in poor alleys and leaky huts,
all honor them,
for the Way truly resides in them.
When Confucius served as Minister of Crime in Lǔ,
Shěnyóu shì dared not water his sheep before market,
Gōngshèn shì divorced his wife,
Shènkuì shì fled across the border,
and in Lǔ, cattle and horse traders stopped inflating prices -
all corrected themselves in anticipation.
Living in Quèdǎng,
the young men of Quèdǎng divided their catch from nets,
giving more to those with parents -
transformed through filial piety and fraternal duty.
When Confucians serve at court,
they improve governance;
when in lower positions,
they improve customs.
Such is the Confucian's conduct in subordinate positions."
The King said:
"Then
how are they in superior positions?"
Xúnzǐ responded:
"Their character becomes magnificent.
With will firmly set within,
ritual propriety cultivated at court,
laws and standards rectified among officials,
loyalty, trust, love, and benefit manifested below.
They would not commit one unjust act
or kill one innocent person
even to gain the whole world.
When righteousness and trustworthiness permeate among people,
reaching throughout the four seas,
then beyond the world,
all respond and cherish them -
why is this?
Because their noble reputation becomes clear and the world becomes well-governed.
Thus those nearby sing praises and rejoice,
while those afar rush eagerly to them,
the four seas become like one family,
and all within reach follow and submit.
This is what is called a teacher of men.
The Book of Songs says:
'From west, from east,
from south, from north,

Tián Zàn, dressed in Confucian robes, went to see the King of Jīng.
The King of Jīng said:
"Sir, your clothing—
how shabby it is!"
Zàn replied:
"There are garments even worse than this."
The King of Jīng said:
"May I hear about them?"
He replied:
"Armor is worse than this."
The King said:
"What do you mean?"
He replied:
"In winter it is cold,
in summer it is hot—
no clothing is worse than armor.
I, Zàn, am poor,
hence my clothing is shabby.
But you, Great King,
lord of ten thousand chariots,
unrivaled in wealth and power,
yet delight in clothing people in armor.
I privately believe this is not worthy of Your Majesty.
Is it because you consider it righteous?
Matters of arms and warfare—
splitting people's heads,
gutting people's bellies,
destroying their city walls,
enslaving their children—
their reputation is especially dishonorable.
Is it because you consider it noble?
If one plans to harm others,
others will surely plan to harm him;
if one plans to endanger others,
others will surely plan to endanger him.
Such nobility
makes people deeply uneasy.
These two reasons
make it unworthy for Your Majesty to pursue."
The King of Jīng had no reply.
Long ago, when Duke Líng of Wèi asked about battle formations,
Confucius spoke of ritual vessels,
showing his disdain for weapons and respect for rites.
Now, Confucian robes
are the attire of ancient kings,
yet the King of Jīng despised them;
while weapons
are the ominous tools of state,
yet the King of Jīng delighted in them.
This is why he was shamed by Tián Zàn and endangered his state.
Thus the *Spring and Autumn Annals* say:
"Those skilled at governing do not maintain armies."
This expresses that meaning.
Duke Āi asked Confucius:
"I have heard
that expanding one's residence eastward is inauspicious.
Is this truly so?"
Confucius said:
"There are five inauspicious things,
and eastward expansion is not among them.
Harming others to benefit oneself—
this is inauspicious for the individual;
neglecting the elderly and favoring the young—
this is inauspicious for the family;
rejecting the worthy and employing the unworthy—
this is inauspicious for the state;
the old not teaching
and the young not learning—
this is inauspicious for customs;
sages living in obscurity—
this is inauspicious for the world.
Thus there are five inauspicious things,
and eastward expansion is not among them.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'Each should respect his demeanor,
for Heaven's mandate does not return.'
I have never heard that eastward expansion relates to destiny."
Yán Yuān was attending Duke Dìng of Lǔ on a terrace,
while Dōngyě Bì was driving horses below.
Duke Dìng said:
"How excellent!
Dōngyě Bì's driving."
Yán Yuān said:
"Excellent it is indeed!
However,
his horses are about to bolt."
Duke Dìng was displeased
and told his attendants:
"I have heard
that a gentleman does not slander others.
Does a gentleman also slander people?"
Yán Yuān, displeased,
descended the steps and left.
Soon after,
news came that the horses had indeed bolted.
Duke Dìng rose hastily from his mat and said:
"Quickly bring my carriage to fetch Yán Yuān."
When Yán Yuān arrived,
Duke Dìng said:
"Earlier I said:
'How excellent!
Dōngyě Bì's driving.'
And you said:
'Excellent it is indeed!
However,
his horses are about to bolt.'
How did you, as a gentleman, know this?"
Yán Yuān said:
"I knew it from principles of governance.
In ancient times,
Shùn was skilled at directing people,
and Zàofǔ was skilled at handling horses.
Shùn never pushed his people to exhaustion,
nor did Zàofǔ overtax his horses.
Thus Shùn never lost his people,
and Zàofǔ never lost his horses.
Now Dōngyě Bì's driving—
mounting the carriage and taking the reins,
his posture is correct;
turning and pacing,
the courtesies are fully observed;
but traversing dangers and going long distances,
the horses' strength is exhausted.
Yet he still drives them relentlessly—
thus I knew they would bolt."
Duke Dìng said:
"Well said.
Could you elaborate further?"
Yán Yuān said:
"A cornered beast will charge,
a cornered bird will peck,
a desperate man will deceive.
From ancient times to the present,
there has never been
one who pushed his subordinates to extremity without facing danger.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'Holding reins like silk threads,
the side horses dance like performers.'
This describes skilled driving."
Duke Dìng said:
"How true!
This was my fault."
When Confucius traveled north to the Shānróng tribe,
he encountered a woman weeping by the roadside,
her cries very mournful.
Confucius stopped his carriage and asked:
"Why do you weep so sorrowfully?"
The woman replied:
"Last year a tiger killed my husband,
and this year a tiger killed my son.
Therefore I grieve."
Confucius said:
"Alas!
If so,
then why not leave this place?"
She said:
"The governance here is fair,
the officials are not harsh.
This is why I cannot leave."
Confucius turned to Zǐgòng and said:
"Remember this, my disciple.
When governance is unjust and officials harsh,
it is worse than tigers and wolves.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'He sent down famine and death,
ravaging all four quarters.'
When governance is unjust,
it ravages all four quarters—
how much more just two people?
No wonder she does not leave!"
Marquis Wén of Wèi asked Lǐ Kè:
"Why did Wú perish?"
Lǐ Kè replied:
"Because it fought frequently and won frequently."
The Marquis said:
"Frequent battles and frequent victories—
this should be a state's blessing.
Why then did it perish?"
Lǐ Kè said:
"Frequent battles exhaust the people;
frequent victories make the ruler arrogant.
With an arrogant ruler governing exhausted people—
this is why it perished."
Therefore, those who love war and exhaust their military strength
never avoid destruction.
Zhào Xiāngzǐ asked of Prince Wéi, saying:
"Why did Wú perish?"
He replied:
"The ruler of Wú was stingy and could not bear to punish."
Xiāngzǐ said:
"Indeed!
That Wú perished.
Stinginess meant he could not reward the worthy,
and inability to bear punishment meant he could not penalize the wicked.
If the worthy are not rewarded,
and the guilty cannot be punished,
what can be expected but ruin?"
Confucius was sitting in attendance upon Jìsūn,
when Jìsūn's steward Tōng said:
"The ruler is sending someone to borrow horses;
should we give them to him?"
Confucius said:
"I have heard that when taking from ministers,
it is called 'taking,'
not 'borrowing'."
Jìsūn understood,
and informed his steward:
"From now on,
when the ruler takes something,
call it 'taking,'
do not say 'borrowing'."
Thus Confucius rectified the name of borrowing horses,
and the principle between ruler and minister was established.
The Analects say:
"There must be the rectification of names."
The Book of Songs says:
"Do not lightly change your words,
do not say 'it is but a trifle'."
Can one not be cautious?
The gentleman says:
"The Son of Heaven dwells within the palace gates,
inside curtains and canopies,
under vast roofs,
upon felt cushions,
yet without stepping beyond the tent flaps,
he knows all under heaven,
because he has worthy aides at his side.
Thus, seeing alone is not as clear as seeing with the multitude,
hearing alone is not as acute as hearing with the multitude."
Jìn Pínggōng asked Shū Xiàng, saying:
"What is the greatest calamity for a state?"
He replied:
"When high ministers value their emoluments and do not remonstrate to the utmost,
when courtiers fear punishment and dare not speak,
and when conditions below are not communicated above—
these are the greatest calamities."
The duke said:
"Well said!"
Thereupon he ordered the state:
"Those wishing to present good counsel,
if the ushers do not admit them,
the crime shall be punishable by death!"
There was a man in Chǔ skilled at physiognomy,
whose predictions never missed the mark,
and he was renowned throughout the state.
King Zhuāng met him and inquired about the circumstances,
to which he replied:
"I am not able to read people's faces,
but I can observe the company they keep.
If a commoner
associates only with those who are filial and fraternal,
sincere, cautious, and law-abiding,
then such a person
will surely see his family prosper daily,
and his person become more secure daily—
this is what is called an auspicious man.
An official,
one who serves the ruler,
if his associates are all honest and trustworthy,
and fond of goodness,
then such a person
will serve the ruler ever better,
and his rank will advance daily—
this is what is called an auspicious officer.
If the ruler is enlightened and his ministers worthy,
his attendants mostly loyal,
and when the ruler errs,
they all dare to dispute and correct him,
then such a state
will become more secure daily,
the ruler more honored daily,
and the realm more prosperous daily—
this is what is called an auspicious ruler.
I am not able to read people's faces,
but I can observe the company they keep."
King Zhuāng said:
"Well said!"
Thereupon,
he summoned and enlisted scholars from all quarters,
striving day and night without cease,
and thus obtained such men as Sūnshū Áo and General Zǐ Zhòng,
filling the positions of ministers and chancellors,
and so achieved hegemonic success.
The Book of Songs says:
"With many officers, ample and grand,
King Wén secured his land."
This expresses it.
King Mǐn of Qí, having lost his state, resided in Wèi.
One day while walking briskly,
he said to Gōngyù Dān:
"I have lost my kingdom,
yet I do not know the reason.
Why did I lose it?"
Gōngyù Dān replied:
"I thought Your Majesty already knew.
Could it be that you still do not know?
The reason you lost your kingdom
is because of your worthiness;
since all the rulers of the world are unworthy,
they hated Your Majesty's worthiness,
and thus joined forces to attack you.
This is why you lost your kingdom."
King Mǐn sighed deeply and said:
"Is being worthy really so bitter?"
Dān then said to King Mǐn:
"In ancient times, there were those who relinquished the world without showing worry.
I have heard of their reputation,
and now I see the reality in Your Majesty.
Your Majesty was known as the Eastern Emperor,
truly possessing the world.
Yet after leaving your state and residing in Wèi,
your appearance remains full,
your complexion radiant,
with no sign of valuing your lost state."
The king said:
"Very good.
Dān, you know that since I left my state and lived in Wèi,
my belt has been loosened three times."
Thus he considered himself worthy,
and became increasingly arrogant without cease.
King Mǐn fled to Wèi.
The ruler of Wèi vacated his palace to lodge him,
addressing him as sovereign and providing all necessities.
King Mǐn showed no humility,
so the people of Wèi encroached upon him.
King Mǐn then left for Zōu and Lǔ,
still wearing an arrogant expression.
Zōu and Lǔ refused him entry,
so he fled to Jǔ.
Chǔ sent Zhuō Chǐ with troops to rescue Qí,
who consequently became King Mǐn's chancellor.
Zhuō Chǐ tore out King Mǐn's tendons,
and hung him from the temple beam,
killing him overnight.
He then divided Qí's territory with Yān.
How tragic!
King Mǐn ruled over the great state of Qí,
with territory spanning thousands of li,
yet his troops were defeated by the feudal lords,
his land taken by King Zhāo of Yān,
his ancestral temple destroyed,
his state altars left without sacrifices,
his palaces empty,
his person fleeing for refuge,
worse than a slave,
still unaware of why he fell—
this is deeply painful.
Yet he still considered himself worthy—
is this not lamentable!
Gōngyù Dān, from among slaves,
led him with flattery and sycophancy—
how extreme!
King Mǐn, unaware,
pursued and praised him,
taking disgrace as honor,
and worry as joy.
His downfall was belated,
and he ultimately was killed.
Earlier,
Jìngguō Jūn brutalized his people,
harmed his ministers,
and the populace was about to rebel and jointly expel him.
His charioteer knew this,
and prepared food in advance.
When rebellion erupted,
Jìngguō Jūn fled into exile,
reaching the countryside starving.
His charioteer produced the prepared food and offered it.
Jìngguō Jūn said:
"How did you know to prepare food?"
The reply was:
"Your tyranny
has long been plotted against by your ministers!"
Jìngguō Jūn angrily refused to eat,
saying:
"My worthiness is widely known—
how can you call me tyrannical?"
His charioteer, frightened, said:
"My words were mistaken.
You are truly worthy,
it's just that your ministers are unworthy,
and collectively harm the worthy."
Only then was Jìngguō Jūn pleased,
and then he ate.
Thus King Mǐn of Qí and Jìngguō Jūn, even unto death,
remained unenlightened for life—
how tragic!
When Duke Zhāo of Sòng fled his state,
reaching the border,
he sighed deeply and said:
"Now I know why I lost my state.
My court has a thousand officials—
when issuing decrees and appointing officers,
none fails to call me sage;
hundreds of attendants and servants,
standing in full attire,
none fails to call me magnificent.
Neither inside nor outside do I hear of my faults—
this is how I came to this."
From Duke Zhāo's perspective,
the reason rulers lose their states and altars
is the multitude of flatterers.
Thus Duke Zhāo, having lost his state, could awaken,
and eventually regained his kingdom.
When Húhài, the Second Emperor of Qín, was still a prince,
he had several brothers.
An edict ordered a feast for the ministers,
summoning all the princes.
The princes, having been fed, were dismissed first.
Húhài descended the steps,
saw the ministers' well-arranged shoes,
and proceeded to trample them ruined before leaving.
All the princes who witnessed this
sighed deeply.
When the Second Emperor ascended the throne,
they all knew the world would inevitably abandon him.
Thus the Second Emperor, deluded by Zhào Gāo,
disrespected his senior ministers,
and disregarded the common people.
Hence, Chén Shèng raised his arm in revolt east of the pass,
and Yán Lè rebelled at Wàngyí Palace.
Yán Lè,
Zhào Gāo's son-in-law,
served as magistrate of Xiányáng.
Pretending to pursue rebels,
he led officers and soldiers into Wàngyí Palace,
attacked and shot at the Second Emperor,
then confronted and enumerated his faults,
intending to kill him.
The Second Emperor, terrified,
retreated to commit suicide,
with one eunuch following him.
The Second Emperor said:
"Why has it come to this?"
The eunuch replied:
"I've known this would happen long ago!"
The Second Emperor said:
"Why didn't you speak earlier?"
The reply was:
"Because I didn't speak,
I survived until now;
had I spoken,
I would have died long ago."
Then the Second Emperor sighed in regret,
and killed himself.
The Marquis of Qí asked Yànzǐ:
"How does a loyal minister serve his ruler?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"He does not die when the ruler faces calamity,
nor see him off when he flees."
The ruler said:
"I grant him land to enrich him,
and bestow titles to honor him.
Yet when I face calamity he doesn't die,
when I flee he doesn't see me off—
can this be called loyalty?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"If his advice is followed,
the ruler never faces calamity—
how then would the minister die?
If his remonstrance is heeded,
the ruler never flees—
how then would the minister see him off?
If his words are ignored
and he dies in calamity,
that is a meaningless death;
if his advice is rejected
and he sees off the fleeing ruler,
that is hypocritical action.
Thus a loyal minister
can fully do good for the ruler,
but cannot join him in calamity."
Sòng Yù, through his friend, was introduced to King Xiāng of Chǔ,
but the king treated him no differently.
Sòng Yù reproached his friend,
and his friend said:
"Ginger and cinnamon grow from the earth,
but their pungency does not come from the earth;
a woman marries through a matchmaker,
but intimacy does not come from the matchmaker.
Your service to the king has not yet borne fruit,
why blame me?"
Sòng Yù replied:
"Not so!
In the past, Qí had a fine rabbit called Dōngguō Jùn,
which could run five hundred lǐ in a single day.
At that time,
Qí also had an excellent hound named Hán Lú,
which could also run five hundred lǐ in a day.
If made to spot from afar and point it out,
then even Hán Lú could not catch up to the dust of an ordinary rabbit;
but if tracking its trail and unleashed on the leash,
then even Dōngguō Jùn could not escape.
Now, in your recommendation of me,
did you track the trail and unleash the leash,
or spot from afar and point it out?
The Book of Songs says:
'When about to be at ease and joyful,
you cast me aside like a discarded thing.'
This refers to such a case."
His friend said:
"I have been at fault,
I have been at fault!"
Sòng Yù served King Xiāng of Chǔ but was not recognized,
his spirit and will unsatisfied,
showing in his countenance.
Someone said to him:
"Why is your discourse not elevated,
and your plans doubted?"
Sòng Yù said:
"Not so!
Have you not seen the black gibbon?
When it dwells among the cinnamon forests,
on the high leaves,
leisurely at play,
soaring and leaping back and forth,
like a dragon rising and birds gathering,
sadly calling and long chanting—
at such times,
even Yì or Péng Méng,
could not look directly at it.
But when it is among the thorny bushes,
fearful and trembling,
cautiously looking and treading carefully,
then everyone feels superior to it.
This is not because its sinews have tightened or its body shortened,
but because its position is unfavorable.
When in an unfavorable position,
how can one measure achievements or compare abilities?
Does the Book of Songs not say?
'I harness those four stallions,
the four stallions thick-necked.'
Long harnessed yet unable to run for long,
their necks thicken—
is that not fitting?
The Book of Changes says:
'The buttocks have no skin,
his walking is hesitant.'
This refers to such a case."
Tián Ráo served Duke Āi of Lǔ,
but was not recognized.
Tián Ráo said to Duke Āi of Lǔ:
"I shall leave you, my lord, and soar like the swan goose!"
The Duke said:
"What do you mean?"
Tián Ráo replied:
"My lord, have you not seen the chicken?
Its head wears a comb—that is culture;
its feet have spurs—that is martial prowess;
it dares to fight enemies before it—that is courage;
it calls to others when seeing food—that is benevolence;
it keeps watch at night without missing the hour—that is trustworthiness.
Though the chicken possesses these five virtues,
you, my lord, still boil and eat it daily.
Why so?
Because it comes from nearby.
The swan goose soars a thousand lǐ at one flight,
alights in your garden pond,
eats your fish and turtles,
pecks your grains and millet—
it lacks these five virtues,
yet you, my lord, still value it,
because it comes from afar.
I beg to soar like the swan goose!"
The Duke said:
"Stop!
I shall write down your words."
Tián Ráo said:
"I have heard that he who eats from a vessel does not break it;
he who shelters under a tree does not break its branches.
Having a scholar but not using him,
what use is writing down his words?"
Thereupon he left for Yān,
where Yān made him chancellor.
After three years,
Yān's governance was greatly peaceful,
and the state had no bandits or thieves.
Duke Āi heard of this,
sighed deeply with regret,
and for this avoided his bedchamber for three months,
reducing his upper garments,
saying:
"Not being cautious beforehand,
and regretting afterward—
how can it be regained?"
The Book of Songs says:
"I will leave you,
and go to that happy land,
go to that happy land,
where I shall find my place."
The Spring and Autumn Annals say:
