"If one grows up with the ruler,
the ruler will take him lightly."
This refers to such a case.
Zǐ Zhāng went to see Duke Āi of Lǔ,
but after seven days, the Duke still did not receive him courteously.
Entrusting a message to a servant, he left, saying:
"I heard that you, my lord, favor scholars,
so I came from beyond a thousand lǐ,
braving frost and dew,
enduring dust and grime,
with blistered feet from a hundred stops,
not daring to rest in order to see you, my lord.
Yet after seven days, you have not received me courteously.
Your fondness for scholars, my lord,
resembles Lord Yè Gōng's fondness for dragons.
Lord Yè Gōng loved dragons;
he carved dragons on hooks,
chiseled dragons on tools,
and decorated his house with dragon patterns.
Thereupon, the dragon heard of this and descended to him,
peeping its head in at the window,
and laying its tail in the hall.
When Lord Yè saw it,
he turned and fled, abandoning all,
lost his spirit and soul,
his face drained of color.
This shows that Lord Yè did not truly love dragons,
but loved what resembles a dragon yet is not a dragon.
Now I heard that you, my lord, favor scholars,
so I came from beyond a thousand lǐ to see you,
yet after seven days without courteous reception,
it shows you do not truly favor scholars,
but favor those who resemble scholars yet are not scholars.
The Book of Songs says:
'Keeping it in my heart,
how could I ever forget it?'
I dare to entrust this message and depart."
Long ago, Mr. Chǔqiū, at seventy years of age,
wearing a fur coat tied with a rope belt,
went to see Lord Mèngcháng.
He wished to hasten forward but could not advance.
Lord Mèngcháng said:
"You are old, sir,
your years are advanced;
what instruction do you have for me?"
Mr. Chǔqiū replied:
"Alas!
Do you consider me old?
Ah!
Would you have me chase carriages and pursue horses?
Hurl stones and leap distances?
Hunt deer and grapple with leopards and tigers?
Then I would already be dead—
what leisure would I have for being old?
But ah!
If you would have me speak forthright words and confront the feudal lords,
resolve doubts and settle indecisions,
then I am just in my prime—
how can I be considered old?"
Lord Mèngcháng retreated respectfully from his mat,
his face showing a shameful expression.
The Book of Songs says:
"The old man is earnest,
the young man is proud."
This means the old man wishes to exhaust his counsel,
but the youth is arrogant and does not accept it.
This is why Lord Mù of Qín was defeated in his campaign,
and why King Zhòu of Shāng lost the empire.
Therefore, the Book of Documents states:
"The words of the yellow-haired [elders]
are without fault."
The Book of Songs says:
"Long life is granted to those tested."
It praises using the words of the elderly to bring stability to the state.
In Qí, there was Lǘqiū Áng,
aged eighteen,
who intercepted King Xuān on the road, saying:
"My family is poor and my parents are old;
I wish to obtain a minor official post."
King Xuān replied:
"You are still too young;
it is not yet possible."
Lǘqiū Áng responded:
"Not so!
In ancient times, Zhuānxū
governed the world at twelve years of age;
and Xiàng Tuó of Qín,
at seven, served as teacher to a sage.
From this perspective,
I may be unworthy,
but my age is not immature."
King Xuān said:
"There has never been a colt with tiny horns that can pull heavy loads over long distances.
From this, it is seen
that a scholar is only useful after his hair has turned white and fallen out."
Lǘqiū Áng replied:
"Not so!
For a foot may sometimes be too short,
an inch sometimes too long.
Huáliú and Lùjì
are the finest horses in the world,
but if made to compete with a weasel between a cauldron and a stove,
their speed may not surpass the weasel's.
The yellow swan and white crane
soar a thousand miles in one flight,
but if tested with bats under the hall eaves
or within a small room,
their agility may not exceed that of the bats.
Pìlǘ and Jùquē,
the sharpest weapons under heaven,
strike stone without chipping,
pierce rock without blunting,
yet if used with a straw to remove a speck from the eye,
their convenience may not surpass the straw.
From this viewpoint,
white-haired and balding elders—
how do they differ from me, Áng?"
King Xuān said:
"Excellent!
You speak wisely;
why have you come to me so late?"
Áng responded:
"When chickens and pigs clamor noisily,
they drown out the sound of bells and drums;
when clouds and mist fill the throat,
they obscure the sun and moon's brightness.
With slanderers at your side,
that is why I am late in appearing.
The Book of Songs says:
'To good words they respond,
to slander they retreat.'
How could I have advanced earlier?"
King Xuān struck his carriage rail and said:
"I have been at fault."
Thereupon, he took him in his carriage, returned with him, and employed him.
Hence, Confucius said:
"The younger generation is to be held in awe;
how can one know they will not surpass the present?"
This expresses that idea.
A man of Jīng named Biàn Hé obtained an uncut jade and presented it to King Lì of Jīng.
The king had the jade minister examine it,
who said:
"It is a stone."
The king deemed Hé deceptive,
and had his left foot cut off.
When King Lì passed away,
and King Wǔ ascended the throne,
Hé again offered the uncut jade to King Wǔ.
King Wǔ had the jade minister examine it,
who said:
"It is a stone."
Again deeming it deception,
he had his right foot cut off.
After King Wǔ's death,
King Gòng came to the throne.
Hé then took the uncut jade and wept in the Jīng mountains,
for three days and three nights,
until his tears were exhausted and followed by blood.
King Gòng heard of this,
and sent someone to ask him:
"Many in the world suffer punishment;
why do you alone weep so bitterly?"
He replied:
"A precious jade is named a stone;
a loyal man is punished as a deceiver—
this is why I grieve."
King Gòng said:
"Alas,
my predecessors' judgment!
So difficult to split a stone, yet so easy to sever a man's feet!
The dead cannot be revived,
the severed cannot be rejoined—
how extreme was their hearing!"
He then had someone polish the uncarved jade and obtained a treasure.
Thus, it was named the Hé Shì Jade.
Hence it is said:
"Pearls and jades
are valued by rulers;
though Hé's offering was beautiful,
it was not used by the jade minister.
If presenting a treasure is so difficult,
how much more so presenting a worthy man?
The worthy and the treacherous minister
are like enemies;
they do not align with the mediocre ruler's will.
To have a treacherous minister recommend his enemy to a disagreeable ruler
is ten thousand times harder than Hé Shì's jade,
and without a minister who has lost both feet to push through the difficulty,
it is like moving a mountain.
Once in a thousand years they may match,
as if stepping in succession,
and then a sage king's rule arises.
Those who are worthy but unused
are too numerous to record;
thus, that men of principle are not executed
is likely because the uncut white jade has not yet been presented."
King Jié built a jade terrace,
exhausting the people's labor,
draining the people's wealth,
creating a pond of wine and embankments of dregs,
indulging in decadent music,
where at one drumbeat, three thousand people drank like cattle.
The ministers held hands and sang:
"The river waters surge and swell,
the boats and oars are broken,
our king is depraved,
let us hasten to return to Bó,
for Bó is also great!"
They also sang: [16"Joyful, oh joyful,
the four steeds are sturdy,
the six reins are sleek,
to leave evil and follow goodness,
how can we not be joyful!"
Yī Yǐn knew the mandate of heaven had arrived,
raised his cup and warned Jié:
"If Your Majesty does not heed your servant's words,
your downfall is imminent!"
Jié slapped his throne and rose,
laughing mockingly:
"What sorcerous talk is this?
I possess the world,
just as heaven possesses the sun.
Can the sun perish?
If the sun perishes,
then I too shall perish!"
Thereupon,
Yī Yǐn gathered his shoes and hastened away,
going to Tāng,
who appointed him as prime minister.
Thus Yī Yǐn left his post and entered Yīn,
and the king of Yīn caused Xià to perish.
King Zhòu built the Deer Terrace,
which took seven years to complete,
measuring three lǐ in breadth,
a thousand feet in height,
overlooking the clouds and rain,
instituted the roasting punishment,
executed the innocent,
seized the people's labor,
inflicted injustice and cruelty upon the common people,
and imposed brutality upon his ministers.
All under heaven rebelled against him,
wishing to submit to King Wén.
When the Zhōu army arrived,
he could not command even those around him,
how lamentable!
At that time,
to seek to be a commoner
was no longer possible—
this was Zhòu's own doing.
The King of Wèi planned to build a mid-heaven terrace,
issuing the order:
"Whoever dares to remonstrate shall die!"
Xǔ Wǎn entered carrying a shovel on his back,
saying:
"I hear Your Majesty plans to build a mid-heaven terrace,
I wish to contribute some effort."
The King asked:
"What effort can you contribute?"
Wǎn replied:
"Though I lack strength,
I can discuss the terrace."
The King said:
"How so?"
He answered:
"I hear heaven and earth
are fifteen thousand lǐ apart,
now if Your Majesty takes half of that,
you should build a terrace seven thousand five hundred lǐ high.
With such height,
its base must cover eight thousand lǐ square.
Even all Your Majesty's lands
are insufficient for the terrace's foundation.
In ancient times, Yáo and Shùn established feudal lords
with territories of five thousand lǐ square.
If Your Majesty must build this terrace,
first raise troops to attack the feudal lords,
seizing all their lands,
and if still insufficient,
then attack the four barbarians,
obtaining eight thousand lǐ square,
to suffice for the terrace's foundation.
The accumulation of timber,
the multitude of laborers,
the storage of granaries—
all would number in trillions.
Beyond the eight thousand lǐ area,
farmland must be designated
to supply the needs of Your Majesty's terrace.
Only when all preparations for the terrace are complete
can construction begin."
The King of Wèi fell silent with no response,
and abandoned the terrace project.
Duke Líng of Wèi dug a pond in cold weather,
Wǎn Chūn remonstrated:
"Starting labor in cold weather
may harm the people."
The Duke asked: [112"Is the weather cold?"
Wǎn Chūn replied:
"You wear fox fur,
sit on bear mats,
with a stove in the warm corner—
therefore you feel no cold.
Now the people wear torn unrepaired clothes,
shoes broken and unmended,
while you feel no cold,
the people truly suffer from cold."
The Duke said:
"Well said!"
And ordered the labor stopped.
His attendants remonstrated:
"You dug the pond
unaware of the cold,
but because Wǎn Chūn knew and you stopped the work,
gratitude will go to Wǎn Chūn,
while resentment falls upon you."
The Duke said:
"Not so!
Wǎn Chūn
was a commoner of Lǔ state,
I promoted him,
yet the people haven't witnessed his qualities.
Now I shall let the people see this through him.
Moreover, when Chūn has virtue,
I possess it too;
Chūn's virtue
is it not also my virtue?"
Duke Líng's judgment of Wǎn Chūn
may be said to understand the way of rulership!
King Xuān of Qí built a great palace,
covering nearly a hundred acres,
with three hundred doors in its hall,
yet despite Qí's great size,
it remained unfinished after three years of preparation,
with no minister daring to remonstrate.
Xiāng Jū asked King Xuān:
"The King of Jīng abandoned the former kings' rites and music
for debauched music—
dare I ask if the state of Jīng has a ruler?"
The King said:
"It has no ruler."
"Dare I ask if the state of Jīng has ministers?"
The King said:
"It has no ministers."
After a pause,
Xiāng Jū said:
"Now Your Majesty builds a great palace,
unfinished in three years,
with no ministers daring to remonstrate—
dare I ask if you have ministers?"
The King said:
"I have no ministers."
Xiāng Jū said:
"I beg to take my leave!"
And hurried out.
The King said:
"Xiāngzǐ, stay!
Why did you remonstrate with me so late?"
Immediately summoning the Secretary,
he said:
"Record this:
I, unworthy,
Zhào Xiāngzǐ was drinking
for five days and five nights without stopping.
He said to his attendant:
"I am truly a hero of the state,
for I have been drinking
for five days and five nights,
yet I am not ill at all."
Yōu Mò said:
"Strive harder, my lord,
you are only two days short of King Zhòu.
King Zhòu drank for seven days and seven nights,
while you have only managed five."
Xiāngzǐ became fearful
and said to Yōu Mò:
"Then am I doomed to perish?"
Yōu Mò replied:
"You will not perish."
Xiāngzǐ said:
"I am only two days short of King Zhòu,
if I'm not doomed to perish, then what awaits me?"
Yōu Mò said:
"The reason Jié and Zhòu perished
was because they encountered Tāng and Wǔ;
now all under heaven are like Jié,
and you are like Zhòu;
with Jié and Zhòu coexisting in the same era,
how could they destroy each other?
Nevertheless, it is still perilous!"
Duke Jǐng of Qí was drinking and enjoying himself,
removed his ceremonial robes and cap,
and personally struck the earthen jar.
He said to his attendant:
"Would a benevolent person also enjoy this?"
Liáng Qiūzǐ said:
"The ears and eyes of a benevolent person
are also like those of ordinary people,
why would they alone not enjoy this?"
The duke said:
"Quickly prepare the carriage to welcome Yànzǐ."
Yànzǐ arrived in full court attire.
The duke said:
"I am very happy.
This joy,
I wish to share with you, Master.
Please let us dispense with ritual."
Yànzǐ replied:
"Your words are mistaken!
Even a child of five feet in Qí,
could overcome me in strength and even surpass you,
the reason they dare not cause disorder
is because they fear ritual.
If those above have no ritual,
they have no means to command those below;
if those below have no ritual,
they have no means to serve those above.
The deer have no ritual,
therefore father and son share the same doe.
What makes humans noble compared to beasts
is because they have ritual.
The Book of Songs says:
'If a man has no ritual,
why does he not quickly die?'
Therefore, ritual cannot be discarded."
The duke said:
"I lack virtue,
my attendants indulge me in excessive drinking,
leading to this state.
I request to have them executed."
Yànzǐ said:
"What crime have your attendants committed?
If you, my lord, favor ritual,
those attendants who practice ritual will come,
and those without ritual will leave;
if you, my lord, dislike ritual,
the same will happen."
The duke said:
"Well said!
I ask to change my robes and cap,
and receive instruction anew."
Thereupon, he ceased drinking and replaced the wine vessels,
sat in court attire,
after three rounds of toasts,
Yànzǐ hurriedly departed.
Marquis Wén of Wèi visited Jī Jì,
whose wall had collapsed but was not repaired.
Marquis Wén asked:
"Why haven't you repaired it?"
He replied:
"It is not the season."
His wall was crooked and not straight,
the Marquis asked:
"Why isn't it straight?"
He said:
"It is naturally so."
The attendants ate peaches from his garden,
Jī Jì stopped them.
A short while later, when the day was late,
he served coarse food,
and soup made from gourds.
After Marquis Wén left,
his servant said:
"You gained nothing from Jī Jì!
Earlier when food was served,
I secretly observed,
it was coarse food,
and gourd soup."
Marquis Wén said:
"How can you say I gained nothing from Jī Jì?
In one meeting with Jī Jì, I gained four lessons.
His wall collapsed but he did not repair it,
saying 'wait for the season'
taught me not to interfere with farming seasons;
the wall was crooked and not straight,
replying 'it is naturally so'
taught me not to encroach on others' boundaries;
when the attendants ate garden peaches,
Jī Jì stopped them -
was it because he cherished the peaches?
No, he was teaching me that subordinates should not encroach upon superiors;
he served me coarse food -
could Jī Jì not afford the five flavors?
He was teaching me not to overtax the people,
and to reduce extravagant consumption."
Shì Yǐn Chí was on a mission from Chǔ to Sòng,
Sīchéng Zǐhǎn hosted him with wine.
The southern neighbor's wall
protruded in front and was not straight,
the western neighbor's drainage
flowed through his residence without being stopped.
Shì Yǐn Chí asked the reason,
Sīchéng Zǐhǎn said:
"The southern family are workers,
they make leather shoes.
I intended to relocate them,
but their father said:
'We rely on making shoes,
this has fed us for three generations.
If we move now,
those in Sòng who seek shoes
will not know our location.
We will have nothing to eat -
I hope the Prime Minister will consider our starvation.'
For this reason, I did not relocate them.
The western house is high,
my residence is low,
so the drainage flowing through my property is convenient,
for this reason I do not stop it."
When Shì Yǐn Chí returned,
Chǔ was about to raise troops
to attack Sòng.
Shì Yǐn Chí advised the king:
"Sòng cannot be attacked.
Their ruler is wise,
their minister is benevolent;
the wise gain the people's support,
the benevolent can employ men effectively.
To attack would be fruitless,
and would make us the laughingstock of the world."
Chǔ gave up attacking Sòng and attacked Zhèng instead.
Confucius heard of this and said:
"Those who cultivate virtue in the court
can repel enemies a thousand miles away -
this describes Sīchéng Zǐhǎn."
Mèng Xiànzǐ of Lǔ visited Jìn,
Xuānzǐ entertained him with wine.
Three times they moved locations,
yet the bells and stone chimes
were all in place without being moved.
Xiànzǐ said:
"How wealthy your household is!"
Xuānzǐ said:
"How does your household's wealth compare to mine?"
Xiànzǐ replied:
"My household is very poor.
I only have two scholars named Yán Huí and Zī Wúlíng -
they bring peace and stability to my state and household,
and harmony among the common people.
These are the only two things I have,
this is my entire wealth."
After the guest left,
Xuānzǐ said:
"He is a true gentleman,
who considers nurturing worthies as wealth.
I am a vulgar man,
who considers bells, stones, gold and jade as wealth."
Confucius said:
"Mèng Xiànzǐ's wealth
deserves to be recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals."
Zōu Mùgōng had issued an order:
"Ducks and geese must be fed with chaff,
and must not be given grain."
Thereupon,
the granary had no chaff and sought to exchange with the people,
getting one shí of chaff for two shí of grain.
The officials considered this wasteful,
and requested to feed them with grain instead.
Mùgōng said:
"Away!
This is beyond your understanding.
The common people plow with well-fed oxen,
and weed under the scorching sun,
laboring diligently without laziness—
is this all for the sake of birds and beasts?
Grain
is the finest food for humans;
how can we use it to feed birds?
Moreover, you only know petty calculations
but fail to grasp the greater scheme.
A Zhōu proverb says:
'What leaks from the bag remains in the storage.'
Have you not heard this?
The ruler
is the parent of the people;
taking grain from the granary
and transferring it to the people—
is this not still my grain?
If the birds eat Zōu's chaff,
it does not harm Zōu's grain supply.
Whether the grain is in the granary or among the people,
what difference does it make to me?"
When the people of Zōu heard this,
they all understood that private stores and public stores were one and the same.
This is called knowing how to enrich a state.
When Yáo ruled the world,
Bóchéng Zǐgāo served as a feudal lord.
When Yáo passed the throne to Shùn,
and Shùn passed it to Yǔ,
Bóchéng Zǐgāo resigned his lordship to farm.
Yǔ went to see him
while he was plowing in the fields.
Yǔ hurried to a lower position and asked him:
"In the past when Yáo ruled the world,
you, sir, stood as a feudal lord;
when Yáo passed authority to Shùn,
you, sir, still remained;
yet now that I am on the throne,
you resign your lordship to farm—
what is the reason?"
Bóchéng Zǐgāo said:
"In the past when Yáo ruled the world,
he elevated the world and passed it to others—
this was the ultimate selflessness;
he selected the worthy and gave them his position—
this was the ultimate impartiality.
By demonstrating this perfectly selfless and impartial conduct to the world,
he needed no rewards yet the people were encouraged;
he needed no punishments yet the people stood in awe.
Shùn was also like this.
Now you employ rewards and punishments, yet the people are covetous and full of selfishness—
this shows that what you cherish is selfishness.
When the common people know this,
the beginning of greed and contention
starts from here.
Virtue declines from this point,
and punishments multiply from this point.
I cannot bear to witness this,
which is why I remain in the wilderness.
Now why do you seek to see me?
You may go now,
do not delay my work."
He continued plowing without looking back.
The Shū says:
"He broadly applied symbolic punishments with clarity."
But Yǔ could not achieve this.
The Chūnqiū says:
"The Five Emperors made no covenants or oaths"—
this shows their trustworthiness and sincerity.
Jié built a pool of wine
large enough to float boats;
a hill of dregs
high enough to see for seven lǐ;
at one drumbeat, three thousand people drank like cattle.
Guān Lóngpáng admonished him:
"As a ruler,
one should personally practice ritual and righteousness,
love the people and conserve resources—
thus the state will be secure and one's life long.
Now you use resources as if they were endless,
and use people as if fearing they won't die.
If you do not reform,
heaven's calamity will surely descend,
and punishment will certainly come.
I beg you to reform."
He remained standing without leaving the court.
Jié then imprisoned him.
The gentleman, hearing of this, said:
"It's hopeless—
such is fate!"
When Zhòu instituted the punishment of the roasting pillar,
Prince Bǐgān said:
"To see a tyrannical ruler and not remonstrate
is to be no loyal minister;
to fear death and not speak out
is to be no courageous man;
to see error and remonstrate,
and die if not heeded—
this is the ultimate loyalty."
Thereupon he went to admonish,
remaining at court for three days without leaving.
Zhòu consequently killed him.
The Shī says:
"Great Heaven is too cruel,
I am truly innocent."
To die innocent—
is this not tragic indeed!
Cáo Gōngzǐ Xǐshí,
courtesy name Zǐzāng,
was a son of Cáo Xuāngōng.
When Xuāngōng joined the feudal lords in attacking Qín,
he died in the campaign.
The people of Cáo sent Zǐzāng to receive the funeral procession,
while making Gōngzǐ Fùchú and the crown prince remain to guard the state.
Fùchú killed the crown prince and established himself.
When Zǐzāng saw that Fùchú was about to become ruler,
after Xuāngōng was buried,
Zǐzāng prepared to leave,
and all the people of the state followed him.
Fùchú was established,
becoming Cáo Chénggōng.
Chénggōng, afraid,
confessed his crime
and begged Zǐzāng to return.
Zǐzāng then came back,
and Chénggōng subsequently became ruler.
Later, the Marquis of Jìn assembled the feudal lords,
seized Cáo Chénggōng,
and took him to the capital,
intending to present Zǐzāng to the Zhōu Son of Heaven and establish him.
Zǐzāng said:
"Ancient records state:
'The sage attains the ultimate integrity,
the next best preserves integrity,
the lowest does not lose integrity.'
To be ruler
is not my integrity.
Though I cannot be a sage,
dare I fail to preserve my integrity?"
Thereupon he fled to Sòng.
The people of Cáo repeatedly pleaded.
The Marquis of Jìn told Zǐzāng that if he returned to his state,
he would release their ruler.
Thereupon,
Zǐzāng returned to the state,
and Jìn then spoke to the Son of Heaven,
returning Chénggōng to Cáo.
Zǐzāng consequently handed over the state to Chénggōng.
When Chénggōng became ruler,
Zǐzāng did not emerge from retirement,
and the state of Cáo was thus pacified.
Zǐzāng yielded a state of a thousand chariots—
this can be called worthy indeed.
Therefore the Chūnqiū honors him and praises his descendants.
Yánlíng Jìzǐ was
the son of the King of Wú.
There were four full brothers by the same mother:
the eldest was È,
the next was Yúzhài,
the next was Yímò,
and the next was Zhá.
Zhá was Jìzǐ,
the youngest and virtuous,
and all his brothers loved him.
After the mourning period was over,
they intended to establish Jìzǐ as king,
but Jìzǐ declined, saying:
"At the death of Duke Xuān of Cáo,
the feudal lords and the people of Cáo considered the Cáo ruler unrighteous,
and intended to establish Zǐzāng,
but Zǐzāng left,
and thus did not act,
thereby enabling the Cáo ruler.
The gentleman said:
'He was able to maintain integrity!'
You, my lord, are the rightful successor;
who would dare to oppose you?
To possess the state
is not my integrity.
Although I, Zhá, lack talent,
I wish to follow Zǐzāng's example,
so as not to lose my integrity."
They insisted on establishing him,
but he abandoned his home and plowed the fields,
so they gave up.
È said:
"If we now abruptly give the throne to Jìzǐ,
Jìzǐ will certainly not accept.
Let us not pass it to sons but to brothers,
with us brothers taking turns as ruler,
and then convey the state to Jìzǐ."
All said:
"Agreed!"
Therefore, those who became rulers
all despised death and acted bravely,
and when eating and drinking, they would pray, saying:
"If Heaven wishes to preserve our state,
may disaster quickly fall upon my person."
Thus, when È died,
Yúzhài was established;
when Yúzhài died,
Yímò was established.
When Yímò died,
the state should have gone to Jìzǐ,
but Jìzǐ was on a mission and had not yet returned.
Liáo was
the elder son's half-brother,
and he set himself up as King of Wú.
When Jìzǐ returned from his mission,
upon arrival, he served him as his lord.
È's son was called Prince Guāng,
also known as Hélǘ,
who was displeased and said:
"What our former ruler did,
not giving the throne to sons but to brothers,
was all for Jìzǐ's sake.
If we follow the former ruler's command,
then the state should go to Jìzǐ;
if we do not follow the former ruler's command and give it to a son,
then I am the one who should be established.
How can Liáo become ruler?"
Thereupon,
he sent Zhuānzhū to assassinate Liáo,
and offered the state to Jìzǐ.
Jìzǐ said:
"You killed my lord,
and I accept the state from you—
this would mean I am joining you in rebellion;
you killed my elder brother,
and if I then kill you,
it would be a cycle of fathers, sons, and brothers killing each other,
with no end for life."
He left and went to Yánlíng,
never entering the state of Wú again for life,
hence he was called Yánlíng Jìzǐ.
The gentleman considers his refusal to accept the state as righteousness,
and his refusal to kill as benevolence.
Therefore, the Spring and Autumn Annals esteemed Jìzǐ and honored him.
Yánlíng Jìzǐ was about to go west on a diplomatic mission to Jìn,
and carrying a precious sword, he passed by the lord of Xú.
The lord of Xú looked at the sword,
and though he did not speak, his expression showed desire for it.
Yánlíng Jìzǐ, because he had a mission to the superior state,
did not present it,
but in his heart, he had promised it to him.
After completing his mission to Jìn,
on his return,
he found that the lord of Xú had died in Chǔ.
Thereupon,
he took off the sword and presented it to the successor lord.
His attendant stopped him, saying:
"This is a treasure of the state of Wú,
not something to be given as a gift."
Yánlíng Jìzǐ said:
"I am not giving it as a gift.
Previously when I came,
the lord of Xú looked at my sword,
and though he did not speak, his expression showed desire for it;
I, because I had a mission to the superior state,
did not present it,
but even so,
in my heart, I had promised it to him.
Now that he is dead, if I do not offer it,
that would be deceiving my heart.
To cherish the sword and be false to my heart
is something a man of integrity would not do."
Thereupon, he took off the sword and presented it to the successor lord.
The successor lord said:
"My late lord left no command,
so I, the orphan, dare not accept the sword."
Thereupon,
Jìzǐ hung the sword on a tree at the tomb of the lord of Xú and left.
The people of Xú praised him and sang of him, saying:
"Yánlíng Jìzǐ, oh, does not forget his old friend,
taking off his sword worth a thousand pieces of gold, oh, and hanging it on the tomb tree."
Duke Dào of Xǔ suffered from malaria,
drank medicine that was poisoned, and died.
The crown prince, Zhǐ, blamed himself for not having tasted the medicine,
and did not assume the throne.
Together with his brother Wěi,
he devoted himself to weeping,
consuming only congee,
unable to swallow a single grain,
grieving over his failure to taste the medicine,
and died within the year.
Therefore, the Spring and Autumn Annals considered him righteous.
Duke Xuān of Wèi had sons: Jí, Shòu, and Shuò.
Jí
was the son of the former wife;
Shòu and Shuò
were sons of the later wife.
Shòu's mother
conspired with Shuò
to kill Crown Prince Jí and establish Shòu instead.
They sent men to make Jí board a boat on the river,
intending to sink and kill him.
Shòu learned of this,
but could not prevent it,
so he boarded the same boat with him,
making the boatmen unable to kill Jí.
While they were boarding the boat,
Jí's governess, fearing his death,
grieved and composed a poem—
this is the poem "Two Men Board a Boat."
The poem says:
"Two men board a boat,
its shadow floats afar;
longing, I think of you,
my heart is full of care."
Then,
Shòu, grieving that his elder brother was about to be harmed,
composed a poem of sorrow—
this is the poem "The Millet Lush."
The poem says:
"I walk with faltering steps,
my heart is deeply troubled.
Those who know me
say my heart is grieved;
those who do not know me
ask what I seek.
Vast, distant heaven,
who has brought this about!"
They again sent Jí to Qí,
instructing bandits to look for the carriage with streamers
and intercept and kill him.
Shòu tried to stop Jí,
but Jí said:
"To abandon my father's command
is not the way of a son;
it cannot be done."
Shòu then went with him.
Shòu's mother, knowing she could not stop him,
thus warned him:
"Shòu, do not go ahead."
But Shòu went ahead anyway,
secretly taking Jí's streamers and proceeding first.
When he was nearly at Qí,
the bandits saw and killed him.
When Jí arrived,
seeing Shòu dead,
he grieved that Shòu had died in his place,
wept in sorrow,
then carried his body,
returned to the border, and took his own life.
Thus, both brothers died.
Therefore, the nobleman honors these two men,
and laments Duke Xuān's heeding of slander.
Duke Xuān of Lǔ
was the younger brother of Duke Wén of Lǔ.
When Duke Wén passed away,
his son Zǐ Chì was established as the Marquis of Lǔ.
Duke Xuān killed Zǐ Chì and seized the state,
becoming the Marquis of Lǔ.
Gōngzǐ Xī,
Duke Xuān's full brother,
condemned Duke Xuān for killing Zǐ Chì.
When Duke Xuān offered him a salary,
he said:
"I have enough;
why should I take my elder brother's food?"
He made a living by weaving sandals,
never eating Duke Xuān's provisions for life.
His benevolence and kindness were profound,
his integrity steadfast.
Thus, the Spring and Autumn Annals praises and honors him.
When the Crown Prince of Duke Xiàn of Jìn went to the Spirit Tower,
a snake coiled around the left wheel of his carriage.
The driver said:
"Your Highness, bow in reverence.
I have heard that for the son of a ruler,
a snake coiling around the left wheel means he will quickly gain the state."
The Crown Prince did not proceed,
but returned to his residence.
The driver went to see the Crown Prince,
who said:
"I have heard that as a son,
one should be entirely harmonious and obedient to the ruler,
not act on selfish desires;
reverently and solemnly carry out commands,
not oppose the ruler's peace.
Now, if I gain the state,
it would mean the ruler loses his peace.
To see the benefit for the state
and forget the ruler's peace
is not the way of a son;
to hear of gaining the state and bow to an omen,
is not the ruler's wish.
To abandon the way of a son is unfilial;
to oppose the ruler's wish is disloyal.
For you to make me do this
seems intended to endanger our state—
this is clear."
He drew his sword to take his life.
The driver stopped him, saying:
"Auspicious signs and ominous portents
are the way of heaven;
reverently carrying out commands
is human conduct.
To bow to auspicious signs and guard against omens
is ritual propriety;
solemnly carrying out commands,
not letting personal resentment affect the ruler,
is filial piety.
Now, Your Highness sees a blessing but does not bow,
losing propriety;
killing yourself and resenting the ruler,
losing filial piety.
Following a perverse heart,
abandoning righteous conduct—
this is not what I have heard is proper."
The Crown Prince said:
"Not so!
My gaining the state
would be the ruler's misfortune;
to bow to the ruler's misfortune
cannot be called propriety.
To see an auspicious sign and forget the ruler's peace
makes one a traitor to the state;
to serve the ruler with a traitorous heart
cannot be called filial.
Holding deceitful intentions to rule the world,
harboring a traitorous heart to serve the ruler—
this is the gravest evil.
For you to make me do this
is clearly intended to endanger the state."
He then fell on his sword and died.
The nobleman said:
"The Crown Prince of Jìn,
merely because his driver urged him to bow to the snake omen,
so detested it that he went to the point of suicide,
for he was suspected of desiring the state.
That he himself did not desire the state, to keep the ruler secure,
was thus made clear.
Due to a foolish driver's mistaken words,
he came to lose his life.
Abandoning the way of a son,
cutting off the sacrifices—
this cannot be called filial,
but he can be said to be a scholar who avoided suspicion and maintained integrity."
Shēn Bāoxū was
a man of the State of Chǔ.
When Wú defeated the Chǔ army at Bǎijǔ,
they advanced into Yǐng,
and King Zhāo fled to Suí.
Shēn Bāoxū, without receiving orders, went to Qín to plead for troops,
saying:
"Wú acts without principle,
behaving like a giant boar or long serpent,
devouring the world like a silkworm,
starting with the great states,
and beginning with Chǔ.
My lord has lost his altars of soil and grain,
and is stranded in the wilderness,
sending your humble servant to report the emergency, saying:
'Wú
is a land of barbarians.
The demands of barbarians are insatiable—
if they destroy Chǔ, they will then share a border with you to the west.
If they become your neighbors,
it will be a calamity for your borders.
While Wú is not yet settled,
may you, my lord, consider this.
If by your divine power,
you can preserve and comfort the State of Chǔ,
we will serve you for generations.'"
The Earl of Qín sent a message declining,
saying:
"My lord has heard your request.
You should go to the guesthouse,
and we will deliberate and inform you."
Shēn Bāoxū replied:
"My lord is stranded in the wilderness,
with no place to rest—
how dare I, your humble servant, seek comfort?"
Leaning against the courtyard wall, he stood weeping,
his cries unceasing day and night,
without taking even water or gruel,
for seven days and seven nights.
Duke Āi of Qín then recited the poem 'No Clothes,'
indicating that troops would now be dispatched.
Bāoxū bowed nine times with his head to the ground and sat.
Duke Āi of Qín said:
"If Chǔ has a minister like this and still perishes,
then if I have no minister like this,
my own downfall is not far off."
Thereupon,
he sent out troops to rescue Chǔ.
Shēn Bāoxū arrived in Chǔ with the Qín army,
led by Qín grand masters Zǐmǎn and Zǐhǔ with five hundred chariots.
Zǐmǎn said:
"I do not yet know Wú's tactics."
He had the Chǔ people first engage the Wú forces and then joined the battle,
decisively defeating the Wú army.
After the Wú army retreated,
King Zhāo restored the state,
and the rewards began with Bāoxū.
Bāoxū said:
"To assist the ruler and secure the state
is not for personal gain;
to rescue from crisis and eliminate harm
is not for fame;
to accept rewards after achieving success
is to sell one's courage.
Since the ruler is now settled,
what more could I seek?"
He then fled from the reward,
and was never seen again for the rest of his life.
The gentleman says:
"Shēnzǐ's going to Qín without orders was
an act of loyalty;
his seven days and seven nights of unceasing cries
showed profound dedication;
his refusal of reward
demonstrated humility.
However, rewards are meant to encourage goodness,
and declining them is not the constant rule."
Cuī Zhù of Qí
was the chancellor of Qí.
He assassinated Duke Zhuāng
and ordered the Grand Historian not to record the ruler's assassination and the perpetrator.
The Grand Historian refused to comply,
and thus wrote of the perpetrator:
"Cuī Zhù assassinated his ruler."
Cuīzǐ killed him;
his younger brother then continued the record,
and Cuīzǐ killed him too,
so two men died.
When another younger brother again continued to record it,
he then spared him.
Nánshǐshì,
of the same clan,
heard that the Grand Historians had all died,
took his bamboo slips and went,
intending to continue the record,
but upon hearing it had already been written,
he returned.
The gentleman says:
"They were the excellent historians of antiquity."
When Qí attacked Lǔ,
they demanded the Céndǐng tripod.
The ruler of Lǔ sent the Céndǐng,
but the Marquis of Qí disbelieved it and returned it,
thinking it was not genuine.
He sent a message to the ruler of Lǔ:
"If Liǔxià Huì confirms it is genuine,
then we will accept it."
The ruler of Lǔ requested Liǔxià Huì's help,
and Liǔxià Huì replied:
"Your wish to present it as the Céndǐng
is to save the state.
But I too have a 'state' here—
to destroy my 'state'
in order to save your state
is something I find difficult."
The ruler of Lǔ then sent the genuine Céndǐng.
Liǔxià Huì can be said to have upheld trustworthiness,
not only preserving his own 'state'
but also saving the ruler's state.
Trustworthiness in a person
is of great importance,
like the crossbar and yoke of a carriage.
Therefore, Confucius said:
"A large carriage without a crossbar,
a small carriage without a yoke—
how can they be driven?"
This refers to such a case.
A man of Sòng obtained a piece of jade
and presented it to Minister of Works Zǐhǎn,
but Zǐhǎn declined it.
The jade presenter said:
"I showed it to a jade expert,
who deemed it a treasure,
so I dared to offer it."
Zǐhǎn said:
"I treasure non-greed as my jewel,
while you treasure jade as yours.
If you give it to me,
we would both lose our treasures—
it is better for each to keep his own treasure."
Thus, the elders of Sòng said:
"Zǐhǎn did not lack treasures;
what he treasured was different.
If you show a child a hundred pieces of gold and a ball of millet,
the child will surely take the millet;
if you show a rustic the Héshì Jade and a hundred pieces of gold,
the rustic will surely take the gold;
if you show a wise person the Héshì Jade and the ultimate words of morality,
the wise person will surely take the ultimate words.
The more refined one's understanding,
the more refined one's choice;
the cruder one's understanding,
the cruder one's choice.
What Zǐhǎn treasured was the ultimate."
Once, someone offered fish to the Prime Minister of Zhèng,
but the Prime Minister declined it.
Someone asked the Prime Minister:
"You are fond of fish—
why did you not accept it?"
He replied:
"It is because I am fond of fish
that I did not accept the fish.
If I accept fish, I will lose my salary,
and have no means to buy fish;
by not accepting it, I keep my salary,
and can eat fish for life."
Yuán Xiàn lived in Lǔ,
in a house surrounded by walls,
thatched with fresh mugwort,
had a door of brushwood and a window like a jar mouth,
with twisted mulberry branches as the pivot,
leaking from above and damp below,
yet he sat upright playing the zither and singing.
Zǐ Gòng heard of this,
rode a well-fed horse,
wore light furs,
with dark red underneath and plain white outside,
his carriage too large for the alley,
and went to see Yuán Xiàn.
Yuán Xiàn, wearing a mulberry leaf hat and leaning on a goosefoot staff, came to answer the door,
when he straightened his hat, the strings broke,
when he adjusted his lapel, his elbows showed through,
and when he put on his shoes, the heels split open.
Zǐ Gòng said:
"Alas!
What ailment afflicts you, sir?"
Yuán Xiàn looked up and replied:
"I have heard that
lacking wealth is called poverty,
but learning without being able to practice it is called an ailment.
I,
am poor,
not ailing.
As for those who act to please the world,
associate with cliques,
study for the sake of others' approval,
teach for their own gain,
pervert benevolence and righteousness,
and adorn themselves with carriages and horses—
these are things I cannot bear to do."
Zǐ Gòng hesitated,
his face showing shame,
and left without saying goodbye.
Yuán Xiàn dragged his staff and shoes,
singing the "Odes of Shāng" as he returned,
his voice filling heaven and earth,
as if emanating from metal and stone.
The Son of Heaven could not make him a minister,
nor could the feudal lords make him a friend.
Thus, those who nurture their will forget their bodies,
and if they do not even love their bodies,
who can burden them?
The Book of Songs says:
"My heart is not a stone,
it cannot be rolled away;
my heart is not a mat,
it cannot be rolled up."
This describes it well.
Yànzǐ went to Jìn,
and saw a man wearing a fur coat and carrying straw, resting by the roadside,
whom he considered a gentleman,
so he sent someone to ask him,
saying:
"Why have you come to this?"
The man replied:
"I was imprisoned by the people of Qí,
my name is Yuè Shífǔ."
Yànzǐ said:
"Alas!"
Immediately, he untied the left trace horse to ransom him,
took him along on the carriage back,
upon reaching his residence,
entered without a word.
Yuè Shífǔ became angry and requested to sever ties.
Yànzǐ sent someone to reply:
"I have never had the chance to befriend you,
now that I've rescued you from distress,
is my treatment of you still unacceptable?"
Yuè Shífǔ said:
"I have heard that a gentleman may be misunderstood by those who do not know him,
but should be trusted by those who do;
that is why I request to sever ties."
Yànzǐ then came out to see him, saying:
"Earlier, I saw your appearance,
but now I see your intent.
I have heard that those who examine reality do not dwell on appearances,
and those who observe actions do not scrutinize words.
May I apologize and not be rejected?"
Yuè Shífǔ said:
"Since you, sir, treat me with courtesy,
how dare I not respectfully comply!"
Yànzǐ then regarded him as a distinguished guest.
Common people, when they achieve something, feel entitled,
and entitlement leads to arrogance.
Yànzǐ had achieved something,
rescuing a man from hardship,
yet instead humbled himself beneath him,
showing how far he was from being common;
this is the way to preserve one's accomplishments.
Zǐ Lièzǐ was impoverished,
his face showing signs of hunger.
A guest spoke to Zhèng Zǐyáng, saying:
"Zǐ Lièzǐ Yùkòu
is likely a man of the Way.
Living in your state and yet impoverished,
does it not reflect poorly on your regard for scholars?"
Zǐyáng ordered an official to send him several tens of carts of grain.
Zǐ Lièzǐ came out to meet the messenger,
bowed twice and declined.
After the messenger left,
Zǐ Lièzǐ went inside,
his wife, looking at him and beating her breast, said:
"I've heard that the wives and children of those who follow the Way enjoy ease and pleasure.
Now, your wife and children show signs of hunger;
the ruler, recognizing his error, sends you grain,
yet you decline it—
is this not fate?"
Zǐ Lièzǐ smiled and said to her:
"The ruler does not know me himself;
he learned of me through others' words,
and through others' words, he sends me grain.
If he were to condemn me,
it would also be based on others' words;
that is why I do not accept it.
Moreover, to accept another's support
and not die for them in their calamity
is unrighteous;
but to die for their calamity
would be to die for an unprincipled man—
is that righteous?"
Later,
the people indeed rebelled,
and killed Zǐyáng.
Zǐ Lièzǐ's foresight in avoiding unrighteousness was profound.
Even when suffering from hunger and cold within,
he still would not take anything improperly,
considering righteousness upon gain,
and harm upon seeing profit—
how much more so when in wealth and honor?
Thus, Zǐ Lièzǐ understood the nature of life and destiny,
and can be said to have upheld integrity.
Qū Yuán, named Píng,
was a senior official from the same clan as the King of Chǔ,
possessed broad and profound knowledge,
and maintained a pure and upright conduct.
King Huái employed him.
Qín intended to annex the feudal lords,
and unite all under heaven.
Qū Yuán was sent east by Chǔ as an envoy to Qí,
to form a strong alliance.
The state of Qín was troubled by this,
and sent Zhāng Yí to Chǔ,
bribing Chǔ's influential ministers such as Senior Grand Master Shàngguān and Jìn Shàng,
up to the Prime Minister Zǐ Lán and Minister of War Zǐ Jiāo,
and internally bribing the Lady Zhèng Xiù,
to collectively slander Qū Yuán.
Qū Yuán was then exiled abroad,
and composed the "Lí Sāo."
Zhāng Yí thus induced Chǔ to sever relations with Qí,
promising to cede six hundred lǐ of land.
King Huái trusted the treacherous schemes of his attendants,
listened to Zhāng Yí's deceitful words,
and thus severed ties with the great support of powerful Qí.
After Chǔ had cut off relations with Qí,
Qín deceived them with only six lǐ.
King Huái was greatly enraged,
raised troops to attack Qín,
engaged in several major battles,
where Qín's forces heavily defeated Chǔ's army,
decapitating tens of thousands.
Qín sent someone offering to apologize to King Huái with the land of Hànzhōng,
but he did not accept,
wishing only to capture Zhāng Yí to satisfy his resolve.
Zhāng Yí said:
"To exchange one Yí for the land of Hànzhōng,
why spare Yí?"
He requested to go,
and thus arrived in Chǔ,
where Chǔ imprisoned him.
Senior Grand Master and his associates jointly spoke to the king on his behalf,
and the king released him.
At this time,
King Huái regretted not having followed Qū Yuán's strategies,
which led to this situation.
Thereupon,
he reinstated Qū Yuán.
Qū Yuán was sent to Qí,
and upon returning, heard that Zhāng Yí had already left;
he vehemently spoke to the king about Zhāng Yí's crimes,
but King Huái sent men to pursue him and failed to catch up.
Later, Qín married a daughter to Chǔ,
and delighted King Huái,
holding a meeting at Lántián.
Qū Yuán believed that Qín could not be trusted,
and advised against attending the meeting,
but all the ministers thought it permissible.
King Huái thus attended,
and was indeed imprisoned,
dying abroad in Qín,
becoming a laughingstock to all under heaven.
King Huái's son, King Qǐng Xiāng, also knew that the ministers had flattered and misled King Huái,
but instead of investigating their crimes,
he listened to the mouths of slanderers,
and again exiled Qū Yuán.
Qū Yuán detested the benighted king and corrupted customs,
the muddled and silent compliance,
taking right for wrong,
and purity for filth.
Unable to bear living in such a world,
he decided to throw himself into the deep.
A fisherman tried to stop him,
but Qū Yuán said:
"The world is all drunk,
I alone am sober;
the world is all turbid,
I alone am clear.
I have heard it said,
those who have newly bathed must shake out their clothes,
those who have newly washed their hair must dust their hats.
How can one, being pure and clean, serve those who are muddled and silent?
I would rather throw myself into the deep and die."
Thereupon, he threw himself into the Mìluó River of the Xiāng waters and died.
King Zhāo of Chǔ had a scholar named Shí Shē,
whose character
was just and fond of righteousness.
The king appointed him as chief judge.
At that time,
there was a murderer in the court,
Shí Shē pursued him,
and it turned out to be his father.
He then returned to the court,
and said:
"The murderer
is my father.
To use my father to establish governance
is unfilial;
to not enforce the ruler's laws
is disloyal.
To release a criminal and abandon the law,
and yet bear the guilt,
is what I uphold.
I prostrate before the execution block,
my fate lies with the lord."
The lord said:
"You pursued but did not catch up,
how could that be a crime?
Attend to your duties!"
Shí Shē said:
"Not to show partiality to one's father
is unfilial;
to not enforce the ruler's laws
is disloyal;
to let a capital offender live
is unjust.
If the lord pardons me,
it is his grace;
but I dare not fail the law,
it is my duty as a subject."
Thus, he did not leave the execution block,
but cut his throat and died in the court.
The gentleman, hearing of this, said:
"How steadfast in law!"
Confucius said:
"A son conceals for his father,
a father conceals for his son,
uprightness lies within this!"
The "Book of Songs" says:
"That man,
is the upholder of rectitude in the state."
This refers to Shí Zǐ.
When Duke Wén of Jìn returned to his state,
Lǐ Lí served as the chief justice.
Having mistakenly executed an innocent person,
he bound himself and declared:
"My crime deserves death."
Duke Wén commanded him:
"Officials have ranks of high and low,
punishments vary in severity.
This is the fault of your subordinate officials,
not your error."
Lǐ Lí responded:
"I hold the highest position in this office,
yet I do not yield my post to subordinates;
I receive the largest salary,
yet I do not share the benefits with those below me.
Having misheard and killed an innocent,
to shift blame to subordinates while fearing death myself -
this is unjust.
My crime truly deserves death."
Duke Wén said:
"If you insist you are guilty,
then I too must bear some fault."
Lǐ Lí replied:
"You measured abilities to assign offices,
I received my duty to handle affairs.
On the day I received the official seal,
you commanded me:
'You must assist governance with benevolence and righteousness,
preferring error in sparing life
over mistake in killing.'
I have failed in my appointed task,
obstructing your kindness and grace.
For such crime as mine,
death is deserved -
how could you be at fault?
Moreover, justice follows laws:
erring in sparing life means sparing,
but erring in killing means dying.
You considered me capable of discerning subtleties and deciding doubtful cases,
hence entrusted me with justice.
Now I, Lí, have been harsh without regard for benevolence and righteousness,
trusting only written records,
without investigating right and wrong;
hearing others' words,
without examining facts thoroughly,
extorting confession from the innocent,
causing the common people to resent.
When the world hears of this,
they will criticize my lord;
when the feudal lords hear of it,
they will despise our state.
Resentment accumulates among the people,
evil reputation spreads throughout the world,
authority diminishes before the feudal lords.
For crime such as mine,
double death would be fitting."
Duke Wén said:
"I have heard that
one who is straight but unbending
cannot go far;
square but not round
cannot long endure.
I wish you would heed me in this."
Lǐ Lí replied:
"For you to harm public law with private favor,
sparing one who deserves death while having killed the innocent -
neither action serves to educate the state.
I dare not accept your command."
Duke Wén said:
"Have you not heard of Guǎn Zhòng as minister?
Though his person suffered disgrace, his lord prospered;
though his conduct was stained, hegemony was achieved."
Lǐ Lí responded:
"I lack Guǎn Zhòng's worthiness,
yet bear the name of disgrace and stain;
without the achievement of hegemon or king,
yet burdened with the weight of mistaken judgment.
To oversee office without capability,
governing people through stained means -
even if you cannot bear to apply the law to me,
I dare not defile office and disrupt governance to preserve my life.
I have heard your command."
Thereupon he fell on his sword and died.
When Duke Wén of Jìn returned to his state,
he feasted his officials with wine,
summoned Jiù Fàn to make him general,
summoned Wěi Líng to make him chancellor,
granting them million-acre fields.
Jiè Zǐtuī received no rank,
yet took his place according to age.
After three rounds of drinking,
Jiè Zǐtuī raised his cup and stood saying:
"There was a majestic dragon
about to lose its place;
a snake followed it,
wandering throughout the world.
The dragon has entered the deep abyss,
gaining its peaceful place;
the snake's fat has dried completely,
alone without sweet rain.
What does this mean?"
Duke Wén said:
"Alas!
This is my fault.
I shall grant you rank for tomorrow's court;
I shall grant you land between Hédōng and Yáng."
Jiè Zǐtuī replied:
"I have heard that in the way of gentlemen,
positions obtained through solicitation
are not occupied by men of principle;
wealth obtained through contention
is not accepted by upright men."
Duke Wén said:
"You were the one who enabled my return to the state,
I wish to establish your reputation."
Jiè Zǐtuī responded:
"I have heard that in the way of gentlemen,
a son who cannot inherit his father's legacy
dare not assume his succession;
a minister unrecognized by his lord
dare not stand in his court.
Thus I seek nothing from the world."
Thereupon he left and went atop Jiè Mountain.
Duke Wén sent people to search for him but couldn't find him,
abstained from his bedchamber for three months,
calling his name for a full year.
The Book of Songs says:
"I will leave you,
go to those happy borders;
go to those happy borders,
who will there long lament!"
This describes it.
Duke Wén waited but he wouldn't come out,
searched but couldn't find him,
thought burning the mountain might make him emerge.
When they burned the mountain,
he still didn't emerge but was burned to death.
Shēntú Dí, disapproving of his era,
was about to throw himself into the river.
Cuī Jiā heard and stopped him, saying:
"I have heard that sage and benevolent men in heaven and earth
act as parents to the people.
Now for fear of wetting your feet,
you won't save drowning people -
is this acceptable?"
Shēntú Dí replied:
"Not so!
Previously, Jié executed Guān Lóngpáng,
Zhòu executed Prince Bǐgān and lost the empire;
Wú executed Zǐxū,
Chén executed Xiè Yě and destroyed their state.
Thus states lost and families ruined
occur not from lack of sages and wise men,
but from not using them."
Thereupon he carried stones and sank into the river.
The gentleman heard of this and said:
"How upright!
As for benevolence and wisdom,
I have not seen them.
The Book of Songs says:
'Heaven indeed ordains it,
what can be said?'
This describes it."
There was great famine in Qí.
Qián Áo prepared food by the roadside,
waiting to feed the starving.
A starving man came, covering his face with sleeves, dragging his shoes,
stumbling along dazedly.
drink in his right, saying:
"Hey!
Come eat!"
The starving man raised his eyes and looked at him:
"I precisely because I won't eat 'hey-come-eat' food
have reached this state!"
Thereupon Qián Áo apologized to him.
But he ultimately didn't eat and died.
Zēngzǐ heard of this and said:
"Was this not excessive?
When called 'hey' one may leave,
but when apologized to, one may eat."
In the east there was a scholar named Yuán Zúmù,
who, while journeying to a destination, grew hungry on the road.
A robber from Húfǔ named Qiū
saw him,
descended and offered his pot of food to him.
After three mouthfuls, Yuán Zúmù regained his sight,
looked up and asked:
"Who are you?"
The reply was:
"I am the robber from Húfǔ named Qiū."
Yuán Zúmù said:
"Alas!
You are a robber!
Why do you feed me?
I will not eat it."
He pressed both hands on the ground and vomited,
but nothing came out,
gagging and choking,
until he collapsed on the ground and died.
The county named Shèngmǔ,
Zēngzǐ would not enter;
the city called Zhāogē,
Mòzǐ turned his carriage around.
Thus, Confucius would not sit unless the mat was straight,
would not eat unless the cut was proper,
and would not drink the water of Dàoquán spring—
this is the accumulation of righteousness;
Zúmù refused to eat and died—
this is the purity of righteousness.
Bào Jiāo, with worn-out clothes revealing his skin,
was carrying a basket of vegetables,
when he met Zǐgòng on the road.
Zǐgòng said:
"Why has my lord come to this state?"
Bào Jiāo replied:
"There are many in the world who abandon virtue and teaching—
why should I not have come to this!
I have heard that
to persist in action when the age does not recognize one—
this is corrupt conduct;
to persist in seeking office when the ruler does not recognize one—
this is to destroy integrity.
With corrupt conduct and destroyed integrity,
yet still not giving up—
this is delusion for profit."
Zǐgòng said:
"I have heard that
one who does not approve of the age
should not enjoy its benefits;
one who defames his ruler
should not tread his land.
Now you, my lord, defame your ruler yet tread his land,
disapprove of the age yet carry its vegetables—
whose fault is this then?"
Bào Jiāo said:
"Alas!
I have heard that the worthy value advancement but disdain retreat,
the upright find shame easy but death light."
Thereupon, he abandoned his vegetables and stood,
until he withered and died by the Luò River.
The gentleman, hearing of this, said:
"How unbending was this upright man!
For if mountains are sharp, they are not high;
if waters are narrow, they are not deep;
one whose conduct is extreme lacks generous virtue;
one whose will rivals heaven and earth—
such a person is inauspicious.
Master Bào can be called inauspicious indeed!
His measure of depth and shallowness
reached its limit and stopped there.
The Book of Songs says:
'Let it be so!
Heaven has truly ordained it—
what is there to say!'"
Gōngsūn Chǔjiù and Chéng Yīng were
retainers of Zhào Shuò, a senior official of Jìn.
When Zhào Chuān of Jìn assassinated Lord Líng,
Zhào Dùn, then a high-ranking minister,
fled without leaving the border,
and upon returning did not punish the assassin,
so the Spring and Autumn Annals held him accountable,
considering Dùn the regicide.
Tú'àn Gǔ,
who had been favored by Lord Líng;
during the reign of Lord Jǐng of Jìn,
Gǔ became the Minister of Justice,
and sought to punish Lord Líng's assassin.
Dùn had already died,
so he aimed to execute Dùn's son Shuò,
announcing to all the generals:
"Although Dùn did not know of the plot,
he was still the chief culprit.
A treacherous minister assassinated the lord,
yet his descendants remain at court—
how can this punish the crime?
I request their execution."
Hán Jué said:
"When Lord Líng was murdered,
Zhào Dùn was abroad;
our former lord deemed him innocent,
hence he was not punished.
Now you all intend to execute arbitrarily.
Arbitrary execution
is called the act of rebellious ministers.
For such major affairs,
if the lord is not informed,
it shows disregard for the lord."
Tú'àn Gǔ did not listen,
so Hán Jué urged Zhào Shuò to flee quickly.
Zhào Shuò refused,
saying:
"If you ensure the Zhào lineage continues,
I will die without regret."
Hán Jué promised,
and feigned illness, staying home.
Gǔ, without seeking permission,擅自 joined the generals in attacking the Zhào family at Xiàgōng,
killing Zhào Shuò, Zhào Tóng, Zhào Kuò, and Zhào Yīngqí,
exterminating their entire clan.
Zhào Shuò's wife,
sister of Lord Chéng,
was pregnant,
and fled to the lord's palace to hide.
Gōngsūn Chǔjiù said to Chéng Yīng:
"Why not die?"
Yīng replied:
"Shuò's wife is with child;
if by luck it's a boy,
I will serve him.
If it's a girl,
then I will die slowly."
Not long after,
Shuò's wife gave birth,
to a boy.
Tú'àn Gǔ heard of it,
searched the palace,
Shuò's wife placed the child in her trousers,
praying:
"If the Zhào line is to perish,
you cry;
if not to perish,
you stay silent."
When they searched for the child,
it made no sound.
Once safe,
Chéng Yīng said to Chǔjiù:
"Now one search failed,
they will surely search again later,
what to do?"
Chǔjiù said:
"Which is harder: raising the orphan or dying?"
Yīng said:
"Raising the orphan is harder."
Chǔjiù said:
"The Zhào ancestors treated you well,
you take the harder task,
I'll take the easier one,
I ask to die first."
So the two plotted,
took another baby,
wrapped it in ornate swaddling,
and hid in the mountains.
Yīng told the generals:
"I am unworthy,
unable to raise the orphan.
Who will give me a thousand pieces of gold,
I'll reveal where the Zhào orphan is."
The generals were pleased,
agreed,
sent troops with Yīng to attack Chǔjiù.
Chǔjiù said:
"Petty man, Chéng Yīng!
During the Xiàgōng disaster,
you couldn't die,
plotted with me to hide the Zhào orphan,
now you sell him out.
Even if you can't raise the orphan,
how can you bear to sell him?"
Holding the child, he cried out:
"Heaven!
What crime has the Zhào orphan committed?
Spare him,
kill only Chǔjiù."
The generals refused,
and killed both Chǔjiù and the child.
The generals thought the Zhào orphan was dead,
and rejoiced.
But the true Zhào orphan survived,
Chéng Yīng eventually hid with him in the mountains.
Fifteen years later,
Lord Jǐng of Jìn fell ill,
divined:
the descendant of Dà Yè was causing the haunt.
Lord Jǐng asked Hán Jué,
who knew the Zhào orphan lived,
and said:
"The lineage of Dà Yè,
in Jìn, whose line was cut off,
must be the Zhào family?
From Zhōngháng Yǎn on,
all were of the Yíng surname.
Zhōngháng Yǎn,
with a human face and bird's beak,
descended to assist Emperor Dà Wù and the Zhou Son of Heaven,
all possessing bright virtue,
down to the tyrannical Yōu and Lì,
when Shū Dài left Zhōu for Jìn,
served from Lord Móu to Lord Chéng,
each generation achieving merit,
never ceasing sacrifices.
Now in your reign,
only the Zhào line is extinguished.
The people mourn them,
hence it appears in the turtle and stalk divination,
I beg you to consider this."
Lord Jǐng asked:
"Does Zhào still have descendants?"
Hán Jué fully informed him,
so Lord Jǐng plotted with Hán Jué to install the Zhào orphan,
summoning him to hide in the palace.
When the generals came to inquire about his illness,
Lord Jǐng used Hán Jué's men to pressure them and presented the Zhào orphan.
The orphan was named Wǔ.
The generals had no choice,
and said:
"The former Xiàgōng disaster,
was Tú'àn Gǔ's doing,
forging your command,
and ordering the ministers.
Otherwise,
who would dare cause trouble?
If not for your illness,
we would have requested to reestablish Zhào's heir.
Now you command,
we are willing."
Thereupon,
they summoned the Zhào orphan and Chéng Yīng,
who bowed to all the generals.
Then together with Chéng Yīng and the Zhào orphan, they attacked Tú'àn Gǔ,
exterminating his clan,
and restored Zhào's lands and cities as before.
When Zhào Wǔ came of age,
and became an adult,
Chéng Yīng declined official rank,
and said to Zhào Wǔ:
"During the Xiàgōng disaster,
all could have died;
I did not die,
thinking to establish Zhào's heir.
Now you are installed,
an adult,
the Zhào line restored,
I will go below to report to Zhào Mèng and Gōngsūn Chǔjiù."
Zhào Wǔ wept and pleaded firmly:
"I wish to toil to repay you until death,
how can you bear to abandon me and die?"
Chéng Yīng said:
"No,
they thought I could accomplish the task,
so they died before me;
if I do not report below,
they will think I failed."
Then he killed himself.
Zhào Wǔ observed mourning for three years,
established a sacrificial estate,
offered sacrifices spring and autumn,
unceasing through generations.
The gentleman says:
"Chéng Yīng and Gōngsūn Chǔjiù can be called faithful and profound friends!
But Yīng's suicide to report below,
was excessive!"
Cuī Zhù assassinated Duke Zhuāng,
ordering the officials and nobles to swear an oath,
all had to remove their swords before entering.
Those who spoke not swiftly,
or whose fingers did not reach the blood would die,
and ten people were killed.
When it came to Yàn Zǐ's turn,
he held the cup of blood, looked up to the sky, and sighed:
"Alas, Cuī Zǐ,
you are about to commit an unrighteous act,
killing your sovereign!"
All the oath-takers looked at him.
Cuī Zhù said to Yàn Zǐ:
"If you side with me,
I will share the state with you;
if you do not side with me,
I will kill you,
with straight blades thrust at you,
and curved hooks pulling you.
Consider it carefully."
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"Yīng has heard that to turn one's back on one's sovereign for profit
is not benevolence;
to lose one's resolve under threat of blades
is not courage.
The Book of Songs says:
'The mild and courteous gentleman,
seeks blessings without turning away.'
Yīng can be said not to turn away.
Thrust straight blades at me,
hook me with curved ones,
Yīng will not turn away."
Cuī Zǐ spared him.
Yàn Zǐ hurried out,
took the carriage strap and hung down,
his driver was about to gallop away.
Yàn Zǐ patted his hand and said:
"Tigers and leopards in the mountains and forests,
their fate lies in the kitchen;
galloping won't increase life,
slowing won't hasten death."
He proceeded with composed steps,
and then departed.
The Book of Songs says:
"That man,
does not change even at the cost of his life."
This refers to Yàn Zǐ.
Bì Xī rebelled with Zhōngmóu,
set a cauldron in the courtyard,
and addressed the officials and nobles:
"Those who side with me will receive fiefs,
those who do not side with me will be boiled!"
All the nobles followed him,
until it came to Tián Bēi,
who said:
"To die for righteousness does not avoid the crime of axe and halberd;
to be impoverished for righteousness does not accept the carriage and crown.
To live without righteousness,
to be wealthy without benevolence,
is worse than being boiled!"
He lifted his garment and approached the cauldron,
Bì Xī took off his shoes and spared him.
The Zhào clan heard of his rebellion,
attacked and captured it.
Hearing that Tián Bēi refused to join,
they sought to reward him.
Tián Bēi said:
"It cannot be.
For one person to rise and ten thousand to bow their heads,
the wise do not do;
to reward one person and shame ten thousand,
the righteous do not take.
If I accept the reward,
it will make the scholars of Zhōngmóu feel ashamed,
which is unrighteous."
He declined the reward and went into seclusion,
saying:
"To impose one's conduct on others,
is unjust;
I shall leave!"
Then he went south to Chǔ.
Chǔ Crown Prince Jiàn was exiled due to Fèi Wújí's slander,
Jiàn had a son named Shèng,
who was abroad.
Zǐ Xī summoned Shèng to govern Bái,
and he was titled Lord Bái.
Shèng resented Chǔ for exiling his father,
and planned to assassinate King Huì and Zǐ Xī.
He wanted to win over Yì Jiǎ,
arrayed troops and showed them to Yì Jiǎ, saying:
"Side with me,
and worry not about wealth and honor;
do not side with me,
then this is the consequence!"
Yì Jiǎ laughed and said:
"You once spoke of my righteousness,
have you forgotten, my friend?
To gain the world by standing,
if unrighteous,
I would not take it;
to threaten me with weapons,
if unrighteous,
I would not comply.
Now you plan to kill your sovereign,
and want me to follow you,
which contradicts my former righteousness.
Though you tempt me with profit,
and threaten me with weapons,
I cannot bear to do it.
You exercise your power,
and I shall also clarify my righteousness.
To oppose you with weapons,
is contention;
to respond to you with voice,
is baseness.
I have heard that a scholar establishes righteousness without contention,
and faces death without baseness."
He folded his hands and awaited the weapons,
his expression unchanged.
Lord Bái Shèng was about to assassinate King Huì of Chǔ,
the king fled,
the Prime Minister and Minister of War both died,
Shèng drew his sword and pressed Qū Lú, saying:
"If you side with me,
I will spare you;
if you do not side with me,
I will surely kill you."
Lú said:
"You kill your uncle and seek fortune from Lú,
is that possible?
I have heard that a man who knows fate
does not waver at profit,
nor fear in the face of death.
As a subject,
one lives when it is time to live,
dies when it is time to die,
this is called the ritual of a subject.
Thus, knowing the Mandate of Heaven above,
and the way of a subject below,
how can he be coerced!
Why don't you sheathe your sword?"
Bái Gōng Shèng then put away his sword.
After Bái Gōng Shèng killed the Prime Minister and Minister of War,
he wanted to establish Prince Lǘ as king,
but Prince Lǘ refused.
Threatened with a blade,
Prince Lǘ said:
"To assist the state of Chǔ as a royal descendant,
and rectify the royal house,
then protect myself,
is Lǘ's wish.
Now you use force to brutalize the royal house,
and kill to disrupt the state.
Even if I die,
I will not follow you."
Bái Gōng Shèng said:
"The weight of the state of Chǔ,
is unmatched under heaven,
Heaven gives it to you,
why do you not accept?"
Prince Lǘ replied:
"I have heard that one who declines the world
does not轻视 its benefits,
but to manifest his virtue;
one who does not become a feudal lord
does not despise the position,
but to purify his conduct.
Now, to see the state and forget the sovereign,
is not benevolent;
to lose righteousness under threat of blades,
is not courageous.
Though you tempt me with profit,
and threaten me with weapons,
I will not do it."
Bái Gōng forced him,
but he would not yield,
so he killed him.
Yè Gōng Gāo led troops to execute Bái Gōng,
and restored King Huì to the state.
During the rebellion of Lord Bái,
a man from Chǔ named Zhuāng Shàn
bid farewell to his mother,
intending to die for his lord.
His mother said:
"Abandoning one's parents to die for one's lord,
can this be called righteousness?"
Zhuāng Shàn replied:
"I have heard that those who serve a lord
should treat his salary as internal and his person as external.
Now, what I use to support my mother
is the lord's salary,
so how can I not die for him?"
He then bid farewell and departed.
When he reached the lord's gate,
he collapsed three times in the carriage.
His servant said:
"You are afraid!"
He replied:
"I am afraid."
"Since you are afraid,
why not turn back?"
Zhuāng Shàn said:
"Fear
is my private concern;
dying for righteousness,
is my public duty.
I have heard that a gentleman does not let private concerns harm public duty."
Upon reaching the lord's gate,
he cut his throat and died.
The gentleman remarked:
"How he loved righteousness!"
When Cuī Zhù of Qí assassinated Lord Zhuāng,
there was a man named Chén Bùzhàn
who, hearing of his lord's peril,
set out to join him.
As he was leaving,
he dropped his spoon during meals,
and lost his grip on the carriage rail when boarding.
The driver said:
"If you are this timid,
what good will going do?"
Bùzhàn replied:
"Dying for one's lord
is righteousness;
lacking courage
is a private matter.
One should not let private matters harm public duty."
He then proceeded,
but upon hearing the sounds of battle,
he died of terror.
People said:
"Bùzhàn may be said to have had the courage of a benevolent man."
During the time of Zhì Bó Áo,
there was a scholar named Zhǎng'ér Zǐyú
who severed ties with Zhì Bó and left him.
Three years later,
as he was heading east to Yuè,
he heard on the road that Zhì Bó Áo had been killed.
He told his driver:
"Turn the carriage around;
I will die for him."
The driver said:
"You severed ties with Zhì Bó and left him three years ago;
now to return and die for him
shows no distinction in your relationship."
Zhǎng'ér Zǐyú said:
"Not so.
I have heard that the benevolent have no leftover affection,
and loyal ministers no leftover salary.
Hearing of Zhì Bó's death stirred my heart;
the leftover salary he bestowed upon me
still remains with me to this day,
so I will go to fulfill my duty to it."
He returned and died.
Lord Yì of Wèi had a minister named Hóng Yǎn
who was away on a distant mission and had not returned.
The Dí people attacked Wèi,
and its people said:
"Those our lord grants salaries and positions to
are his cranes;
those he enriches
are his palace attendants.
Let the lord send his palace attendants and cranes to fight;
why should we fight?"
They then dispersed and fled.
The Dí pursued and caught Lord Yì at Yíngzé,
killed him,
ate all his flesh,
and only spared his liver.
When Hóng Yǎn arrived,
after reporting on his mission to the liver,
he cried out to heaven and wailed,
expressing his grief fully before stopping.
He said:
"I request to serve as a coffin."
Thereupon, he stabbed his own abdomen,
inserted Lord Yì's liver inside, and died.
Lord Huán of Qí heard of this and said:
"Wèi fell due to its lack of virtue,
but now it has such a minister;
we cannot let it perish."
Thus,
he restored Wèi at Chǔqiū.
There was a man named Yù Yǐn Wén,
a driver of deer and swine in Jīng.
When Sīmǎ Zǐqī was hunting in Yúnmèng,
the flags on his carriage dragged on the ground.
Yù Yǐn Wén drew his sword and cut them level with the carriage bed.
The attendant in the second carriage drew a bow from its case,
took an arrow from the quiver,
and aimed but did not shoot.
Sīmǎ Zǐqī leaned on the carriage rail and asked:
"Have I offended you, sir?"
He replied:
"It is because your flags drag on the ground.
A ruler's flags should be level with the carriage bed,
a senior official's flags level with the rail.
Now you are a renowned senior official of Jīng,
yet you lower them by three grades.
My cutting them
is surely justified!"
Zǐqī was pleased,
and took him to the king.
The king said:
"I heard there is one who cut your flags;
where is this man?
I will have him killed."
Zǐqī reported Wén's words,
and the king was pleased,
appointing Wén as magistrate south of the Yangtze, where he governed excellently.
Biàn Zhuāngzǐ was fond of valor,
but cared for his mother,
and fled three times in battle.
His friends criticized him,
and the ruler shamed him.
After his mother died three years later,
in winter, when fighting against Lǔ,
Biàn Zhuāngzǐ requested to join,
and said to the Lǔ general:
"While my mother was alive,
I fled three times for her sake;
now she has died,
I ask to redeem my duty and let my spirit find rest."
He then charged the enemy,
took one armored head and presented it, saying:
"This redeems one flight."
He charged again,
took another head and said:
"This redeems the second flight."
He charged once more,
took a third head and said:
"This redeems the third flight."
The general said:
"Do not wipe out your family line;
you should stop now,
and let us be as brothers."
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"The three flights were to care for my mother,
which was a son's duty.
Now I have partly fulfilled a soldier's integrity and redeemed my responsibility.
I have heard that
a man of integrity does not live in disgrace."
He then turned back to the enemy,
killed ten men, and died.
The gentleman remarked:
"Redeeming the three flights,
yet ending his lineage and family line—
this is not a complete fulfillment of filial piety."
During the reign of Duke Huán of Qí,
the states of Jiāng and Huáng,
being small states,
were located between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
close to Chǔ.
Chǔ,
a large state,
repeatedly invaded and attacked,
intending to conquer and annex them.
The people of Jiāng and Huáng were troubled by Chǔ,
while Duke Huán of Qí was then engaged in preserving the perishing and restoring the severed,
rescuing the endangered and supporting the falling,
honoring the Zhōu royal house,
and repelling the barbarians.
He convened the meeting at Yánggǔ,
and the covenant at Guànzé,
preparing with the feudal lords to attack Chǔ.
The people of Jiāng and Huáng, admiring Duke Huán's righteousness,
came to join the covenant at Guànzé.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Jiāng
and Huáng are far from Qí and near to Chǔ.
Chǔ is a state that seeks profit.
If we attack and are unable to rescue them,
we will have no means to lead the feudal lords,
so we should not accept them."
Duke Huán did not listen,
and proceeded to form a covenant with them.
After Guǎn Zhòng died,
the people of Chǔ attacked Jiāng and destroyed Huáng,
and Duke Huán could not rescue them,
which the gentlemen pitied.
Thereafter, Duke Huán's credibility was damaged and his virtue declined,
the feudal lords did not submit to him,
and he gradually declined without being able to revive.
Now, the plans of the benevolent and wise
consider the progression of events;
if one's strength cannot save them,
one should not accept their allegiance.
Duke Huán accepted them,
which was a mistake.
Guǎn Zhòng can be said to have been good at planning.
The Book of Songs says:
"If this is not heeded,
the great mandate will topple."
This refers to such a case.
During the time of Duke Wén of Jìn,
King Xiāng of Zhōu faced the trouble of his younger brother, Prince Tàishū,
and fled to live in Zhèng,
unable to return.
He sent messages seeking help to Lǔ, Jìn, and Qín.
The following spring,
the Earl of Qín stationed his troops by the river,
intending to restore the king.
Hú Yǎn said to Duke Wén of Jìn:
"To seek the allegiance of the feudal lords, nothing is better than diligently serving the king,
and moreover, it is a great righteousness,
which the feudal lords will trust.
Continuing the work of Duke Wén,
and gaining trust among the feudal lords,
now is the time to act!"
Bǔ Yǎn performed a divination and said:
"Auspicious!
It encountered the omen of the Yellow Emperor's battle at Bǎnquán."
The Duke said:
"I am not worthy."
He replied:
"The rites of Zhōu have not changed;
the king of today
is the emperor of ancient times."
The Duke said:
"Perform a milfoil divination."
They performed the divination,
and encountered the hexagram Dàyǒu changing to Kuí,
and said:
"Auspicious!
It encountered the hexagram 'the duke is entertained by the son of Heaven,'
victory in battle and the king's feast,
a highly auspicious plan.
Moreover, in this hexagram,
heaven becomes a marsh facing the sun,
the son of Heaven lowers his heart to welcome you,
is that not acceptable?
Dàyǒu departs from Kuí and returns,
which is also its place."
The Marquis of Jìn declined the Qín troops and moved down,
on the day Jiǎchén in the third month,
encamped at Yángfán,
the right army besieged Wēn,
and the left army welcomed the king.
On the day Dīngsì in the summer fourth month,
the king entered the royal city.
They captured Prince Tàishū at Wēn,
and killed him at Xíchéng.
On the day Wǔwǔ,
the Marquis of Jìn attended the king's court,
the king offered sweet wine,
commanded him to assist,
and granted him the lands of Yángfán, Wēn, Yuán, and Cuánmáo,
thus Jìn began to open up the territory of Nányáng.
Three years later,
Duke Wén then again assembled the feudal lords to attend the son of Heaven,
the son of Heaven bestowed upon him bows, arrows, and black millet wine,
appointing him as the regional lord.
Duke Wén of Jìn's mandate was thus,
ultimately achieving hegemony,
due to Hú Yǎn's planning.
Now, both Qín and Lǔ were hesitant,
but Jìn had Hú Yǎn's excellent strategy,
which accomplished the achievement of hegemony.
Thus, when plans are made within the tent,
their achievements extend throughout the world;
this refers to Hú Yǎn.
Yú and Guó
were both small states.
Yú had the strategic barrier of Xiàyáng,
which Yú and Guó jointly defended,
so Jìn could not capture them.
Thus, Duke Xiàn of Jìn wanted to attack Yú and Guó,
and Xún Xī said:
"Why does my lord not use the steeds of Qūchǎn
and the jade disc of Chuíjí
to borrow a path through Yú?"
The Duke said:
"These are the treasures of Jìn.
If they accept our jade
but do not lend us the path,
what then?"
Xún Xī said:
"This is how small states serve large states;
if they do not lend us the path,
they certainly will not dare accept our gifts;
if they accept our gifts and lend us the path,
then it is like we take from the inner treasury
and place it in the outer treasury,
take from the inner stable
and place it in the outer stable."
The Duke said:
"Gōng Zhīqí is there,
he will certainly not allow them to accept."
Xún Xī said:
"Gōng Zhīqí is indeed knowledgeable.
Even so,
his character
is perceptive but timid,
and he grew up with the ruler since youth.
Being perceptive, his words are concise;
being timid, he cannot remonstrate forcefully;
having grown up with the ruler,
the ruler takes him lightly.
Moreover, the delights are before the eyes and ears,
while the disaster lies beyond the state;
only those of average intelligence or above
can consider it,
