and I estimate the ruler of Yú is below average intelligence."
The Duke then borrowed the path to attack Guó,
and Gōng Zhīqí remonstrated, saying:
"The envoy from Jìn,
his gifts are heavy,
his words humble,
it certainly bodes ill for Yú.
As the saying goes:
'When the lips are gone, the teeth feel the cold!'
Thus, Yú and Guó rescue each other,
not as a favor to one another.
Today Guó perishes,
and tomorrow Yú will perish."
The ruler did not listen,
accepted the gifts,
and lent them the path,
then returned.
Four years later,
they turned around and captured Yú.
Xún Xī led the horses and held the jade, coming forward,
saying:
"How was my plan?"
Duke Xiàn said:
"The jade is still the same,
but my horses' teeth have grown longer."
Duke Xiàn of Jìn used Xún Xī's plan and captured Yú.
Yú did not use Gōng Zhīqí's plan and perished.
Thus, Xún Xī was not an assistant for a hegemon or king,
but a minister for the annexation of the Warring States.
As for Gōng Zhīqí,
he can be said to have had the planning of a loyal minister.
Duke Wén of Jìn and Duke Mù of Qín jointly besieged Zhèng,
because it had been disrespectful and allied with Chǔ.
Yì Zhīhú, a senior official of Zhèng, said to the ruler of Zhèng:
"If you send Zhú Zhīwǔ to meet with the ruler of Qín,
the siege will surely be lifted."
The ruler of Zhèng agreed,
summoned Zhú Zhīwǔ and sent him.
He declined, saying:
"In my prime,
I was still not as capable as others;
now that I am old,
I can do nothing."
The ruler of Zhèng said:
"I failed to employ you earlier,
and now in desperation I seek your help—
this is my fault.
However, if Zhèng perishes,
you too will suffer不利."
Zhú Zhīwǔ consented,
went out at night to see the ruler of Qín, and said:
"Qín and Jìn besiege Zhèng,
and Zhèng knows it is doomed.
But if its destruction benefits you,
how dare I trouble your officers?
Zhèng lies east of Jìn,
Qín lies west of Jìn;
to cross Jìn and take Zhèng,
you know how difficult it is.
Why use Zhèng's fall to strengthen Jìn?
Jìn
is your neighbor.
A strong neighbor
is your worry.
If you spare Zhèng to serve as your host in the east,
for envoys coming and going,
supplying their provisions,
it would cause no harm.
Moreover, you helped install the ruler of Jìn,
and he promised you Jiāo and Xiá.
Yet by morning he entered,
and by evening he set up defenses and drew borders—
this you know.
As for Jìn,
what satisfaction does it have?
Having taken Zhèng in the east,
it will seek to expand west;
if not at Qín's expense, where will it take land?
Harming Qín to benefit Jìn—
I hope you will consider this."
The Earl of Qín was pleased,
withdrew his troops and returned.
Jiùfàn of Jìn requested to attack them,
but Duke Wén said:
"No!
Without that man's strength,
we could not have weakened Zhèng.
To use another's strength and then harm them
is unkind;
to lose an ally
is unwise;
to replace order with chaos
is unworthy.
Let us return."
They too left,
and the siege of Zhèng was thus lifted.
Zhú Zhīwǔ can be called adept at strategy;
with one word he preserved Zhèng and pacified Qín.
The ruler of Zhèng's failure to employ such wisdom earlier
is why his state declined;
realizing in crisis,
is how it survived.
King Líng of Chǔ ascended the throne,
desiring hegemony,
and convened the lords,
sending Jiāo Jǔ to Jìn to seek their participation.
Jiāo Jǔ delivered the message:
"My lord sends me to say,
'You have shown favor,
granting a covenant at Sòng,
saying:
"Followers of Jìn and Chǔ
shall meet mutually."
Due to the year's troubles,
I wish to foster joy with you lords,
sending Jǔ to request an opportunity.
If you have no concerns from the four quarters,
then I hope to borrow your prestige to invite the lords.'"
The ruler of Jìn wished to refuse,
but Sīmǎ Hóu said:
"No!
King Chǔ is now arrogant;
perhaps Heaven wishes to fill his heart to deepen his poison,
then bring down punishment—
it is unknown;
whether he can end well
is also unknown.
Only what Heaven assists
cannot be contested;
you should agree.
Cultivate virtue and await his outcome:
if he turns to virtue,
we would still serve him,
let alone the other lords?
If he goes to excess in cruelty,
Chǔ will abandon him,
and with whom would we contend?"
The duke said:
"Jìn has three invulnerabilities—
what enemy can it have?
The state is secure and rich in horses,
Qí and Chǔ face many troubles;
with these three,
what direction would not succeed?"
He replied:
"Relying on horses and security,
and delighting in neighbors' troubles—
these are three vulnerabilities.
The Sì Yuè and Sān Tú mountains,
Yángchéng and Dàshì,
Jīngshān and Zhōngnán—
these are the secure places of the nine provinces,
yet they do not belong to one clan.
North of Jìzhōu,
where horses are bred,
has no thriving states.
Relying on security and horses
is insufficient for firmness—
so it has been since ancient times.
Thus, former kings pursued virtuous reputation
to please spirits and people;
we do not hear they pursued security and horses.
Some, through many troubles, strengthened their states
and expanded their territories;
others, without troubles, lost their states
and their domains—
why delight in troubles?
Qí had the trouble of Zhòngsūn,
yet gained Duke Huán,
and relies on it to this day;
Jìn had the trouble of Lǐ Kè,
yet gained Duke Wén,
thus becoming hegemon.
Wèi and Xíng had no troubles,
yet the Dí tribes destroyed them.
So others' troubles
cannot be delighted in.
Relying on these three,
without cultivating governance and virtue,
leaves no leisure before downfall—
how can one succeed?
You should agree.
Zhòu practiced cruelty,
King Wén practiced kindness—
thus Yīn fell,
thus Zhōu rose;
how could it be about contending for lords!"
So he agreed to King Líng of Chǔ,
who then held the Shēn assembly,
joined lords to attack Wú,
built the Zhānghuá Terrace,
launched the Gānxī campaign—
the people were exhausted,
resentful below,
ministers rebellious above.
Prince Qìjí rebelled,
King Líng fled,
and died in the wild.
Thus it is said:
"Jìn did not break a spear, yet Chǔ destroyed itself."
This was Sīmǎ Hóu's strategy.
King Píng of Chǔ killed Wǔ Zǐxū's father;
Zǐxū fled into exile,
carrying a bow to seek audience with Hé Lǘ.
Hé Lǘ said:
"Extreme in greatness,
extreme in courage."
For this reason, he wished to raise an army to attack Chǔ.
Wǔ Zīxū remonstrated, saying:
"It cannot be done!
I have heard it said,
a nobleman does not raise armies for the sake of an ordinary man,
and serving one's ruler is like serving one's father.
To compromise the ruler's righteousness
to avenge one's father's enemy—
this is something I cannot do."
Thereupon, he desisted.
Duke Zhāo of Cài paid a court visit to Chǔ,
possessing a fine fur robe.
Chǔ's Prime Minister Náng Wǎ sought it,
but Duke Zhāo did not give it.
Thereupon,
he detained Duke Zhāo in Yǐng for several years,
and only then sent him back.
As Duke Zhāo crossed the Hàn River,
he sank a jade disc, saying:
"Should any feudal lord attack Chǔ,
I request to lead the vanguard."
The people of Chǔ heard this and were angered,
thereupon raising an army to attack Cài.
Cài requested aid from Wú.
Wǔ Zīxū remonstrated, saying:
"Cài is not at fault;
the people of Chǔ are without principle.
If my lord has a heart concerned for the central states,
then now is the time to act."
Thereupon,
they raised an army to attack Chǔ,
and subsequently defeated the Chǔ army at Bǎijǔ, establishing hegemony—
this was due to Wǔ Zīxū's strategy.
Therefore, the "Spring and Autumn Annals" praises and commends him.
Duke Xiào of Qín wished to adopt Wèi Yāng's advice,
instituting stricter laws and harsher punishments,
altering the systems of the ancient Three Dynasties.
Fearing his ministers would not comply,
he then
summoned the three senior officials Wèi Yāng, Gān Lóng, and Dù Zhì to attend him,
to ponder the changes in worldly affairs,
deliberate on the fundamentals of proper law,
and the way to guide the people.
The ruler said:
"Succeeding to the throne without losing the altars of soil and grain is the way of a ruler;
implementing laws focused on clarifying the ruler's leadership is the conduct of a minister.
Now I wish to change the laws to educate the people,
but I fear the criticism of all under heaven."
Gōngsūn Yǎng said:
"I have heard that hesitant action gains no fame,
hesitant endeavors achieve no merit.
My lord should quickly resolve on the plan for changing the laws
and implement it without hesitation or doubt,
heedless of the criticism of all under heaven.
Moreover, those with actions surpassing others
are bound to bear censure from the world;
those with uniquely wise plans
are sure to be scorned by the people.
As the saying goes:
'The foolish understand only after things are done;
the wise see what is yet to sprout.
One cannot plan the beginning with the common people,
but can share the joy of success with them.'
Guō Yǎn's laws state:
'Those who discuss ultimate virtue do not conform to custom;
those who achieve great merit do not consult the multitude.'
Laws are meant to love the people;
rites are meant to facilitate affairs.
Therefore, if a sage can govern the state,
he does not imitate the old ways;
if he can benefit the people,
he does not adhere to the old rites."
Duke Xiào said:
"Excellent!"
Gān Lóng said:
"Not so!
I have heard that sages do not change the people to teach them,
and the wise do not alter the laws to govern.
Teaching according to the people brings success without toil;
governing based on existing laws makes officials familiar and people content.
Now my lord changes the laws, not following the old ways,
and alters the rites to teach the people.
I fear the criticism of all under heaven against you,
and urge you to consider this carefully."
Gōngsūn Yǎng said:
"What you speak of is known to the世俗.
Ordinary people are comfortable with their habits;
scholars are immersed in what they have heard.
These two types
are fit to hold office and maintain laws,
but not to discuss matters beyond the classical laws.
The Three Dynasties ruled differently yet all became kings;
the Five Hegemons used different laws yet all achieved hegemony.
The wise create laws,
and the foolish are bound by them;
the worthy change rites,
and the unworthy are constrained by them.
Those who cling to rites are not worth discussing affairs with;
those who are bound by laws are not worth deliberating governance with.
My lord, have no doubts."
Dù Zhì said:
"Without hundredfold benefit,
do not change the laws;
without tenfold gain,
do not replace tools.
I have heard that following antiquity incurs no error,
adhering to rites avoids deviation.
I urge you to consider this."
Gōngsūn Yǎng said:
"The teachings of former ages differed—which antiquity should we follow?
Imperial kings did not repeat each other—which rites should we adhere to?
Fúxī and Shénnóng taught without punishment;
Huángdì, Yáo, and Shùn punished without wrath.
By the time of Wén and Wǔ,
each established laws according to their time,
and instituted rites based on circumstances.
Rites and laws were both established,
with regulations and decrees each appropriate.
Armor, weapons, and equipment
were each suited to their use.
Therefore I say:
'Governing the world does not rely on one way;
benefiting the state does not require antiquity.'
Thus, Tāng and Wǔ became kings without following the old ways;
Yīn and Xià perished without changing their rites.
Hence, those who oppose antiquity should not be faulted;
those who adhere to rites do not deserve praise.
My lord, have no doubts."
Duke Xiào said:
"Excellent!
I have heard that remote regions breed many strange tales,
and biased learning fosters much argument.
The laughter of fools
is mourned by the wise;
the joy of madmen
is worried over by the worthy.
Bound by worldly opinions,
people's minds would never doubt!"
Thereupon,
Duke Xiào rejected the good counsel of Lóng and Zhì,
and followed Wèi Yāng's excessive words.
The laws were strict and cruel,
punishments severe and inevitable,
upheld with impartiality,
achieving strength at that time.
Subsequently, he enfeoffed Yǎng as Lord of Shāng.
When Duke Xiào died,
the people of the state resented Lord Shāng,
to the extent of having him torn apart by chariots.
The troubles spread gradually until Qín Shǐhuáng's time,
with red-clad convicts filling the roads,
bands of robbers covering the hills,
ultimately leading to chaotic downfall—
all resulting from harshness and lack of kindness.
The Three Dynasties accumulated virtue and became kings;
Qí Huán restored broken lines and became hegemon;
Qín's severity and tyranny led to its fall;
the Hàn king extended benevolence and became emperor.
Therefore, kindness and benevolence
are the foundation of strategy.
During the reign of King Huì of Qín,
Shǔ was in turmoil,
with its people attacking each other,
and they urgently appealed to Qín for help.
King Huì intended to send troops to attack Shǔ,
but considered the route treacherous and difficult to reach,
while the people of Hán came to invade Qín.
King Huì of Qín wanted to attack Hán first,
but feared the chaos in Shǔ;
if he attacked Shǔ first,
he worried that Hán would take advantage of Qín's vulnerability,
so he hesitated and could not decide.
Sīmǎ Cuò and Lord Zhāng debated before King Huì,
with Sīmǎ Cuò advocating for attacking Shǔ,
and Lord Zhāng saying:
"It would be better to attack Hán."
The King said:
"Please explain your reasoning."
He replied:
"Be friendly with Wèi and maintain good relations with Chǔ,
send troops to Sānchuān,
block the pass at Shígǔ,
secure the route to Túnliú,
have Wèi cut off Nányáng,
and Chǔ approach Nánzhèng,
while Qín attacks Xīnchéng and Yíyáng,
thereby reaching the outskirts of the two Zhōu domains,
punishing the King of Zhōu for his crimes,
and encroaching upon the territories of Chǔ and Wèi.
When Zhōu realizes it cannot save itself,
the nine tripods and precious vessels will surely be surrendered.
By seizing the nine tripods,
examining the maps and records,
and controlling the Son of Heaven to command the world,
no one under heaven would dare disobey—
this is the path to kingship.
Now, Shǔ is a remote western state,
akin to the barbarian tribes.
Exhausting troops and wearying the masses
would not suffice to achieve fame;
gaining its land
would not bring substantial benefit.
I have heard that those contending for fame do so at court,
and those contending for profit do so in the marketplace.
Now, Sānchuān and the Zhōu court
are the court and marketplace of the world,
yet Your Majesty does not contend there,
but instead contends with barbarians—
this is far from the way of kingship!"
Sīmǎ Cuò said:
"Not so!
I have heard that
those who wish to be wealthy
must expand their territory;
those who wish to be strong
must enrich their people;
those who wish to be kings
must broaden their virtue.
When these three foundations are complete,
kingship will follow.
Now, Your Majesty's land is small and the people poor,
so I propose starting with what is easier.
Shǔ is a remote western state,
yet a leader among the barbarian tribes.
It suffers from tyranny like that of Jié and Zhòu,
and for Qín to attack it
is like sending a wolf to chase a flock of sheep.
Gaining its land
will suffice to expand the state;
taking its wealth
will suffice to enrich the people,
and we can arm ourselves without harming the masses and subdue it.
Subduing one state
will not be seen as brutality by the world;
exhausting the benefits of the western seas
will not be viewed as greed by the feudal lords—
this is achieving both fame and substance in one move.
Moreover, we gain a reputation for ending tyranny and quelling chaos.
Now, attacking Hán and coercing the Son of Heaven
brings infamy,
and may not even yield benefits.
Having the name of unrighteousness
and attacking what the world does not desire
is perilous!
Allow me to state the reason:
Zhōu
is the ancestral house of the world;
Qí and Hán are its allies.
If Zhōu realizes it will lose the nine tripods,
and Hán knows it will lose Sānchuān,
they will unite efforts and conspire together,
relying on Qí and Zhào,
and seek resolution with Chǔ and Wèi,
giving the tripods to Chǔ,
and land to Wèi—
giving the tripods to Chǔ,
and land to Wèi—
Your Majesty would be unable to stop it.
This is what I call perilous;
it is better to attack Shǔ and secure our position."
King Huì of Qín said:
"Excellent!
I shall follow your advice."
He ultimately raised troops to attack Shǔ,
capturing it in the tenth month,
and thus pacified Shǔ.
The King of Shǔ was demoted to a marquis,
and Chén Shū was appointed as chancellor of Shǔ.
Once Shǔ belonged to Qín,
Qín grew increasingly strong, wealthy, and powerful, dominating the feudal lords—
all due to Sīmǎ Cuò's strategy.
The state of Chǔ sent Huáng Xiē to Qín.
King Zhāo of Qín had dispatched Bái Qǐ to attack Hán and Wèi.
Hán and Wèi submitted and served Qín,
and King Zhāo was about to order Bái Qǐ to join Hán and Wèi in attacking Chǔ together.
Huáng Xiē happened to arrive
and learned of this plan.
At that time,
Qín had already sent Bái Qǐ to attack Chǔ,
capturing several counties,
and King Qǐng Xiāng of Chǔ had moved eastward.
Huáng Xiē submitted a letter to King Zhāo of Qín,
intending to persuade Qín to ally with distant Chǔ and attack Hán and Wèi instead, in order to relieve pressure on Chǔ.
The letter stated:
"Under heaven, none are stronger than Qín and Chǔ.
Now I hear Your Majesty wishes to attack Chǔ—
this is like two tigers fighting each other.
When two tigers fight,
a worn-out dog benefits from their exhaustion.
It would be better to befriend Chǔ.
Allow me to explain my reasoning.
I have heard that
when things reach an extreme, they reverse—
such as winter and summer;
reaching great heights brings danger—
as with piling up chess pieces.
Now, Your Majesty's vast territory
spans two borders across the realm,
something unprecedented
since the beginning of humankind,
for a land of ten thousand chariots.
Your Majesty sent Shèng Qiáo to oversee affairs in Hán,
and Shèng Qiáo brought its lands into Qín—
this was achieved without Your Majesty using arms,
without exerting authority,
yet gaining a hundred lǐ of territory.
Your Majesty may be called capable indeed.
You then raised troops to attack Wèi,
blockaded the gates of Dàliáng,
seized Hénèi,
captured Yān, Suānzǎo, Xū, and Táo,
entered Xíng,
while Wèi's forces hovered like clouds but dared not rescue—
Your Majesty's achievements are numerous.
After resting troops and people for two years, you resumed campaigns,
taking Mǎn, Yǎn, Shǒu, and Yuán,
advancing to Rén, Píngqiū, Huáng, Jìyáng, and Zhēnchéng, forcing Wèi to submit.
You further cut off the north of Púlì,
channeling it to the strategic point between Qín and Qí,
severing the spine of Chǔ and Zhào,
so that the states under heaven, though gathered five or six times, dared not aid each other—
Your Majesty's might is unparalleled.
If you can maintain these achievements and uphold your authority,
tempering the desire for war with the richness of benevolence and righteousness,
ensuring no future troubles,
then even three kings would not suffice to be four,
nor five hegemons to be six.
But if you rely on the multitude of your forces,
the strength of your weapons,
and the prestige from crushing Wèi,
seeking to subdue the lords of heaven by force,
I fear there will be future troubles.
The 'Book of Songs' says:
'Nothing is without a beginning,
but few reach the end.'
The 'Book of Changes' states:
'A fox crosses water,
wetting its tail.'
This means starting is easy,
but ending is hard.
How do we know this is so?
Zhì Bó saw the advantage in attacking Zhào,
but did not foresee the disaster at Yúcì;
Wú saw the convenience in attacking Qí,
but did not anticipate defeat at Gānsuì.
These two states
were not without great achievements,
but they pursued profit upfront
and overlooked troubles later.
Wú, trusting Yuè,
went to attack Qí,
and though it defeated the Qí army at Àilíng,
it was captured by Yuè at the shores of Sānzhǔ;
Zhì Bó, trusting Hán and Wèi,
attacked Zhào,
besieging the city of Jìnyáng,
and victory seemed imminent,
but Hán and Wèi betrayed him,
killing Zhì Bó Yáo on the Cóngtái terrace.
Now, Your Majesty resents Chǔ for not being destroyed,
but forgets that destroying Chǔ would strengthen Hán and Wèi.
I consider this unwise for Your Majesty.
The 'Book of Songs' says:
'The great martial [king] keeps distant dwellings and does not tread there.'
From this perspective,
Chǔ is an ally,
a support;
neighboring states
are enemies.
The 'Book of Songs' also says:
'The swift hare leaps,
met by hounds and caught;
others have intentions,
I can surmise them.'
Now, Your Majesty, midway, trusts that Hán and Wèi are well-disposed toward you—
this is like Wú trusting Yuè.
I have heard that
enemies cannot be lent aid,
and opportunities must not be lost.
I fear Hán and Wèi use humble words to avert disaster,
but in reality deceive your great state.
Why?
Your Majesty has no lasting virtue toward Hán and Wèi,
but generations of grievances.
The fathers, sons, brothers
of Hán and Wèi who have died at the hands of Qín
span nearly ten generations.
Their states are ruined,
their altars of grain and soil damaged,
their ancestral temples destroyed.
Bellies ripped, intestines severed,
necks broken, skulls smashed,
bodies and heads separated,
bones exposed in marshes,
heads fallen stiff,
visible across the borders.
Those bound as ministers or tied as sons, becoming masses of captives,
fill the roads.
Spirits wander with nowhere to feast,
the people have no means to live,
clans scatter,
and those fleeing into servitude
overflow the realm.
Thus, that Hán and Wèi have not perished
is a worry for Qín's altars of grain and soil.
Now, if you supply them to attack Chǔ,
is that not a mistake?
Moreover, when you attack Chǔ,
how will you deploy troops?
Will you seek passage through your enemy states Hán and Wèi?
From the day the army sets out,
you will worry about its return.
This would mean using your troops to aid your enemies Hán and Wèi.
If you do not seek passage from enemy Hán and Wèi,
you must attack the right bank of the Suí River.
These are vast rivers and great waters,
mountains, forests, streams, and valleys—
land that yields no food.
Even if you possess it,
it counts not as gained territory.
Thus, you would have the name of destroying Chǔ
but not the reality of gaining land.
Furthermore, when you attack Chǔ,
the four states will surely all raise troops in response.
The forces of Qín and Chǔ
will engage and not separate.
Hán and Wèi will send troops to attack Liú, Fāngyǔ, Zhì, Húlíng, Dàng, Xiāo, and Xiāng,
ensuring the old Sòng territory is fully taken.
The Qí people facing south,
the north of Sì River will surely be seized.
These are all flat plains accessible in all directions,
fertile lands,
yet you let them attack alone.
By defeating Chǔ, you would fatten Hán and Wèi in the central states and strengthen Qí.
When Hán and Wèi grow strong,
they will be enough to oppose Qín.
Qí, with the Sì River as its southern border,
the sea to the east,
and the river to the north,
will have no rear worries.
No state under heaven will be stronger than Qí and Wèi then.
If Qí and Wèi gain land, secure advantages, and cautiously serve your officials,
within a year,
though they may not yet claim the title of emperor,
they will have more than enough to make the king of Chǔ an emperor.
With Your Majesty's broad territories,
multitude of people,
and strong arms,
to act once and incur Chǔ's enmity,
while causing Hán and Wèi to honor Qí with imperial status—
this is a miscalculation by Your Majesty.
For your sake, I consider
nothing better than befriending Chǔ.
If Qín and Chǔ unite to face Hán,
Hán will surely yield submissively.
Your Majesty can then impose the strategic barriers of the Eastern Mountains,
encircle them with the benefits of the winding river,
and Hán will become a marquis within your passes.
If then you send a hundred thousand troops to attack Zhèng,
Liáng will be terrified,
Xǔ and Chǎnglíng will fortify their cities,
while Shàngcài and Zhàolíng cease communication—
thus, Wèi too will become a marquis within the passes.
Once you befriend Chǔ,
with two kings of ten thousand chariots as marquises within your gates,
and direct territory toward Qí,
the right bank of Qí can be taken effortlessly.
Your Majesty's land will then stretch across the two seas,
dominating all under heaven.
Thus Yan and Zhao would be without Qi and Chu,
and Qi and Chu without Yan and Zhao.
Then, by threatening Yan and Zhao,
you can directly shake Qi and Chu.
These four states
will submit without needing to be thoroughly defeated."
King Zhāo said:
"Excellent!"
Thereupon, he stopped Bái Qǐ,
apologized to Hán and Wèi,
sent envoys to bribe Chǔ,
and formed an alliance as allied states.
Huáng Xiē accepted the agreement and returned to Chǔ.
Resolving the disaster for the weakened Chǔ,
and preserving the strength of Qín's army—
this was Huáng Xiē's strategy.
Qín and Zhào battled at Chángpíng,
Zhào was not victorious,
and lost one commandant.
King of Zhào summoned Lóu Chāng and Yú Qīng, saying:
"Our army is not winning in battle,
the commandant has been captured and died,
I shall don my armor and lead the charge myself."
Lóu Chāng said:
"That would be of no benefit,
it would be better to send an envoy with precious treasures to sue for peace."
Yú Qīng said:
"When Chāng speaks of suing for peace,
he believes that if we do not seek peace,
our army will surely be defeated,
but the power to decide on peace lies with Qín.
Moreover, in Your Majesty's assessment of Qín,
do they want to destroy Your Majesty's army?
Or not?"
The King said:
"Qín has spared no effort,
and will certainly destroy Zhào's army."
Yú Qīng said:
"If Your Majesty listens to your servant,
send envoys with precious treasures to ally with Chǔ and Wèi.
Chǔ and Wèi, desiring Your Majesty's precious treasures,
will surely admit our envoys.
Once our envoys enter Chǔ and Wèi,
Qín will certainly suspect the other states,
fearing that the alliances under heaven will unite as one.
In this situation,
then peace can be negotiated."
The King of Zhào did not listen,
but sent Píngyáng Jūn to negotiate peace,
dispatching Zhèng Zhū to Qín,
and Qín admitted him.
The King of Zhào summoned Yú Qīng and said:
"I sent Píngyáng Jūn to negotiate peace with Qín,
and Qín has already admitted Zhèng Zhū.
What does Yú Qīng think of this?"
He replied:
"Your Majesty will not obtain peace,
and your army will surely be defeated!
All under heaven who congratulate the victors are in Qín.
Zhèng Zhū,
an esteemed man,
has entered Qín.
The King of Qín and Yìnghóu will certainly display and honor him to show to all under heaven.
Chǔ and Wèi, believing that Zhào is suing for peace,
will surely not come to Your Majesty's rescue,
so peace cannot be achieved."
Yìnghóu indeed displayed Zhèng Zhū to show to all under heaven who congratulated the victors,
and ultimately refused to make peace.
At Chángpíng, there was a great defeat,
and subsequently Hándān was besieged,
becoming the laughingstock of all under heaven,
because they did not follow Yú Qīng's strategy.
After Qín lifted the siege of Hándān,
the King of Zhào went to pay court,
sent Zhào Hào to settle matters with Qín,
ceding six counties to make peace.
Yú Qīng said to the King of Zhào:
"When Qín attacked Your Majesty,
did they retreat because they were weary?
Or was it that their strength could still advance,
but they spared Your Majesty and did not attack?"
The King said:
"When Qín attacked us,
they spared no effort,
so they must have retreated due to weariness."
Yú Qīng said:
"Qín used its strength to attack what it could not take,
and retreated wearily;
if Your Majesty then gives them what their strength could not take,
this is helping Qín attack yourself.
Next year when Qín attacks Your Majesty again,
Your Majesty will have no means of rescue!"
The King told Zhào Hào what Yú Qīng had said.
He said:
"Can Yú Qīng measure the extent of Qín's strength?
Does he truly know where Qín's strength cannot reach?
If we do not give these small pieces of land,
and cause Qín to attack Your Majesty again next year,
would Your Majesty not have to cede inner territories to make peace?"
The King said:
"I ask to follow your advice to cede land,
but can you guarantee that Qín will not attack again next year?"
Zhào Hào said:
"That is not something your servant dares to take responsibility for.
In the past,
the relations of the Three Jìn with Qín were similar.
Now Qín is friendly with Hán and Wèi but attacks Your Majesty,
so the way Your Majesty serves Qín
must be inferior to that of Hán and Wèi.
Now your servant, to relieve you from the attack due to severed relations,
open borders and facilitate exchanges,
and align with Hán and Wèi,
yet by next year you alone are attacked by Qín.
This means Your Majesty's service to Qín
must lag behind Hán and Wèi.
This is not something your servant dares to guarantee."
The King told this to Yú Qīng,
and Yú Qīng replied:
"Hào says:
'If we do not make peace,
and next year Qín attacks Your Majesty again,
would Your Majesty not have to cede inner territories to make peace?'
Now if we make peace,
Hào cannot guarantee that Qín will not attack again,
so what good does ceding do?
If they attack again next year,
and we again cede what their strength could not take to make peace,
this is a strategy of self-destruction,
better not to make peace at all.
Though Qín is skilled in attack,
it could not take the six counties;
though Zhào may not be able to defend,
it would not lose six cities either.
Qín retreated wearily,
its troops must be exhausted;
if we use five counties to win over all under heaven to attack the weary Qín,
then we lose to all under heaven,
but gain compensation from Qín,
which still benefits our state.
How does this compare to sitting back, ceding territory, weakening ourselves, and strengthening Qín?
Now Hào says:
'The reason Qín is friendly with Hán and Wèi but attacks Zhào
must be that Your Majesty's service to Qín is inferior to that of Hán and Wèi.'
This would have Your Majesty serve Qín with six cities annually,
sitting until your land is exhausted.
When Qín comes again next year to demand territory,
will Your Majesty give it?
If not,
you abandon previous efforts and provoke Qín's wrath;
if you give,
soon you will have no land to offer.
As the saying goes:
'The strong are good at attacking,
while the weak cannot defend.'
Now if we sit back and obey Qín,
Qín's troops, without being worn out, gain much land,
thus strengthening Qín and weakening Zhào.
To strengthen an already powerful Qín by cutting from an increasingly weak Zhào,
their military schemes will surely not cease.
Moreover, Your Majesty's land is finite, but Qín's demands are endless;
to meet endless demands with finite land,
the situation will inevitably lead to the end of Zhào!"
Before the plan was decided,
Lóu Huǎn arrived from Qín,
and the King of Zhào consulted with Lóu Huǎn, saying:
"Is it more auspicious to give Qín land or not?"
Huǎn declined, saying:
"This is not something your servant can know."
The King said:
"Even so,
try to speak your private opinion."
Lóu Huǎn replied:
"Have you heard of the mother of Gōngfǔ Wénbó?
Gōngfǔ Wénbó served in Lǔ,
fell ill and died,
and two women killed themselves in his room.
His mother heard of this,
but refused to weep.
Her steward said:
'How can there be a mother who does not weep when her son dies?'
His mother said:
'Confucius,
a worthy man,
was driven from Lǔ, and this man did not follow;
now that he is dead, two women have killed themselves for him.
This being the case,
he must have been neglectful of the worthy and generous to women.'
Thus, following the mother's words,
she is considered a worthy mother;
following the wife's words,
she would inevitably be deemed a jealous woman.
The words are the same,
but if the speakers differ, people's views change.
Now your servant has newly come from Qín,
and if I say not to give,
that would not be a good plan;
if I say to give,
I fear Your Majesty would think I am acting for Qín,
so I dare not respond.
But if your servant may plan for Your Majesty,
it would be better to give."
The King said:
"Agreed!"
Yú Qīng, hearing of this, said:
"This is deceptive talk,
Your Majesty must be careful not to give."
Lóu Huǎn, hearing of this,
went to see the King,
and the King again told Lóu Huǎn what Yú Qīng had said.
Lóu Huǎn replied:
"Not so,
Yú Qīng understands one aspect,
but not the other."
When Qín and Zhào were locked in conflict,
all under heaven rejoiced.
Why was this?
The answer was:
"We shall rely on the strong and exploit the weak."
Now Zhào's troops are besieged by Qín,
and those under heaven who congratulate the victor
will surely all side with Qín.
Therefore, it would be better to quickly cede territory to make peace,
thereby sowing doubt among the states and appeasing Qín's ambitions.
If not,
the world will take advantage of Qín's wrath
and exploit Zhào's weakness to carve it up.
When Zhào faces destruction,
what schemes can it plot against Qín?
Hence it is said:
"Yú Qīng understood one aspect,
but not the other."
I hope Your Majesty will decide accordingly,
and not deliberate further."
When Yú Qīng heard this,
he went to see the king and said:
"How perilous!
This is why Lóu Huàn acts for Qín's benefit.
Does this not further alienate the world while failing to truly appease Qín?
He simply fails to mention that this would reveal our weakness to all!
Moreover, when I advised against granting territory,
it was not merely about refusal.
Since Qín demands six cities from Your Majesty,
you should instead use these six cities to bribe Qí.
Qí
is Qín's bitter enemy.
Having received six cities from Your Majesty,
they will join forces to attack Qín from the west.
Qí will heed Your Majesty
before the words are fully spoken.
Thus, what you lose to Qí will be reclaimed from Qín.
And the enmity between Qí and Zhào
can be avenged,
while demonstrating to the world our capability.
If Your Majesty acts on this proposal,
before troops even approach our borders,
I foresee Qín sending lavish gifts to seek reconciliation with Your Majesty.
Should you then align with Qín,
when Hán and Wèi hear of it,
they will surely hold Your Majesty in high esteem.
Esteeming Your Majesty, they will present precious treasures to gain your favor first.
Thus, with one move, Your Majesty would secure alliances with three states and reverse positions with Qín."
King of Zhào said:
"Excellent!"
He immediately sent Yú Qīng east to meet the King of Qí
and conspire against Qín.
Yú Qīng's strategy was implemented, and Zhào achieved hegemony.
This was the pivotal mechanism of survival,
and the activation of such a mechanism
allows no time for hesitation.
Thus, with one word from Yú Qīng, Qín trembled with fear,
swiftly sending envoys to request preparedness.
Therefore, are not ministers skilled in strategy
crucial to the state?
Without Yú Qīng,
Zhào would have perished.
When Wèi requested to form an alliance,
King Xiàochéng of Zhào summoned Yú Qīng for counsel,
passing by Lord Píngyuán.
Lord Píngyuán said:
"I hope you will advocate for the alliance."
Yú Qīng entered for an audience,
and the king said:
"Wèi has requested an alliance."
He replied:
"Wèi is mistaken."
The king said:
"We have not yet agreed to it."
He replied:
"Your Majesty is mistaken."
The king said:
"Wèi requests an alliance,
and you say
Wèi is mistaken;
We have not agreed,
yet you say
We are mistaken.
Then,
is the alliance ultimately impossible?"
He replied:
"I have heard that when a small state engages with a large state,
if there is benefit,
the large state receives the blessing;
if there is failure,
the small state suffers the disaster.
Now Wèi, as a small state, requests disaster upon itself,
while Your Majesty, as a large state, declines the blessing.
Therefore, I say:
Your Majesty is mistaken,
and Wèi is also mistaken.
I privately believe that the alliance is advantageous."
The king said:
"Excellent!"
Thereupon, he formed an alliance with Wèi.
Had Yú Qīng been long employed in Zhào,
Zhào would surely have achieved hegemony.
But encountering the affair of Wèi Qí,
he abandoned his marquisate, resigned his ministry, and returned,
left unused,
and Zhào soon perished.
The Lord of Pèi and Xiàng Jí both received orders from King Huáiyáng of Chǔ,
which stated:
"He who enters Xiányáng first shall rule it."
The Lord of Pèi planned to enter through Wǔguān,
but encountered resistance at Nányáng,
where the governor Yǐ defended the city of Wǎn,
holding firm and not surrendering.
The Lord of Pèi led his troops to surround Wǎn in three layers,
and the governor of Nányáng intended to kill himself,
but his retainer Chén Huī stopped him, saying:
"It is not too late to die."
Thereupon,
Huī scaled the wall to see the Lord of Pèi and said:
"I have heard that you pledged to rule whoever enters Xiányáng first,
yet now you linger here, besieging Wǎn all day.
Wǎn
is the capital of a great commandery,
with dozens of interconnected cities,
a large population,
and abundant reserves.
Its officials and people believe surrender means death,
so they all steadfastly defend the walls.
If you attack them,
casualties will surely be high.
The dead will lie unburied,
the wounded unhealed.
If you prolong this, your mission will stall;
if you lead your troops away,
Wǎn will repair its damaged armor,
sharpen its weary soldiers,
and follow behind you.
Then, ahead, you would break the pledge about Xiányáng;
behind, you would face the threat of a strong Wǎn.
I fear for your peril.
For your sake,
nothing compares to offering terms for Wǎn's surrender,
enfeoffing its governor,
then having him maintain defense,
while leading his armored troops
west with you to attack.
Other cities not yet taken
will, upon hearing this, compete to open their gates and await you,
allowing you to pass unhindered."
The Lord of Pèi said:
"Excellent!"
He then made the governor of Wǎn the Marquis of Yīn,
enfeoffed Chén Huī with a thousand households,
led his troops west,
and there was none who did not surrender,
thus he entered Xiányáng first.
This was due to Chén Huī's strategy.
The King of Hàn, having adopted the advice of Téng Gōng and Xiāo Hé,
promoted Hán Xìn to the rank of Supreme General,
and invited him to take the seat of honor.
The King asked:
"The Chancellor has repeatedly spoken of you, General.
What strategies do you have to teach me?"
Hán Xìn expressed his humility,
then inquired of the King:
"Now, in contending for power over the world to the east,
is it not against King Xiàng?"
The King replied:
"Indeed."
"In your own estimation, Great King, how do you compare with King Xiàng in courage, benevolence, and strength?"
The King of Hàn remained silent for a long while and said:
"I am not his equal."
Hán Xìn bowed twice in congratulation and said:
"Even I, Xìn, believe that you are not his equal.
However, I once served Chǔ,
and beg to speak of King Xiàng's character.
King Xiàng roars and bellows,
causing a thousand men to be paralyzed,
yet he cannot entrust and employ capable generals;
this is merely the courage of a common man.
King Xiàng appears respectful and cautious towards others,
his words are gentle,
and when someone is ill,
he weeps and shares his food and drink.
But when it comes to rewarding merit,
and it is time to confer titles,
he wears out the seal and tatters the ribbon,
grudging and unwilling to give them;
this is what is called the benevolence of a woman.
Although King Xiàng dominates the world and subjugates the feudal lords,
he does not reside in Guānzhōng,
but establishes his capital at Péngchéng;
moreover, he violated the covenant with the Righteous Emperor,
and enfeoffed his favorites as kings over the feudal lords,
which is unjust.
When the feudal lords saw King Xiàng banish the Righteous Emperor to Jiāngnán,
they all likewise expelled their own lords,
and made themselves kings over favorable territories.
Wherever King Xiàng passes through,
there is none not devastated and filled with resentment,
the common people do not support him,
but are merely coerced by his might,
forcibly submitting.
Though in name he is the Hegemon King,
in reality he has lost the hearts of the world.
Therefore it is said:
'His strength can easily be weakened.'
Now if you, Great King, truly reverse his ways,
employing the brave and martial of the world,
who would not be vanquished?
Enfeoffing meritorious officials with the cities and towns of the world,
who would not submit?
Leading righteous troops followed by men longing to return east,
Moreover, the three Qín kings were generals of Qín,
and for years the sons and brothers of Qín whom they led to death and flight
are beyond counting;
furthermore, they deceived their masses into surrendering to the feudal lords,
until at Xīn'ān,
King Xiàng treacherously buried alive over two hundred thousand surrendered Qín soldiers,
with only Sīmǎ Xīn, Dǒng Yì, and Zhāng Hán escaping.
The elders and brothers of Qín hold a deep grudge against these three men,
their hatred piercing to the marrow.
Now Chǔ has forcibly made these three kings through intimidation,
and the people of Qín feel no affection for them.
When you, Great King, entered Wǔguān,
you caused not the slightest harm.
You abolished Qín's harsh laws,
and made a pact with the people of Qín,
that the laws would be only three articles;
there is none among the people of Qín who does not wish for you to be their king.
According to the covenant with the feudal lords,
you should have been king over Guānzhōng,
and the people all know it.
When you were deprived of your rightful position and sent to Shǔ,
there was none among the people who did not resent it.
Now if you raise your army and march east,
the three Qín regions can be secured by mere proclamations."
Thereupon,
the King of Hàn was delighted,
and felt that he had obtained Hán Xìn too late.
He then followed Hán Xìn's strategy,
deploying his generals to their respective targets.
In the eighth month,
the King of Hàn marched east,
and the people of Qín turned to Hàn.
The King then eliminated the three Qín kings,
secured their territories,
gathered the troops of the feudal lords,
marched against King Xiàng,
and established the imperial enterprise.
This was due to Hán Xìn's strategy.
When the land of Zhào fell into chaos,
Wǔ Chén, Zhāng Ěr, and Chén Yú pacified it,
establishing Wǔ Chén as King of Zhào,
with Zhāng Ěr as Chancellor and Chén Yú as General.
The King of Zhào went out alone and
was captured by the army of Yān.
Yān imprisoned him,
intending to return the king only after dividing his land into three parts.
Messengers sent to Yān
were invariably killed,
to insist firmly on the demand for territory.
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú were troubled by this.
A laborer-soldier took leave of his hut companions, saying:
"I will go to Yān on your behalf
and bring back the King of Zhào in our carriage."
All his hut companions laughed at him, saying:
"Ten batches of messengers have gone and died;
how could you possibly retrieve the king?"
The laborer-soldier said:
"This is beyond your understanding."
He then washed and groomed himself, went to see Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú,
and was sent on his mission to meet the King of Yān.
The King of Yān questioned him,
and he replied:
"A lowly man rarely sees a noble one;
I beg for a cup of wine."
After drinking,
he was questioned again.
He repeated:
"A lowly man rarely sees a noble one;
I beg for another cup of wine."
Wine was given to him.
The soldier then said:
"Does the King know what I desire?"
The King of Yān said:
"You wish to retrieve your king, that is all."
The soldier said:
"Does my lord know what kind of men Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú are?"
The King of Yān said:
"They are worthy men."
The soldier said:
"Does my lord know what their intentions are?"
The King said:
"They wish to retrieve their king, that is all."
The Zhào soldier laughed and said:
"My lord does not understand what these two men truly desire.
Now, Wǔ Chén, Zhāng Ěr, and Chén Yú, wielding horsewhips,
conquered dozens of cities in Zhào;
surely each of them also desires to face south and call himself king—
how could they be content with being ministers?
The relationship between minister and lord
can hardly be spoken of in the same breath!
It was only because the situation was just stabilizing
that they dared not divide the land into three and become kings.
Moreover, considering age and seniority,
they first established Wǔ Chén as king
to steady the hearts of Zhào.
Now that the land of Zhào is already pacified,
these two also wish to divide Zhào and become kings themselves,
but the time is not yet ripe.
Now that you, my lord, have imprisoned the King of Zhào,
these two, in name, seek the king's return,
but in truth, they wish for Yān to kill him,
so that they may divide Zhào and establish themselves.
With one Zhào alone, it would still be easy to overcome Yān;
how much more so with two wise kings supporting each other,
holding forth righteousness to condemn an unrighteous and weak Yān?
Your destruction would be imminent!"
The King of Yān found this reasoning sound,
and thus released the King of Zhào.
The laborer-soldier drove the carriage back,
and thus the king was able to return to his state,
and was restored as king.
This was the strategy of the Zhào soldier.
Lì Yìjī, known as Master Lì,
persuaded the King of Hàn, saying:
"I have heard that
those who understand the nature of Heaven
can accomplish royal affairs;
those who do not understand the nature of Heaven
cannot accomplish royal affairs.
A king regards the people as Heaven,
and the people regard food as Heaven.
Now, the Áocāng granary
has long been the hub for grain transport across the realm.
I have heard that beneath it lies a vast store of grain.
The Chǔ forces captured Yíngyáng,
yet failed to secure Áocāng firmly;
instead, they withdrew eastward,
leaving only conscripted soldiers to guard Chénggāo.
This is Heaven's way of aiding Hàn.
Now that Chǔ is vulnerable to attack, yet Hàn retreats instead,
forfeiting this advantage—
I humbly believe this is a mistake.
Moreover, two heroes cannot stand together;
the prolonged stalemate between Chǔ and Hàn
has stirred unrest among the people,
shaken the realm,
caused farmers to abandon their plows,
and weavers to leave their looms.
The hearts of the people
remain unsettled.
I urge Your Majesty to swiftly advance your troops again,
recapture Yíngyáng,
seize the grain stores of Áocāng,
secure the strategic pass at Chénggāo,
block the Tàiháng road,
guard the Fēihú pass,
and hold the ferry at Báimǎ.
By demonstrating such strategic dominance to the feudal lords,
the realm will know where to pledge allegiance."
The King of Hàn replied:
"Excellent!"
He then followed this plan,
reoccupied Áocāng,
and thus ensured an endless supply of provisions,
leading to the capture of the Xiàng clan.
Later,
when Wú and Chǔ rebelled,
Generals Dòu Yīng and Zhōu Yàfū
again secured Áocāng and blocked Chénggāo as before,
defeating Wú and Chǔ.
All this was due to Master Lì's strategy.
Master Lì advised the King of Hàn:
"Now that Yān and Zhào have been pacified,
only Qí remains unconquered.
Tián Héng now holds a thousand lǐ of Qí's territory,
while Tián Jiān stations two hundred thousand troops at Lìchéng.
The Tián clan is powerful,
backed by the sea,
protected by the Huáng Hé and Jì River,
bordering Chǔ to the south.
The people are cunning and unpredictable.
Even if Your Majesty sends hundreds of thousands of troops,
it may take years to subdue them.
I request to carry your clear decree and persuade the King of Qí
to pledge allegiance as an eastern vassal."
Thereupon,
he sent Lì Yìjī to persuade the King of Qí, who said:
"Does the King know where the realm's allegiance lies?"
The King replied:
"I do not."
Lì Yìjī said:
"If the King knows where the realm's allegiance lies,
then Qí can be preserved;
if he does not know,
then Qí cannot be safeguarded."
The King of Qí asked:
"Where does the realm's allegiance lie?"
He answered:
"With Hàn."
The King said:
"How does the Master justify this?"
He replied:
"The King of Hàn and the King of Chǔ
joined forces to attack Qín from the west,
pledging that whoever entered Xiányáng first would rule it.
The King of Hàn entered Xiányáng first,
yet the King of Chǔ broke the pact and instead made him ruler of Hànzhōng.
The King of Chǔ also moved and murdered the Righteous Emperor.
The King of Hàn raised troops from Shǔ and Hàn,
attacked the Three Qín,
marched through the passes,
and demanded justice for the Righteous Emperor.
He gathered the realm's armies,
restored the descendants of feudal lords,
enfeoffed generals who surrendered cities,
shared spoils with his soldiers,
benefiting all under Heaven alike.
Heroes and talents
gladly serve him.
Armies from the feudal lords
arrive from all directions;
grain from Shǔ and Hàn
flows down the rivers on boats.
The King of Chǔ bears the stigma of breaking covenants
and the guilt of murdering the Righteous Emperor.
He records no merits of others,
yet never forgets their faults.
Those who win battles receive no rewards,
those who capture cities gain no fiefs;
none but the Xiàng clan hold power.
He carves seals of enfeoffment,
yet wears them smooth without granting them;
when cities are taken and spoils won,
he hoards wealth without rewarding others.
The realm rebels against him,
talents resent him,
and none will serve him willingly.
Thus, the affairs of the realm
naturally incline to the King of Hàn—
this can be foreseen even while seated.
For the King of Hàn, starting from Shǔ and Hàn,
pacified the Three Qín,
crossed beyond the Western River,
mobilized the troops of Shàngdǎng,
descended Jǐngxíng,
executed Chéng'ān,
crushed Northern Wèi,
and captured thirty-two cities.
Such armies rival those of Chīyóu,
achieved not by mere human strength.
Now he holds the grain of Áocāng,
secures the strategic pass at Chénggāo,
guards the ferry at Báimǎ,
blocks the slopes of Tàiháng,
and guards the Fēihú pass.
Those who submit last to him will perish first.
If the King swiftly submits to the King of Hàn,
the altars of Qí
may yet be preserved;
if he does not,
peril and ruin await imminently."
Tián Héng found this reasonable,
immediately heeded Master Lì,
disbanded the defenses and troops at Lìxià,
and spent days drinking freely with Lì Yìjī.
This was Master Lì's strategy.
Later, when Kuǎi Tōng of Qí advised Hán Xìn, saying:
"You have received orders to attack Qí;
why have you halted?
To lead three armies
yet achieve less than a petty scholar's feat—
you should strike Qí while it is unprepared."
Hán Xìn followed this advice.
Master Lì was then killed by Tián Héng.
Later, neither Hán Xìn nor Kuǎi Tōng met a good end,
due to their lack of benevolence.
In the third year of the Hàn dynasty,
Xiàng Yǔ urgently besieged King of Hàn at Xíngyáng,
the King of Hàn was fearful and worried,
and consulted with Lì Shēng on a plan to weaken Chǔ's power.
Lì Shēng said:
"In ancient times, when Tāng attacked Jié,
he enfeoffed his descendants at Qǐ;
when King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
he enfeoffed his descendants at Sòng.
Now Qín, devoid of virtue and having abandoned righteousness,
invaded and attacked the altars of the feudal lords,
exterminated the descendants of the six states,
leaving them without even a place to stick an awl.
If Your Majesty truly reestablishes the descendants of the six states,
and fully bestows upon them their seals,
then these rulers, ministers, and common people
will surely all revere Your Majesty's virtue,
none will fail to turn towards your influence and admire your righteousness,
willing to become your subjects.
Once virtue and righteousness have been implemented,
Your Majesty, facing south, can claim hegemony,
and Chǔ will certainly straighten their garments and come to pay homage."
The King of Hàn said:
"Excellent!
Quickly carve the seals,
you, sir, shall take them and bestow them."
Before Mr. Lì could depart,
Zhāng Liáng came from outside seeking an audience.
The King of Hàn was just eating,
and said:
"Zǐfáng, come forward,
a guest has devised a plan for me to weaken Chǔ's power."
He fully informed him of Shíqí's words, saying:
"What do you think of this, Zǐfáng?"
Liáng said:
"Whoever devised this plan for Your Majesty,
Your Majesty's cause is lost!"
The King of Hàn said:
"Why so?"
Liáng replied:
"I beg to borrow your chopsticks to illustrate."
He said:
"In ancient times, when Tāng attacked Jié and enfeoffed his descendants at Qǐ,
that was because he could control Jié's fate;
can Your Majesty control Xiàng Jí's fate?"
He said:
"I cannot."
"That is the first reason it is not feasible.
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu and enfeoffed his descendants at Sòng,
that was because he could obtain Zhòu's head;
can Your Majesty obtain Xiàng Jí's head now?"
He said:
"I cannot."
"That is the second reason it is not feasible.
When King Wǔ entered Yīn,
he honored Shāng Róng's village,
bowed at Jīzǐ's gate,
and built a mound over Bǐgān's tomb;
can Your Majesty build mounds over the tombs of sages,
honor the villages of worthies,
and bow at the gates of the wise?"
He said:
"I cannot."
"That is the third reason it is not feasible.
He distributed the grain from Jùqiáo,
scattered the money from Lùtái,
to bestow upon the poor and weak;
can Your Majesty scatter the treasury to bestow upon the poor and weak?"
He said:
"I cannot."
"That is the fourth reason it is not feasible.
After the affairs of Yīn were concluded,
he converted war chariots into civilian carriages,
inverted the carrying of shields and spears,
to show the world that arms would no longer be used;
can Your Majesty convert chariots and invert shields and spears?"
He said:
"I cannot."
"That is the fifth reason it is not feasible.
He pastured horses on the sunny side of Huàshān,
to show they were of no further use;
can Your Majesty pasture horses as having no use?"
He said:
"I cannot."
"That is the sixth reason it is not feasible.
He rested oxen at Táolín,
to show that grain would no longer be transported;
can Your Majesty rest oxen and no longer transport grain?"
He said:
"I cannot."
"That is the seventh reason it is not feasible.
Moreover, the wandering scholars of the world,
who have left their relatives,
abandoned their ancestral graves,
and parted from their old friends,
to follow Your Majesty in your endeavors,
all day and night hope for a tiny piece of land.
If now the descendants of Hán, Wèi, Yān, Zhào, Qí, and Chǔ are reestablished,
and their kings are all reinstated,
the wandering scholars will each return to serve their own lords,
rejoin their relatives,
and return to their old friends and ancestral graves;
with whom will Your Majesty strive to conquer the world?
That is the eighth reason it is not feasible.
Moreover, if only Chǔ remains unsubdued and strong,
and the six states, weakened, submit to it,
how will Your Majesty be able to make them your subjects?
If you truly follow this guest's plan,
Your Majesty's cause is lost."
The King of Hàn stopped eating, spat out his food,
and cursed, saying:
"That stupid Confucian nearly ruined your lord's affairs!"
He ordered the swift destruction of the seals,
and stopped the mission.
Thereafter, he united the armies of the world,
executed Xiàng Jí,
and stabilized the realm.
This was due to Zhāng Zǐfáng's strategy.
In the fifth year of Hàn,
while pursuing and attacking King Xiàng,
they halted the army south of Yángxià,
and scheduled a meeting with Marquis of Huáiyīn Hán Xìn and Marquis of Jiànchéng Péng Yuè to jointly attack the Chǔ army,
but they did not meet at Gùlíng.
Chǔ attacked the Hàn army,
and greatly defeated it.
The King of Hàn again entered his fortifications,
deepened the moats, and defended,
saying to Zhāng Zǐfáng:
"The feudal lords are not adhering to the agreement;
what is to be done?"
He replied:
"The Chǔ army is about to be defeated,
yet they have not been allotted territories;
it is only natural they do not come.
If you, O King, can share the world with them,
they can be summoned immediately;
if not,
the outcome is uncertain.
If you, O King, can grant the land from Chén eastward to the sea,
entirely to Hán Xìn;
and from Suīyáng north to Gǔchéng,
entirely to Péng Yuè,
enabling each to fight for themselves,
then Chǔ can be easily defeated."
The King of Hàn then sent envoys to inform Hán Xìn and Péng Yuè, saying:
"Join forces to attack Chǔ;
once Chǔ is defeated,
the land from Chén eastward to the sea
will be granted to the King of Qí;
from Suīyáng north to Gǔchéng,
will be granted to Chancellor Péng."
When the envoys arrived,
Hán Xìn and Péng Yuè were both pleased,
and reported:
"We request to advance troops now."
Hán Xìn then marched from Qí,
Péng Yuè's troops came from Liáng,
the feudal lords came to join,
and they defeated the Chǔ army at Gāixià,
pursuing and executing King Xiàng at Huáijīn.
The achievements of these two lords
were due to Zhāng Zǐfáng's strategy.
In the sixth year of the Han dynasty, during the first month,
meritorious officials were enfeoffed.
Zhāng Zǐfáng had never achieved any battle merits,
yet Emperor Gāo stated:
"Devising strategies within the tent,
deciding victory a thousand miles away—
this is Zǐfáng's achievement.
Zǐfáng may personally select thirty thousand households in Qí for his fief."
Liáng replied:
"When I first rose from Xiàpī,
and met with Your Majesty at Liú,
it was Heaven delivering me to Your Majesty.
Your Majesty employed my strategies,
and by fortune they occasionally proved accurate.
I would be content to receive Liú as my fief,
and dare not claim thirty thousand households in Qí."
Thus, Liáng was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Liú,
along with Xiāo Hé and others.
The remaining meritorious officials
had not yet been enfeoffed.
The ministers grew suspicious,
fearing they would not receive fiefs,
all feeling unsettled,
harboring intentions of unrest.
Thereupon,
Emperor Gāo ascended the tower of the Southern Palace in Luòyáng,
and saw the ministers frequently sitting together on the sand, conversing.
The Emperor asked:
"What are they discussing?"
The Marquis of Liú said:
"Does Your Majesty not know?
They are plotting rebellion!"
The Emperor said:
"The empire is now at peace—
why would they rebel?"
The Marquis of Liú replied:
"Your Majesty rose from common origins,
and with these people secured the empire.
Now that Your Majesty is sovereign,
those enfeoffed are all old acquaintances like Xiāo and Cáo,
while those executed are all personal enemies.
Now when military officers calculate achievements,
the entire empire proves insufficient for universal enfeeffment.
These people fear Your Majesty cannot enfeoff them all,
and also suspect their past faults may lead to execution,
hence they gather to plot rebellion."
The Emperor then worriedly said:
"What should be done?"
The Marquis of Liú asked:
"Among those Your Majesty has always despised,
whom all ministers commonly know,
who is the most extreme?"
The Emperor said:
"Yōng Chǐ has history with me—
he repeatedly humiliated and distressed me.
I wished to kill him,
but due to his numerous merits,
I could not bring myself to do it."
The Marquis of Liú said:
"Now urgently enfeoff Yōng Chǐ first,
to demonstrate to the ministers.
When they see Yōng Chǐ receiving a fief,
everyone will immediately feel assured."
Thereupon,
the Emperor held a banquet and enfeoffed Yōng Chǐ as Marquis of Shífāng;
while urgently ordering the Chancellor and Imperial Secretary
to evaluate achievements and conduct enfeeffments.
After the ministers concluded the banquet,
they all rejoiced, saying:
"If even Yōng Chǐ becomes a marquis,
our kind need not worry!"
Thus, treacherous intentions were reversed,
devious plots dissolved,
bringing stability to the state,
and securing peace for generations—
this was achieved through Zhāng Zǐfáng's strategy.
In the fifth year of Emperor Gāozǔ,
Lóu Jìng from Qí, garrisoning Lǒngxī,
passed through Luòyáng,
removed the harness from his carriage,
and said to General Yú, also from Qí:
"I wish to see the emperor to discuss matters of advantage."
General Yú wanted to give him fine clothes.
Lóu Jìng said:
"If I wear silk,
I'll see him in silk;
if I wear coarse cloth,
I'll see him in coarse cloth.
I dare not change."
General Yú went in and reported to the emperor,
who summoned Lóu Jìng for an audience,
granted him food, and then questioned him.
He replied:
"Your Majesty has made Luòyáng the capital—
is it to rival the glory of the Zhōu dynasty?"
The emperor said:
"Indeed!"
Jìng said:
"Your Majesty's way of gaining the empire
differs from that of the Zhōu.
The ancestors of Zhōu began with Hòujì,
whom Yáo enfeoffed at Tái,
accumulating virtue and good deeds for over ten generations.
Gōngliú avoided Jié by dwelling at Bīn,
and King Tàiwáng left Bīn due to attacks from the Dí,
driving his horse to settle at Qí,
where the people contended to follow him.
By the time King Wén became the Earl of the West,
he adjudicated the dispute between Yú and Ruì,
beginning to receive the Mandate,
while Lǚ Wàng and Bó Yí came from the seashore to join him.
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
eight hundred lords met spontaneously at Mèngjīn,
and they overthrew Yīn.
Upon King Chéng's accession,
the Duke of Zhōu and others assisted as regents,
then built the city of Chéngzhōu at Luòyì,
considering it the center of the realm.
Lords from all directions presented tribute there,
as the distances were equal.
With virtue, it was easy to rule;
without it, easy to perish.
Those who dwelled there
wished Zhōu to focus on virtue to attract people,
not to rely on natural barriers,
lest later generations become arrogant and oppressive to the people.
When Zhōu declined,
it split into two,
and none in the realm paid court,
which Zhōu could not control—
not due to lack of virtue,
but because its strategic position was weak.
Now, Your Majesty rose from Fēng and Peì,
gathered three thousand troops,
and marched straight forth,
rolling up Shǔ and Hàn,
and securing Sān Qín.
You fought seventy major battles and
forty minor ones against Xiàng Yǔ,
causing the people's blood to stain the ground,
with fathers and sons bleaching their bones in the wilderness—
too many to count.
The sound of weeping has not ceased,
the wounded have not yet risen,
and yet you wish to rival the glory of the eras of Kings Chéng and Kāng or the Duke of Zhōu.
I humbly believe it is not comparable.
Moreover, the land of Qín is girded by mountains and rivers,
fortified on all sides,
so that in sudden emergency,
a million troops can be assembled.
Leveraging Qín's foundations,
and its rich, fertile resources,
it is what is called a 'storehouse of nature.'
If Your Majesty enters the passes and establishes the capital there,
even if the lands east of the mountains are in turmoil,
the old territory of Qín can be fully retained.
To struggle with others without gripping their throat and striking their back
is not complete victory."
Emperor Gāozǔ was hesitant,
and asked his ministers,
who were mostly from east of the mountains.
They mostly urged him to capitalize at Luòyáng:
"To the east lies Chénggāo,
to the west, Yáo and Miǎn,
backed by the river and sea,
facing Yī and Luò—
its defenses are sufficient to rely on.
Moreover, the Zhōu kings lasted centuries,
while Qín fell in two generations—
it is better to capitalise where Zhōu did."
Marquis Liú Zhāng Liáng said:
"Though Luòyáng has these defenses,
its territory is small,
not exceeding a few hundred lǐ,
with narrow fields,
and it is vulnerable on all sides—
this is no land for military dominance.
Now, Guānzhōng has Yáo and Hán to the left,
Lǒng and Shǔ to the right,
and a thousand lǐ of fertile plains.
To the south, the riches of Bā and Shǔ;
to the north, the advantages of the old Yuān—
protected on three sides,
it defends one corner,
and controls the lords from the east.
When the lords are stable,
the Huáng Hé and Wèi rivers transport goods from across the realm,
supplying the western capital;
if the lords rebel,
we can sail downstream,
ensuring ample supply.
This is what is called 'a thousand lǐ of impregnable walls,
the land of a storehouse of nature.'
Lóu Jìng's advice is correct."
Thereupon,
Emperor Gāozǔ that very day set off westward,
and established the capital in Guānzhōng.
Hence, the state enjoyed peace and stability;
despite the plots of Péng Yuè, Chén Xī, and Lú Wǎn,
the armies of Jiǔjiāng, Yān, and Dài,
and the crises of Wú and Chǔ,
with troops from east of the passes,
even if a million strong,
could not inflict harm—
all because they preserved the grace of benevolent virtue,
and guarded the strength of Guānzhōng.
The state thus enjoyed eternal peace,
thanks to the strategies of Lóu Jìng and Zhāng Liáng.
The emperor said:
"The one who originally proposed capitalizing in Qín was Lóu Jìng.
'Lóu'
is 'Liú'."
He bestowed upon him the surname Liú,
appointed him as a Langzhōng,
styled him Fèngchūn Jūn,
and he later became the Marquis of Jiànxìn.
Marquis of Liǔ, Zhāng Zǐfáng,
after Hàn was stabilized,
suffered from frequent illnesses,
practiced dǎoyǐn and abstained from grains,
shutting his door and not going out.
Over a year later,
the Emperor wanted to depose the Crown Prince,
and install the son of Lady Qī, the King of Zhào, Rúyì.
Many ministers contested this,
but none could achieve a firm resolution.
Empress Lǚ was fearful,
not knowing what to do.
Someone said to Empress Lǚ:
"The Marquis of Liǔ is skilled at devising strategies,
and the Emperor trusts and employs him."
Empress Lǚ then sent her brother Lǚ Zé to compel the Marquis of Liǔ, saying:
"You have always planned for the Emperor,
now he wishes to change the Crown Prince,
how can you rest easy on your high pillow?"
The Marquis of Liǔ replied:
"Initially, the Emperor was often in dire straits,
and fortunately used my services.
Now the empire is stable,
out of love for a younger son,
he wishes to change the Crown Prince.
In matters of flesh and blood,
what use are even over a hundred officials like us?"
Lǚ Zé insisted urgently:
"Devise a plan for me."
The Marquis of Liǔ said:
"This is difficult to contest with words alone.
However, there are four men the Emperor has been unable to summon:
Yuán Gōng, Qǐlǐ Jì, Xià Huánggōng, and Lùlǐ Xiānshēng.
These four are elderly,
and because the Emperor insulted and disrespected scholars,
they fled and hid in the mountains,
on principle refusing to serve as Hàn officials.
Yet the Emperor holds these four in high regard.
If you can spare no expense in gold, jade, silks, and fabrics,
have the Crown Prince write a letter,
with humble words and a comfortable carriage to welcome them,
and send persuasive envoys to firmly invite them,
they should come.
Once they come, treat them as guests,
have them accompany the Crown Prince to court from time to time,
so the Emperor sees them.
When the Emperor sees them, he will surely be surprised
and ask about them.
Upon inquiry,
the Emperor knowing these four men
would be a help."
Thereupon,
Empress Lǚ ordered Zé to send someone with the Crown Prince's letter,
using humble words and generous gifts to welcome the four men.
The four arrived
and stayed at Lǚ Zé's residence.
By the twelfth year,
when the Emperor returned from defeating Qíng Bù's army,
his illness worsened,
and he desired even more to change the Crown Prince.
The Marquis of Liǔ advised against it but was not heeded,
so he pleaded illness and ceased attending to duties.
The Grand Tutor Shūsūn Tōng cited ancient precedents,
risking death to contend for the Crown Prince.
The Emperor pretended to agree
but still intended to change him.
During a banquet,
when wine was served
and the Crown Prince was in attendance,
the four men followed him.
All over eighty years old,
with white hair and eyebrows,
and majestic in dress and bearing,
the Emperor, surprised, asked:
"Who are you?"
The four came forward to respond,
each stating their names.
The Emperor then exclaimed in astonishment:
"I sought you gentlemen for years,
yet you avoided me.
Why now do you accompany my son?"
The four replied together:
"Your Majesty belittles scholars and is quick to insult,
we could not bear the humiliation on principle,
so we fled in fear and hid.
Hearing that the Crown Prince is filial as a son,
benevolent, respectful, and loving towards scholars,
all under heaven crane their necks,
willing to die for the Crown Prince,
hence we have come."
The Emperor said:
"I trouble you gentlemen to kindly take care of and protect the Crown Prince."
After the four offered their toasts,
they rose to leave.
The Emperor watched them go,
then summoned Lady Qī,
pointing to the four and saying:
"I wished to replace him,
but those four assist him.
His wings are fully formed,
hard to shake now!
The Lǚ clan truly will be your master."
Lady Qī wept.
The Emperor said:
"Dance for me the Chǔ dance,
and I will sing you a Chǔ song."
He sang:
"The swan goose flies high,
soaring a thousand miles at once.
Its wings and feathers are fully grown,
traversing the four seas.
Traversing the four seas,
what can be done?
Though there are arrows and lines,
where can they be applied?"
After several verses of the song,
Lady Qī sobbed and shed tears.
The Emperor rose and left,
ending the banquet.
In the end, the Crown Prince was not changed,
thanks to the Marquis of Liǔ's strategy of summoning the four men.
In the eleventh year of Hàn,
Qíng Bù of Jiǔjiāng rebelled,
and the Gāo Emperor was ill,
desiring to send the Crown Prince to strike him.
At that time, Yuán Gōng, Qǐlǐ Jì, Xià Huáng Gōng, and Lùlǐ Xiānshēng were already attending the Crown Prince.
Upon hearing that the Crown Prince was going to attack Qíng Bù,
the four spoke to each other, saying:
"We all came here
for the sake of preserving the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince leading troops
is a dangerous matter."
Then they persuaded Hóu Jiànchéng, saying:
"If the Crown Prince leads the troops,
having achievements will not enhance his position;
without achievements,
he will suffer disaster.
Furthermore, the generals with the Crown Prince
are all formidable leaders who helped establish the realm with His Majesty;
to have the Crown Prince command them
is no different from having a sheep leading wolves,
none will be willing to put forth full effort,
the lack of success is certain.
We have heard that 'a mother's love is embraced by her son.'
Now, Madame Qī is constantly in attendance,
and the King of Zhào is often embraced at the forefront.
His Majesty has said:
'I will never let an unworthy son surpass a beloved son.'
It is clear that replacing the Crown Prince is certain.
Why don't you urgently inform Lady Lü,
and during an interval, weep to His Majesty saying:
'Qíng Bù
is a fierce general under heaven,
skilled in the art of war,
and the generals are all your former equals.
To command the Crown Prince to lead these
is no different from having a sheep lead wolves.
They will not act,
and if Bù hears of it,
he will immediately march westward.
Although you are ill,
while bedridden give protection,
the generals will dare not hold back their full efforts.
Though it's difficult,
strengthen yourself for the sake of your wife and children,
lie down in the supply cart and proceed.'"
Thus, Lǚ Zé met Lady Lü that very night,
and Lady Lü wept and spoke to His Majesty
according to the intent of the four.
His Majesty said:
"I cannot dispatch a child, thus I shall go myself."
Thereupon,
His Majesty led the army eastward,
while the ministers stayed to guard
and escorted him to Bàshàng.
Liúhóu was ill,
but forced himself to rise to Qǔyóu,
where he said to His Majesty:
"I should follow,
but I am very ill.
The Chǔ people are swift,
I wish that you do not clash arms with them."
Then he advised His Majesty, saying:
"Have the Crown Prince be the General,
to oversee the troops of the princes within Guānzhōng."
His Majesty said:
"Though Zǐfāng is ill,
force yourself to rise and assist the Crown Prince."
At that time,
Uncle Sūntōng was already the Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince,
and Liúhóu acted as the Assistant Tutor.
Thus, Hàn crushed Qíng Bù,
the Crown Prince remained at peace,
the state was tranquil,
and this was the strategy of the four.
The Qí Dàohuì King
was the older brother of Emperor Xiào Huì.
In the second year,
Dàohuì King entered the court,
and Emperor Xiào Huì feasted and drank with him,
observing the household rites,
sharing the same seat.
Lady Lü was angry,
and presented poisoned wine.
Emperor Xiào Huì knew and
wanted to drink it himself but
stopped.
Dàohuì King feared he might not leave the city,
so when he mounted the carriage he sighed,
the Interior Minister accompanied him,
inquiring about the reason.
Dàohuì King explained the situation to the Interior Minister.
The Interior Minister said:
"Would you rather lose ten cities
or the entire state of Qí?"
Dàohuì King said:
"I only wish to preserve my life,
how dare I cherish the cities?"
The Interior Minister replied:
"Lord Lǚ Yuán is the daughter of Her Majesty,
and your sister.
You rule over more than seventy cities in the state,
yet Lady Lǚ's bride price is minimal.
If you sincerely offer ten cities as her bride price,
internally you would honor kinship,
and externally you would please Her Majesty.
The empress will surely be pleased,
and you'll lose ten cities but secure sixty."
Dàohuì King said:
"Excellent!"
Upon reaching his residence,
he presented the offer of ten cities as Lady Lǚ Yuán's bridal gift,
which delighted the empress and she accepted the cities.
She richly rewarded Dàohuì King and sent him back home,
thus securing peace for the state.
This was the strategy of the Qí Interior Minister.
On October 13, during the reign of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
Dàháng Wáng Huī frequently advised on the advantages of attacking the Xiōngnú,
stating it would eliminate the threat at the borders
and sever the agreement of peace and marriage.
Yùshǐ Dàfū Hán Ānguó believed that military action should not be taken.
Emperor Xiàowǔ summoned his ministers and asked,
"I have bestowed my daughters in marriage to the Chányú,
and given gifts of brocades and silk
as substantial tributes.
Now the Chányú defies commands and shows disrespect,
continually raiding and plundering.
The border regions are often alarmed,
and I am deeply concerned.
I now wish to raise the army to attack the Xiōngnú,
what do you think?"
Dàháng minister Huī bowed twice and said,
"Excellent!
Even if Your Majesty had not mentioned it, I would have requested it.
I have heard that during the Quándài period,
there were always strong Hú enemies in the north
internally supported by the Chinese army.
Yet they still managed to care for the elderly and the young,
plant trees in due season, warehouses were always full,
and defense preparations were adequate,
so the Xiōngnú did not dare invade lightly.
Now with Your Majesty's power,
the entire realm is as one family.
The world assumes the same responsibilities.
Young nobles are sent to defend the frontier,
grain is transported and delivered as preparation,
but the Xiōngnú persist in their invasions and thefts.
The reason is simply,
they do not feel a serious threat.
I believe it is advantageous to strike."
Yùshǐ Dàfū minister Ānguó bowed twice and said,
"No!
I have heard that Emperor Gāo was once surrounded at Píngchéng,
and the Xiōngnú arrived and threw bridles around the city several times over.
At the Píngchéng disaster,
he went seven days without food,
and the world lamented it.
After escaping the siege and returning to his throne,
he showed no sign of resentment or anger.
Although he gained the empire, he did not avenge the Píngchéng grievance,
not because he lacked strength.
A sage ruler considers the world at large,
not letting personal anger harm public righteousness.
Hence he sent Liú Jìng to establish peace and marriage,
which has benefited us through generations.
Emperor Xiàowén once gathered the elite troops of the empire at Chángqí and Guǎngwǔ,
achieving no measurable success,
worrying every commoner in the realm.
Emperor Xiàowén realized the military should not be maintained permanently,
so he made a pact of peace and marriage,
which benefits future generations to this day.
I believe the precedents set by the two rulers
are enough for example,
therefore I say 'Do not attack; it is advantageous.'"
Dàháng said,
"No!
One who is wise about appearances
divides only by affairs;
those who understand movement
use opportunity without losing advantage;
those who comprehend stillness
reside in tranquility, avoiding disaster.
Emperor Gāo undertook arduous tasks
to eliminate threats from the world.
He faced arrows and stones,
endured wind and rain,
marching for decades.
The bodies of the dead filled lakes,
and the piled heads resembled mountains.
Seventy percent perished,
thirty percent survived.
Those who walked wept,
exhausted from war.
The people of the empire were weary of endless warfare,
which benefited the Xiōngnú, who reveled in leisure.
Hence the peace and marriage agreement
was established to rest the people of the empire.
Emperor Gāo was wise regarding form and acted appropriately,
adapting to changing circumstances.
The five emperors did not find the same joy,
and the three kings did not inherit the same rites—
not intentionally opposing each other,
but tailoring to the needs of the time.
Teachings evolve with time,
defenses adapt to threats.
Rigid adherence to one path
does not suffice to govern.
The Xiōngnú have indulged themselves for a long while,
with unending raids and thefts,
capturing people,
and causing soldiers’ deaths and injuries.
The roads in China are lined with coffins awaiting burial;
this is lamentable to benevolent men.
Thus, I say 'It is advantageous to strike.'"
Yùshǐ Dàfū said,
"No!
I have heard that the skillful in warfare use abundance against hunger,
stable marches and secured camps
to wait out their weariness;
they organize properly and enforce virtue,
to withstand chaos;
restrain troops and mobilize the masses,
deeply strike nations, topple cities,
thus sitting and using enemy nations,
this is the weapon of the sages.
When a strong wind weakens,
it cannot lift feathers;
the force of a spent crossbow is insufficient to pierce fine silk.
What flourishes must decay,
just as morning turns to evening.
Now, if we rashly take up arms and advance lightly,
penetrate deeply with a long drive,
it will be difficult to achieve success.
A lateral attack will cut off supplies,
following roads will be pressed and squeezed,
if slow, benefits come late,
if fast, provisions will run out.
Not before a thousand miles
will people and horses face hunger,
encountering the enemy exhausted,
exactly providing opportunities to be captured.
Unless there is some extraordinary cleverness,
to capture them, I cannot see it.
Otherwise, I do not see the advantage of deep incursions.
Thus, I say 'Not attacking is advantageous.'"
The Chief Grandee said:
"Not so!
In regard to frost and fog among the grasses and trees,
they cannot pass away with the wind;
clear water and a bright mirror
cannot hide the form;
with a person who sees through matters,
one cannot use words to bewilder them.
When I speak of attacking them,
it is not to launch deeply into an offensive.
Instead, it is to conform to the desires of the Chányú,
luring him to the border.
I will station light soldiers and sharp fighters to await him,
secretly blocking dangerous routes to prepare against him.
Our position is thereby established.
Some may strike from the left,
some from the right,
some from the front,
some from the rear.
We can capture the Chányú,
and ensure complete victory.
Thus, I believe there is an opportunity to 'strike him with advantage.' ”
Thereupon,
they followed the words of the Chief Grandee,
and Emperor Xiàowǔ personally led the army,
setting an ambush in Mǎyì,
to lure in the Chányú.
Once the Chányú entered the passes,
he realized the situation,
and fled hastily.
Thereafter, conflicts and clashes ensued,
grievances and calamities intertwined,
with mutual assaults lasting ten years.
The troops were worn out and the people exhausted,
the common people left impoverished,
corpses lined the roads,
and coffins followed one after another.
Bandits and thieves filled the mountains,
and the world was shaken.
