Emperor Xiàowǔ later regretted it.
The Grand Historian Sāng Hóngyáng requested to cultivate Lúntái,
but the edict refused, saying:
“The current task
is to prohibit violence,
and stop extraordinary taxation.
Now, to cultivate far to the west
is not a way to comfort the people.
I cannot bear to hear of it.”
The Chancellor was given the title of Fùmín Marquess,
and military matters were no longer spoken of,
bringing peace to the state,
and stability to the succession.
This followed the original plan of Hán Ānguó.
During Emperor Xiàowǔ's time,
the palace counselor Zhǔfù Yǎn devised a plan, saying:
“In ancient times, the territories of nobles did not exceed a hundred lǐ,
making it easy to control the dynamics of strength and weakness.
Now, some princes hold dozens of cities,
spanning a thousand lǐ.
If they are allowed peace, they become arrogant,
prone to debauchery;
if pressured, they stand firm in strength,
and unite in conspiracy against the capital.
Now, by law to divide them,
if dissent arises,
as in the past with Cháo Cuò.
Now, some princes have numerous sons,
and when the main heir succeeds,
the rest, though kin,
are without even a measure of land.
Thus, the way of benevolence and filial piety is not demonstrated.
I wish for Your Majesty to authorize the princes to distribute favor among their sons,
granting them land as marquessates,
bringing them joy in receiving their desires.
The sovereign governing by virtue,
while in fact sealing their states,
and gradually weakening themselves.”
Thus,
the emperor followed his plan.
As a result,
horses and crossbows could not pass through,
cutting off the paths of persuasion,
reinforcing the laws of honoring the nobles,
and harshly penalizing mistakes by their lords.
Consequently, the feudal lords weakened,
and alliances were no longer made.
This was the stratagem of Zhǔfù Yǎn.
The King of Qí asked Mòzǐ:
"The scholars of old learned for themselves,
but today's scholars learn for others,
what is your view on this? "
He replied:
"The scholars of old, upon gaining a word of goodness, attached it to themselves;
today's scholars, upon gaining a word of goodness,
aim to please others."
"Běitáng Shūchāo" Volume 83, "Tàipíng Yùlǎn" Volume 607.
Lǐ Sī asked Xúnqīng:
"In the present times,
what should be done for Qín? "
Sūnqīng said:
"Restrain the power of force,
and promote the power of righteousness,
that is the way for Qín."
"Xúnzǐ Qiángguópiān" noted by Yáng Jiàng.
Zǐchǎn resolved the difficulty of Dèngxī Jiāo’s teaching the people,
establishing an agreement,
with major lawsuits concerning robes and clothes,
minor ones concerning jackets and trousers,
and the number of people offering robes and trousers was innumerable.
He made wrong as right,
and right as wrong,
causing great chaos in the state of Zhèng,
and the people raised their voices in complaint.
Zǐchǎn was deeply troubled by this.
Therefore, he punished Dèngxī severely,
and the people submitted,
so that right and wrong were finally settled.
"Xúnzǐ Zhèngmíngpiān" annotated.
Liáng Chēxīn, newly appointed as magistrate of Yè,
was visited by his sister.
It was dusk,
the city gates were closed,
so she climbed over the walls to enter,
and Liáng Chēxīn consequently cut off her foot.
Zhào Chénghóu deemed him unkind,
and thus stripped him of his seal and dismissed him from office.
"Yùlǎn" Volume 517.
Duke Āigōng of Lǔ built a large hall,
and Minister Gōng Yízi remonstrated, saying:
"If the hall is large,
with many people inside, it will be noisy,
with few people, it will be desolate.
I wish the duke would consider this."
He said:
"I have heard your command."
Yet, construction of the hall continued uninterrupted.
The next day,
Gōng Yízi advised again:
"With the state small and the hall large,
the people will surely resent our lord;
when the lords hear of it,
they will inevitably look down on our country."
The duke said:
"I have heard your command."
Yet, construction of the hall continued uninterrupted.
The next day,
he advised once more, saying:
"With Shào Mù on the left and Mù on the right,
to build a large hall above the two former princes,
isn't it harmful to filial piety?"
Then Duke Āigōng dismantled the hall and stopped.
"Yùlǎn" Volume 174.
Duke Jǐnggōng of Qí wandered atop Niú Mountain and looked north toward Qí,
saying:
"What a beautiful land!
Were it not for the inevitability of death,
what would I, the lonely ruler, do with parting from this!"
And he wept, soaking his collar.
Gāozi said:
"Indeed.
Thanks to the duke's grace,
coarse food and spoiled meat
are still available to us;
slow horses and rickety carts
can still be ridden.
Moreover, not wishing to die
is something I share with my lord!"
He lowered his head and wept.
Yànzi clapped his hands and laughed, saying:
"How delightful,
today's outing indeed reveals much!
I've seen one fearful lord and two flattering ministers.
If there were no death in ancient times,
then the Grand Duke and Dīng Gōng would still be here.
Our lord would be clad in woven rushes,
standing among the furrows in the fields,
too preoccupied to even think about death!"
Duke Jǐnggōng felt ashamed.
"Yùlǎn" Volume 428.
Zhōu Chāng was
a man from Pèi,
who was enfeoffed as Marquis of Fényīn and appointed Imperial Secretary due to military achievements.
Emperor Gāozǔ intended to depose Emperor Huì
and establish Rú Yì, son of Lady Qī,
Ministers firmly opposed it,
but none could succeed.
Chāng vehemently argued against it at court,
The Emperor asked for his reasoning,
Chāng had a speech impediment,
and said:
"Though my mouth cannot speak well,
I know this cannot be done.
If Your Majesty wishes to depose the Crown Prince,
I stubbornly refuse to obey the decree."
From Imperial Readings volume 740.
In Qí there was a gentleman named Tián Bā,
who cultivated his conduct inwardly
and demonstrated wisdom outwardly.
The King heard of his worthiness,
summoned him,
and intended to consult him on governance.
Tián Bā donned new attire,
adjusted his cap and sash,
turned to ask his concubine,
who said:
"Handsome."
As he was about to leave,
he asked his attendant,
who said:
"Handsome."
Passing by the Zī River,
he saw his reflection,
and realized he was quite ugly.
Then he met the King of Qí.
The King asked about governance,
to which he replied:
"Governance lies in rectifying oneself,
the foundation of self-rectification
rests with the ministers.
When Your Majesty summoned me,
I changed my attire and groomed myself,
asked my concubine:
'How do I look?'
She, fond of me,
flattered me saying 'handsome';
asked my attendant,
who fears me,
also flattered me saying 'handsome'.
But when I looked at my reflection in the Zī River,
then I knew my own ugliness.
Now those in Qí who flatter Your Majesty
are not just two people.
If Your Majesty could look into the Zī River,
see your own faults,
and correct them upon realization,
then Qí would be well-governed."
From Imperial Readings volumes 63 and 382.
Confucius met Róng Qǐqī of Sòng,
who was old,
white-haired,
worn clothes,
yet happily playing the zither.
Confucius asked:
"Sir, you are old and poor,
why are you so happy?"
Qǐqī replied:
"I have three joys.
Heaven created all things with humans as most noble -
I have the fortune to be human,
that is my first joy;
among humans, males are considered more noble -
I have the fortune to be male,
that is my second joy;
human life often meets injury or early death -
I am ninety years old,
that is my third joy.
Poverty is the scholar's constant state,
death is everyone's end -
dwelling in constancy and awaiting the end,
why should I not be happy?"
From Imperial Readings volume 383.
When Cuī Zhù assassinated Duke Zhuāng,
Shēn Kuǎi was fishing at sea and arrived later,
intending to enter and die for his lord.
His charioteer stopped him, saying:
"The lord's lack of virtue
is known throughout the land -
you need not die for him."
Shēn Kuǎi said:
"You tell me too late -
how can I accept the salary of a disorderly lord
yet die for a well-governed state?
You are excused,
do not die."
His charioteer said:
"If you would die for your disorderly lord,
how could I not die for my well-governed master?"
Shēn Kuǎi reached the gate and said:
"Shēn Kuǎi has heard of our lord's death,
I request to enter and mourn."
The gatekeeper reported to Cuī Zhù,
who ordered not to admit him.
Shēn Kuǎi said:
"Do you doubt me?
I'll give you my arm."
Then he cut off his left arm and gave it to the gatekeeper.
The gatekeeper showed it to Cuī Zhù,
who arrayed eight rows of guards,
and ordered him admitted.
Shēn Kuǎi drew his sword, cried to heaven,
leapt three times,
then fought,
killing seven rows,
but fell before reaching Cuī Zhù's row.
His charioteer also died outside the gate.
The gentleman heard of this and said:
"Kuǎi
can be said to have maintained integrity and died for righteousness!"
From Imperial Readings volumes 369,
and 438.
Once Zǐ Qí, at eighteen,
was sent by the Lord of Qí to govern Ā.
After he departed,
the lord regretted it.
He sent a messenger to pursue him,
saying:
"If you reach him before Ā,
overtake him,
and bring him back;
if he has already arrived,
do not recall him."
The messenger overtook him but did not bring him back.
The lord asked why,
to which he replied:
"I saw that those traveling with him
were white-haired elders.
With the wisdom of the old
and the decisiveness of the young,
he will certainly govern Ā well,
therefore I did not bring him back."
From Imperial Readings volume 268.
Lord Jǐng of Qí was traveling on the sea,
enjoying it so much
he didn't return for six months,
ordering that anyone suggesting return would be killed.
Yán Chù remonstrated:
"If you enjoy governing the sea
but not governing the state,
should someone else govern the state,
how could you still enjoy sailing on the sea?"
The lord raised his halberd to strike him.
Chù straightened his clothes and awaited, saying:
"Why don't you strike!
In the past, Jié killed Guān Lóngpáng,
Zhou killed Prince Bǐgān -
why don't you strike,
and let me join these two men -
wouldn't that be fitting!"
The lord then returned.
From Imperial Readings volume 353.
The King of Chāngyì had ten side-worn caps made,
and bestowed them upon scholarly teachers and friends.
Later he gave the remaining caps to slaves.
Gǒng Suì took off his cap and returned it,
saying:
"The King bestowed caps upon scholars,
down to your servant.
Now giving the extra caps to slaves
means the King treats his ministers like slaves."
From Imperial Readings volume 500.
When the King of Chāngyì was summoned to become Emperor,
reaching Yíngyáng,
he acquired two thorned bamboo staffs.
Gǒng Suì remonstrated:
"Thorned bamboo staffs
are for arrogant young men.
Your Majesty is attending a great funeral -
you should use a plain bamboo staff."
From Imperial Readings volume 710.
The King of Chāngyì had the lords and ministers wear ribbons of black and yellow,
granting them to his attendants.
Gōng Suì remonstrated, saying:
"The Grand Emperor established five types of colored ribbons,
yet Your Majesty bestows them upon commoners.
I consider this inappropriate,
and wish Your Majesty to retract them."
Yùlǎn 682.
In ancient times,
the people were simple and honest,
so the Three Sovereigns governed without punishment,
commanded respect without force,
hence those who were skilled did not require instruction;
this was the virtue of the Three Sovereigns.
By the time of the Five Emperors,
there were preparations for military service but no use for them,
thus those skilled in warfare did not arrange battle lines;
this refers to the Five Emperors.
Tāng overthrew Jié,
King Wén attacked Chóng,
King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
all set up battle lines but did not fight;
hence those skilled in battle did not engage,
referring to the Three Kings.
When the Xià Hòu clan attacked Yǒu Hù,
the great ancestor of Yīn battled Guǐfāng,
Zhōu Xuān Wáng's campaign against Xūnyù without bloodshed,
all demonstrated the benevolence and wisdom of the time,
the influence of the era.
When Duke Huán of Qí invaded Cài, Cài dissolved,
attacked Chǔ and Chǔ submitted,
prompting strong Chǔ to offer tribute of grass and rushes to the Zhōu court,
attacked the northern tribes to attend court,
saved three from extinction,
restored one lineage,
united the vassal states nine times,
stabilized the world once,
hosted eleven assemblies in full attire,
even when fighting great battles, did not shed blood.
By the time of Duke Wén of Jìn, he demonstrated the power of the tiger skin,
devised the deceit of dragging branches,
defeating the Chǔ forces and securing the Central States,
thus it is said he who fights well does not die,
referring to Duke Wén of Jìn.
King Zhāo of Chǔ suffered the calamity of Hélǘ,
the country was destroyed,
King Zhāo fled,
the old and young welcomed and wept for him.
King Zhāo said:
"I am unworthy,
unable to protect the altars,
the elders have reversed roles,
why worry about having no ruler,
I shall enter the sea from here.”
The elders said:
"Such a sage ruler!”
Then Shēn Bāoxū pleaded for assistance,
weeping in the court of Qín for seven days,
moved by compassion, the Qín monarch aided him,
aligning the hearts of Qín and Chǔ,
ultimately driving away the Wú forces,
returning King Zhāo to his state.
Thus it is said those who die well are not vanquished,
referring to King Zhāo.
Therefore, from Duke Wén of Jìn onward to the Warring States,
military aggression began to grow.
At this time, the strong annexed the weak,
the large devoured the small.
Thus strong states focused on attack,
weak states prepared for defense,
forging alliances and coalitions,
collectively waging wars.
Hence, in battle, one speaks of Sūn Wǔ,
in defense, one mentions Mò Dí.
By the time of Qín, through force, it unified the realm,
exhausting its military might and perished.
Then Xiàng Yǔ embraced ruthlessness and was destroyed,
and the Hàn rose through benevolence and tolerance,
thus it could sweep away the harsh violence of Qín.
Emperor Xiàowǔ subdued the barbarians,
thereafter, the world was at peace.
Thus those who engage in warfare,
their deeds are easily observed.
Yùlǎn 271.
Tāng resided in Bó, seventy lǐ away,
neighboring the lord of Gē.
Gēbó was dissolute and did not offer sacrifices,
Tāng sent someone to give him cattle and sheep,
Gēbó consumed them,
but still did not perform sacrifices.
Tāng sent someone to inquire:
"Why do you not offer sacrifices?"
He replied:
"There is nothing to offer."
Tāng again commanded the people of Bó to till the fields for him,
the elderly and weak brought food.
Gēbó led his people,
blocking those with wine and millet and robbing them,
killing those who resisted.
There was a young boy delivering millet and meat,
he was killed, and the food was stolen.
The Shū states:
"Gēbó seeks vengeance for the feast."
This is what is meant.
Seeking to avenge this boy, he attacked.
The people within the four seas all said:
"It was not for enriching the world,
but for avenging a common man and woman."
Yùlǎn 305.
Gōngsūn Ào asked Master Bóxiàng:
"Now, sir, you have gathered the techniques of the realm,
observed the regions for a long time,
yet are unable to aid the rulers' governance,
clarify ruler and minister relations;
this is akin to gold stored in a treasury,
or bamboo slats in a basket."
Yùlǎn 811.
Gōngsūn Ào said:
"Even jade, stones, gold, and iron can be cut and polished into useful tools,
how much more so with people."
Yùlǎn 813.
King Zhòu of the world,
killed the cook when the bear stew was undercooked.
Yùlǎn 861.
The King of Chǔ sent Xǔ Guāng to greet someone,
who was playing the yu with a blind man,
Gōng Suì thus departed.
Yùlǎn 581.
Yǔ crossed the Jiāng to the south,
a yellow dragon carried the boat,
everyone on the boat lost their color,
Yǔ looked up to heaven and sighed:
"I have received the command of Heaven,
to die is destiny."
The dragon lowered its head and departed.
Yùlǎn 60.
A brave warrior let out a shout,
the entire army recoiled,
such is the sincerity of the warrior.
The brave warrior Mèng Bèn,
walking through water did not avoid dragons,
on land did not avoid tigers and wolves,
when angry, exhaled with a roar,
the sound echoed across the skies.
At his death,
his head and body severed.
Thus, using might and not benevolence,
brings temporary gratification,
but life surely does not endure,
therefore Confucius diligently practiced benevolence.
Yùlǎn 437.
Qí sent Chúnyú Kūn to Chǔ,
Kūn being short of stature,
the King of Chǔ looked down upon him.
He said:
"Is there no one in Qí?
They sent you,
how can you be tall?"
He replied:
"I have no particular length,
but the seven-foot sword at my waist,
wishes to cut down the scandalous king."
The king said:
"Stop,
I was merely jesting."
Then they drank together.
Yùlǎn 437.
The King of Qín offered five hundred lǐ of land in exchange for Yānlíng,
but the Lord of Yānlíng declined to accept it.
He sent Táng Jū to apologize to the King of Qín.
The king, enraged, changed countenance and angrily said:
"Have you ever witnessed the wrath of a Son of Heaven?"
Jū replied:
"Your subject has never seen it."
The king said:
"The wrath of a Son of Heaven
leaves a million corpses lying prostrate,
with blood flowing for a thousand lǐ."
Jū said:
"Has Your Majesty ever witnessed the wrath of a scholar in coarse cloth and leather girdle?"
The king said:
"The wrath of a scholar in coarse cloth and leather girdle
involves removing his cap and going barefoot,
dashing his head against the ground—
what is hard to know about that?"
Jū said:
"This is merely the wrath of a common man or ordinary person,
not that of a true scholar in coarse cloth and leather girdle.
When Zhuān Zhū assassinated King Liáo,
a comet swept across the sun,
and shooting stars appeared in daytime;
when Yāo Lí assassinated Prince Qìngjì,
a gray eagle struck the terrace;
when Niè Zhèng assassinated the King of Hán,
a white rainbow pierced the sun.
These three
were all instances of scholars' wrath,
and with your servant, they would make four.
When a scholar is not angered, all is well;
once angered,
two corpses will fall,
with bloodshed within five paces."
Thereupon he grasped his dagger;
rising, he looked at the King of Qín and said:
"It is about to happen now!"
The king's face changed color,
and he knelt, saying:
"Sir, please take your seat.
I understand now.
That Yānlíng alone remains with its fifty lǐ
is surely because of you, sir."
From "Imperial Readings" chapter 437.
Lín Jì, wearing leather garments, attended court of Duke Jǐng of Qí.
Duke Jǐng said:
"Is this the attire of a gentleman
or that of a petty man?"
Lín Jì, with a stern expression, said:
"How can clothing suffice to gauge a scholar's conduct?
In the past, Jīng wore long swords and tall hats,
yet Lord Chancellor Zǐ Xī emerged from there.
Duke Huán of Qí wore short clothes and a gutter-like hat,
yet Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng emerged from there.
Yuè tattooed their bodies and cut their hair short,
yet Fàn Lǐ and Minister Wén Zhǒng also emerged from there.
The Western Róng wore left-fastening clothes and coiled their hair in knots,
yet Yóu Yú also emerged from there.
If it were as you say,
then one wearing dog fur should bark like a dog,
and one wearing sheep fur should bleat.
Now you, my lord, wear fox fur to court—
should you not then change accordingly?"
Duke Jǐng said:
"Do you consider yourself brave and fierce?"
He replied:
"To look down from heights and over peril without blinking,
and without shifting one's feet—
this is the bravery of craftsmen.
To enter deep waters,
capture flood dragons,
and bring out giant turtles—
this is the bravery of fishermen.
To enter deep mountains,
stab tigers and leopards,
and carry out bears—
this is the bravery of hunters.
To not hesitate to have one's head severed and belly split,
with bones exposed and blood flowing in the wilderness—
this is the bravery of warriors.
Now I stand in the great court,
with a stern expression arguing,
risking the anger of my ruler—
though there may be rewards of carriages ahead,
I am not moved by them;
though there may be the threat of execution behind,
I am not frightened by it.
This is why I am considered brave and fierce."
From "Imperial Readings" chapter 437.
When King Wén buried desiccated bones,
it did not benefit the multitude,
yet the multitude was pleased—
such was the moving power of kindness and righteousness.
From "Imperial Readings" chapter 375.
Carrying Mount Tài under one's arm to leap over the North Sea.
From "Imperial Readings" chapter 39.
The walls of the feudal lords had the color of whitewash,
lacking the brilliance of vermilion and azure.
From "Imperial Readings" chapter 187.
To treat as lowly as vipers and pigs.
From commentary by Yáng Liàng on "Xúnzǐ: Wáng Bà Piān".
Yī Yǐn endured shame and disgrace,
carrying cauldrons and stands to seek out Tāng.
From commentary in "Hòu Hàn Shū: Cuī Yīn Zhuàn".
Yíng
means to measure.
Quoted in commentary on "Wén Xuǎn: Dōng Jīng Fù".
The King of Chǔ carried the Fán Ruò bow
and Wàng Guī arrows,
to hunt rhinoceroses in Yúnmèng.
Quoted in commentary on Jī Shūyè's "Poem Presented to a Scholar Joining the Army" in "Wén Xuǎn".
Gōngsūn Lóng said to Plain Lord:
"When I was in Lǔ, I heard from afar,
admiring your wisdom, sir,
and delighting in your conduct, sir."
Quoted in commentary on Zōu Yáng's "Letter to the King of Wú" in "Wén Xuǎn".
Confucius said:
"Though sages are born in different eras,
they follow each other as with compass and square."
Quoted in commentary on Sūn Zǐjīng's "Letter to Sūn Hào for Shí Zhòngróng" in "Wén Xuǎn".
Zhào Liáng said to Lord Shāng:
"Your demise can be expected by merely lifting a foot."
Quoted in commentary on Chén Kǒngzhāng's "Proclamation to Wú Officers and Troops" in "Wén Xuǎn".
Great King Dǎnfǔ settled at the foot of Qí Mountain,
and the common people, supporting the old and carrying the young, followed and returned to him.
In one year, a settlement formed;
in two years, a capital was established;
in three years, it was five times its initial size.
Quoted in commentary on Yú Lìngshēng's "General Discussion of the Jìn Annals" in "Wén Xuǎn".
By the time of King Dìng,
the royal house had declined.
Quoted in commentary on Lù Shìhéng's "Discourse on the Fall of Wú, Part 1" in "Wén Xuǎn".
When Zhōu, grandson of Duke Xiāng of Jìn, became ruler of Jìn,
he shared weal and woe without betraying his roots.
Quoted in commentary on Pān Ānrén's "Lament for Yáng Zhòngwǔ" in "Wén Xuǎn".
Zāngsūn implemented harsh governance,
and Zǐgòng criticized him for it.
Zāngsūn summoned Zǐgòng and asked:
"Am I not lawful?"
The reply was:
"You are lawful."
"Am I not incorruptible?"
The answer:
"You are incorruptible."
"Am I incapable of handling affairs?"
The response:
"You are capable."
Zāngsūn said:
"I feared I might fail in these three aspects,
yet now I excel in all.
Why then do you still criticize me?"
Zǐgòng said:
"You are lawful,
but you use it to harm others;
you are incorruptible,
but it makes you arrogant toward superiors;
you are capable in affairs,
but you employ it to oppress subordinates.
Governance is like tuning a zither—
if the thick strings are too tight, the thin ones will snap.
Thus, those in high positions must not have shallow virtue,
those with great authority must not govern narrowly,
those with vast territories must not rule restrictively,
and those governing many people must not enforce harsh laws,
for such is the natural order.
Hence it is said,
proper punishment stops wickedness,
and appropriate rewards bring joy to the people.
From this perspective,
your harmful intentions are already evident.
Have you not heard of Zǐchǎn's governance of Zhèng?
He assessed talent, promoted the worthy, and recommended the capable,
suppressing evil while exalting good.
For those with great strategies,
he overlooked their shortcomings;
for those with profound virtue,
he ignored minor flaws;
for those with significant achievements,
past wrongs were forgiven.
He helped others accomplish good,
not evil.
His way of shepherding the people
was to nurture them with benevolence,
educate them with ritual,
and motivate them with righteousness,
refining laws and teachings
to follow what the people delighted in.
Thus, he placed them according to their convenience,
gave them what they desired,
and encouraged them in their preferences.
When rewards were uncertain, he erred on the side of generosity;
when punishments were doubtful, he leaned toward leniency.
His penalties were careful,
his rewards clear,
his punishments minimal,
his virtue pure,
and his governance simple, yet education flourished.
After seven years governing Zhèng, customs became harmonious,
disasters did not occur,
the state had no criminals,
and prisons stood empty.
Upon his death,
the people heard of it,
all beating their chests and weeping,
saying:
'Zǐchǎn has died;
where shall we turn now?
If Zǐchǎn's life could be exchanged,
we would not spare even one from our families.'
In life, he was loved;
in death, he was mourned.
Officials wept in the court,
merchants in the market,
farmers in the fields,
maidens in their chambers,
gentlemen ceased playing music,
ministers removed their jade pendants,
women took off their hairpins and earrings,
all weeping in the streets.
This illustrates the way of benevolence and forgiveness.
The gentleman's governance
begins imperceptibly and ends beyond reach,
meaning just this.
For those with deep virtue, rewards are beautiful;
for those with great enmity, calamities are profound.
Hence it is said,
no virtue is greater than benevolence,
and no disaster greater than harshness.
Goodness cannot be sought through force,
nor evil eradicated through chaos.
Now, you are ill,
and the people rejoice, congratulating each other:
'Zāngsūnzǐ has fallen ill.'
They hope he will die.
When your illness slightly improves,
the people fearfully say to one another:
'Zāngsūnzǐ's illness has improved again;
how unfortunate our fate is.
Zāngsūnzǐ will not die after all.'
Your illness
brings people joy;
your survival
brings them terror.
Your harmful intentions run deep indeed.
Governing in such a manner,
how can I not criticize you?"
Then Zāngsūnzǐ felt ashamed,
withdrew, and relinquished his position.
From "Essentials of Governance from the Collected Books."
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ wished to dominate the world,
and said to his minister:
"In Zhào there is Dú Chōu,
in Jìn there is Duó Míng,
and in Lǔ there is Kǒng Qiū.
If I kill these three,
I can rule the world."
Thereupon, he summoned Dú Chōu and Duó Míng to discuss governance,
and then killed them.
He sent an envoy to invite Kǒngzǐ from Lǔ,
meeting him at the river with fattened beef.
The envoy told the boatman:
"Once Kǒngzǐ boards the boat,
mid-river, push him into the current to kill him."
When Kǒngzǐ arrived,
the envoy delivered his message,
presenting the fattened beef.
Kǒngzǐ looked up to heaven and sighed:
"How splendid is the water,
so vast and majestic!
That I do not cross this river must be fate!"
Zǐlù hurried forward and asked:
"What do you mean?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Dú Chōu and Duó Míng
were worthy ministers of Jìn.
When Zhào Jiǎnzǐ had not yet achieved his ambition,
he relied on them in governance;
once he succeeded, he killed them.
A yellow dragon does not return to a dried marsh,
a phoenix does not approach a trapping net.
Thus, if you cut open wombs and burn forests, the qílín will not come;
if you overturn nests and break eggs, the phoenix will not soar;
if you drain the pond to fish, the tortoise and dragon will not appear.
Even birds and beasts know to avoid the unkind—
how much more should I?
For when a tiger roars, the valley wind rises;
when a dragon ascends, bright clouds appear;
strike the courtyard bell, and the huángzhōng responds within.
Things of the same kind influence each other,
spirits and minds resonate—
like an echo answering a sound,
a shadow following a form.
Thus, the gentleman avoids harming his kind.
Now that he has killed my kind,
why should I go there?"
So he turned his carriage around,
returning without crossing the river.
From "Annotations to the Records of the Three Kingdoms, Liú Yì's Biography."
Zǐ Qí was sixteen years old.
The ruler of Qí sent him to govern Ā,
but soon regretted it,
dispatching a messenger to recall him.
The messenger returned and said:
"Zǐ Qí will surely govern Ā well,
for his companions are all white-haired elders.
With the wisdom of the old
and the decisiveness of the young,
he is certain to govern Ā effectively."
When Zǐ Qí arrived in Ā,
he melted weapons to make farming tools,
opened granaries to relieve the poor,
and Ā county became greatly well-governed.
Wèi, hearing that a youth governed the city,
with no weapons in the armory
and no grain in the granaries,
raised an army to attack.
The people of Ā, fathers leading sons,
elder brothers leading younger brothers,
fought with their private weapons
and defeated the army of Wèi.
From "Forest of Ideas."
Mèngzǐ met King Xuān of Qí at the Xuě Palace.
The king looked around and said:
"Do virtuous men also have such pleasures?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"Yes.
When people cannot obtain them,
they blame their superiors.
Those who cannot obtain them and blame their superiors
are wrong;
those who are above the people
yet do not share pleasures with them
are also wrong.
Those who take pleasure in what pleases the people,
the people will also take pleasure in their pleasures;
those who worry about what concerns the people,
the people will also worry about their worries.
Taking the world's pleasures as one's own,
taking the world's worries as one's own,
yet failing to become a true king -
such a thing has never happened."
From "Qún Shū Zhì Yào".
Zǐlù governed Pú for three years.
When Confucius passed through,
upon entering the territory he said:
"How excellent is Yóu!
He is reverent and trustworthy."
Entering the city,
he said:
"How excellent is Yóu!
He is loyal, trustworthy, and generous."
Reaching the court,
he said:
"How excellent is Yóu!
He is discerning and decisive."
Zǐgòng, holding the reins, asked:
"Master, you have praised Yóu three times without seeing him -
may I hear your reasoning?"
Confucius said:
"Entering his territory,
I saw fields all cultivated,
wastelands well cleared,
and irrigation ditches deeply dug -
this shows his reverence and trustworthiness,
hence his people work diligently.
Entering his city,
I saw walls and buildings well maintained,
and trees flourishing -
this shows his loyalty, trustworthiness and generosity,
hence his people are not negligent.
Entering his court,
I found it orderly and calm -
this shows his discernment and decisiveness,
hence his people are not disturbed."
From "Qún Shū Zhì Yào".
The writings of Shēnzǐ
say that rulers should master statecraft without relying solely on punishment,
following established ways to supervise and hold ministers accountable.
His accountability was severe,
hence called 'statecraft'.
What Shāng Yāng wrote
was called 'law',
both were termed 'punishment and name',
hence called writings on punishment, name, law and statecraft.
. From "Shǐjì Hán Fēi Zhuàn Jíjiě".
Duke Xiào of Qín secured the strong defenses of Xiáo and Hán,
expanding the territory of Yōngzhōu,
annexing Héxī to the east,
and capturing Shàngjùn to the north.
The state grew wealthy and army strong,
dominating other feudal lords.
The Zhōu court sent tribute,
all regions came to congratulate,
becoming a hegemon of the Warring States.
Qín thus grew powerful,
and after six generations united all feudal lords -
all due to Lord Shāng's strategies.
Lord Shāng exerted himself single-mindedly,
completely public-spirited without personal considerations,
making people focus on farming and weaving internally to enrich the state,
emphasizing military rewards externally to encourage warriors.
Laws and decrees were strictly enforced,
internally not favoring the noble and privileged,
externally not partial to strangers.
Thus orders were followed and prohibitions observed,
laws issued and wickedness ceased.
Though the Shū says "no bias, no factions",
the Shī says "the Zhōu way is like a whetstone,
straight as an arrow",
the Sīmǎ Fǎ encourages warriors,
and Zhōu's Hòujì promotes agriculture -
none surpass this,
this is how they united the feudal lords.
Hence Xúnzǐ said:
"Four generations of victory
is not luck,
but inevitability."
Yet being untrustworthy,
feudal lords feared but did not befriend him.
Hegemonic rulers like Duke Huán of Qí and Duke Wén of Jìn -
Huán did not break the Kē alliance,
Wén did not violate the Yuán agreement -
so feudal lords feared their strength yet trusted them.
They preserved the perishing and continued the severed,
all regions submitted to them -
this was Guǎn Zhòng and Jiù Fàn's strategy.
But Lord Shāng betrayed former kindness to Prince Áng,
abandoned clear faith with Wèi,
deceitfully captured three armies,
so feudal lords feared his strength but distrusted him.
Had Duke Xiào encountered Duke Huán or Duke Wén,
gained command of feudal lords' forces,
united feudal lords' rulers,
and led the world's troops against Qín,
Qín would have perished.
The world lacked rulers like Huán and Wén,
so Qín could annex the feudal lords.
Wèi Yāng initially thought he understood hegemonic virtue,
but examining his deeds proves otherwise.
When Zhōu and Shào implemented good governance,
after their death,
later generations remembered them -
the "Lush Sweet Pear" poem shows this.
They once rested under trees,
later generations recalling their virtue couldn't bear to cut those trees -
how much less harm their persons!
Guǎn Zhòng took three hundred households from Bó's fief,
yet there were no complaints.
But Wèi Yāng internally imposed harsh saw-blade punishments,
externally severe axe executions,
fining those stepping over six chǐ,
executing those dumping ash on roads.
Once sentencing over seven hundred prisoners by the Wèi River,
the river turned completely red,
cries shaking heaven and earth,
accumulated hatred like mountains.
None could hide from him,
none find refuge with him.
He died torn by chariots,
exterminated with his clan -
far from a hegemonic assistant.
Yet King Huì killing him was also wrong -
he could have been guided and used.
Had Wèi Yāng implemented lenient laws,
added kindness,
and emphasized trustworthiness,
he might have approximated a hegemonic assistant!
. From "Shǐjì Shāng Jūn Zhuàn Jíjiě".
While Sī was being exiled,
he submitted a memorial to the First Emperor on the road,
who sent someone to intercept him at Líyì,
whereupon he returned.
. From "Shǐjì Lǐ Sī Zhuàn Jíjiě".
Confucius said to Zēngzǐ:
"When gentlemen don't harm righteousness for profit,
how can shame and disgrace arise?
Officials slacken after achieving office,
illness worsens after slight recovery,
disaster comes from laziness,
filial piety declines after marrying -
recognizing these four,
be as cautious at the end as the start."
From Xuē Jù's "Kǒngzǐ Jíyǔ".
Duke Huán of Qí favored women's charms,
marrying his aunts and sisters,
so many in the state committed incest.
From Mǎ Sù's "Yì Shǐ" 44.2.
Farming had no abandoned fields,
countryside no empty land.
Cited in "Běi Táng Shū Chāo" vol. 39.
Earl of Liáng indulged in drink,
wallowed in lust,
mind confused and ears blocked,
liked building great cities but not living there,
exhausting the people severely.
Cited in "Imperial Reader" 192.
Duke Xiāng of Shàn said:
"Warped by heaven,
woofed by earth,
warp and woof never err -
this is heaven's pattern."
. Cited in "Wén Xuǎn: Ode to Wèi Capital" commentary.
